entries.x: Learning Objective Explain the epidemiology of osteoporosis, including the treatment care gap. The assessment and treatment sections below go beyond that single objective, following the structure of the lecture notes. See the source line at the bottom for which parts came from the slides and which from the Canadian guideline.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Definition: Three Doors In Osteoporosis is not one number. Any one of these establishes the diagnosis: Route Criterion The catch Clinical Presence of a fragility fracture Excludes fractures of the skull, hands, feet and ankles, and any fracture with significant trauma. A hip fracture from a standing-height fall counts; a skull fracture does not. Densitometric BMD T-score < −2.5 A number, not a symptom — and most people who fracture are not below this line. Risk-based > 20% 10-year fracture risk Applies in the absence of both a fragility fracture and a T-score < −2.5 — the third door for people the first two miss. Why Three Definitions Rather Than One Each catches a different failure of the others. A T-score alone misses the majority of people who actually fracture, because bone quality and fall risk are not measured by densitometry. A fracture alone is a diagnosis made too late. The risk-based door exists to identify the person who has not yet fractured and whose density is not yet dire, but whose combined risk factors already put them where treatment helps.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Epidemiology: Bigger Than You Think Annual incidence in Canadian women — osteoporotic fractures against the diseases that get far more attention: Osteoporotic fractures outnumber heart attacks and breast cancer combined, by a wide margin. Stroke, also shown on the original slide, sits between the two right-hand bars. Canadian hip-fracture data from Leslie et al., Osteoporos Int 2010; non-hip extrapolated from Burge et al., J Bone Miner Res 2007; CIHI 2009; Canadian Cancer Society 2009.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: The Treatment Gap Here is the comparison the whole lecture is built around: A fracture is to osteoporosis what a heart attack is to cardiovascular disease — a sentinel event that should trigger secondary prevention. One of these is treated like that; the other is not. Bessette et al., Osteoporos Int 2008; Austin et al., CMAJ 2008. The gap has been widening . Treatment rates were higher a decade ago; as bisphosphonates fell out of favour — driven largely by fear of the rare harms covered below — prescribing declined without the risk of fracture declining with it. What undertreatment costs Outcome Figure Lifetime risk of hip fracture, age > 50 12.1% 1 year after hip fracture — unable to carry out more than one IADL 80% 1 year after hip fracture — unable to walk independently 40% 1 year after hip fracture — death 29% 5-year mortality after hip fracture 23.5% 5-year mortality after vertebral fracture 15.7% Note the 1-year and 5-year hip figures are not a contradiction — they come from different cohorts and different eras. The point they share is that hip fracture mortality is measured in tens of percent, not fractions of one.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Clinical Presentation It is a silent disease. Most patients have no symptoms until they fracture — which is exactly why case-finding depends on risk factors and densitometry rather than on how the patient feels. Vertebral fractures are graded by the loss of vertebral body height. Moderate and severe grades are the ones that feed prediction models — and many are found incidentally, never having caused a recognised episode of back pain. Accumulated vertebral fractures produce the kyphotic spine — the visible end-stage of a disease that was silent throughout. Physical signs worth looking for Sign Threshold Prospective height loss (measured over time) > 2 cm Historical height loss (versus recalled peak height) > 6 cm Rib-to-pelvis distance < 2 finger-breadths Occiput-to-wall distance > 5 cm All four are surrogates for the same thing — vertebral height that has already been lost. Falls risk assessment belongs in the same examination.

entries.t: Assessment: T-Score, Z-Score and Who to Scan
entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Assessment: T-Score, Z-Score and Who to Scan T vs Z — Different Comparators, Different Jobs T-score compares the patient's bone density to a healthy young adult at peak bone mass. That is the comparison the diagnostic threshold of −2.5 is built on, because the question it answers is "how much bone have you lost from your best?" Z-score compares them to people of their own age and sex . Losing bone with age is expected, so a normal Z-score is unremarkable — but a markedly low Z-score means the patient is losing bone faster than their peers, which points at a secondary cause rather than ordinary ageing. That is the score that should prompt you to go looking. Who gets a BMD scan Age Indication ≥ 70 Screen — no risk factors required 65–69 With 1 risk factor 50–64 With a prior fracture or ≥ 2 risk factors The risk factors: previous fragility fracture after age 40 · glucocorticoids (> 3 months in the last year at prednisone > 5 mg/day) · ≥ 2 falls in the last year · parent who fractured a hip · BMI < 20 kg/m 2 · a condition causing secondary osteoporosis · current smoking · alcohol ≥ 3 drinks/day . Blood work A short, targeted panel — aimed at excluding secondary causes and at making sure the treatment you are about to give is safe: Test Why Calcium, corrected for albumin Screens for hyperparathyroidism and malignancy — and hypocalcemia must be corrected before starting an antiresorptive. See corrected calcium . CBC Anemia or cytopenias point toward myeloma and other marrow disease Creatinine Renal function constrains drug choice — bisphosphonates are contraindicated at low clearance Alkaline phosphatase Raised in Paget's disease, osteomalacia, and bone metastases TSH Thyrotoxicosis causes bone loss — see subclinical hyperthyroidism , which is explicitly associated with it 25-OH vitamin D Deficiency must be corrected alongside any pharmacotherapy Fracture risk tools FRAX CAROC Status Preferred in the 2023 Canadian guideline Acceptable alternative Inputs More clinical risk factors, including glucocorticoids, smoking, alcohol, rheumatoid arthritis, parental hip fracture; BMD optional but better with it Age, sex, femoral neck T-score, with adjustment for fragility fracture and glucocorticoid use Output 10-year probability of major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture 10-year risk category — low, moderate, high Trade-off More granular, captures more of the risk that BMD alone misses Simpler, faster, fewer inputs Either way, the number that matters downstream is

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Treatment 1: Lifestyle Comes First This applies to everyone, treated or not. Recommendation Exercise Balance, functional training and progressive resistance training, more than twice weekly — to reduce falls and maintain physical function and bone strength. Weight-bearing is the operative principle. Falls prevention A formal falls-risk assessment. Most fractures require a fall; removing the fall removes the fracture. Calcium Meet the RDA from food where possible — women > 50 and men > 70: 1200 mg/day ; men 50–70: 1000 mg/day . If dietary intake is adequate, supplementation is not recommended to prevent fractures. Vitamin D RDA 600 IU/day (51–70) and 800 IU/day (> 70). Because that is hard to reach from diet, a minimum 400 IU daily supplement is suggested alongside vitamin D-rich foods. The Nuance People Get Wrong Calcium and vitamin D are not a treatment for osteoporosis — they are the nutritional floor that the actual drugs are built on. Supplementing calcium in someone already meeting the RDA through diet does not prevent fractures, and the trials that established every drug below gave their participants a minimum of roughly 400 IU of vitamin D and up to 1000 mg of calcium. That is the context in which those drugs work, not a substitute for them.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Treatment 2: Choosing a Drug The drug classes, mechanisms and adverse-effect profiles are covered in detail in Drugs Affecting Vitamin D & Calcium Homeostasis . What matters here is the sequence : Pharmacotherapy pathway, 2023 Osteoporosis Canada guideline. A bisphosphonate is the default; the two side branches are the specific situations that override it. Note that anabolic therapy is never the endpoint — it must be followed by an antiresorptive. The classes, in one line each Class Agents Role Antiresorptive stop bone being broken down Bisphosphonates — alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid First line for almost everyone Denosumab (RANKL antibody) When bisphosphonates can't be used — but commits the patient to uninterrupted therapy Raloxifene (SERM) Second line; vertebral fracture reduction Hormone therapy Menopausal symptom control with a bone benefit, rather than a primary osteoporosis drug Anabolic build new bone Teriparatide , romosozumab First for severe or multiple vertebral fractures — then hand off to an antiresorptive

entries.t: The Two Harms That Created the Gap
entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: The Two Harms That Created the Gap These are the adverse effects that made prescribing fall — worth knowing precisely, because the fear of them is out of proportion to their frequency. Osteonecrosis of the jaw Atypical femoral fracture Caused by Bisphosphonates and denosumab Bisphosphonates and denosumab Where Jaw — typically after dental extraction or with poor dental health Subtrochanteric — below the lesser trochanter, in the femoral shaft Warning sign Exposed bone, non-healing dental socket New thigh or groin pain, often prodromal and often bilateral Frequency Rare — and the reason the drug holiday exists, since risk rises with cumulative duration Keeping the Risk in Proportion Both harms are real, both are rare, and both scale with how long treatment continues — which is precisely why the guideline builds in a defined treatment period and a drug holiday rather than treating indefinitely. Set against them: a 29% one-year mortality after hip fracture, and a 12.1% lifetime hip fracture risk over the age of 50. The treatment gap exists because the rare, nameable, drug-attributable harm feels more salient than the common, diffuse, disease-attributable one. Recognising that asymmetry is the actual clinical skill this lecture is teaching.

Learning Objectives Describe the clinical presentation of primary hyperparathyroidism and primary hypoparathyroidism. Explain the differential diagnosis of hypercalcemia and the etiologies of hyperparathyroidism. Explain the differential diagnosis of hypocalcemia and the etiologies of hypoparathyroidism. Describe the acute and chronic treatment of hypercalcemia and hypocalcemia, accounting for the underlying etiology.

Calcium Homeostasis: The Numbers The full loop — parathyroid, bone, kidney, gut and vitamin D — is covered in Drugs Affecting Vitamin D & Calcium Homeostasis : falling plasma Ca ++ triggers PTH, which pulls calcium from bone, reclaims it in the kidney, and (via vitamin D, made from sunlight or diet ) absorbs more from the gut; rising calcium then shuts PTH off. What that lecture skips is the numbers. Serum calcium exists in three forms, and only one of them is biologically active: Composition of total serum calcium. Only the ionized fraction is free and biologically active; the rest is bound to albumin or complexed to anions. This is why a total-calcium result misleads when albumin is abnormal — the bound fraction moves with the albumin while the active fraction may not have changed at all.

Corrected Calcium A lab reports total calcium — ionized plus protein-bound plus complexed. Since roughly 40% rides on albumin, a low albumin drags the total down while the active ionized fraction is unchanged; a high albumin does the reverse. Correcting avoids calling a hypoalbuminemic patient hypocalcemic, or missing real hypercalcemia. The Formula Corrected Ca (mmol/L) = Measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − Albumin [g/L]) A change in albumin of 1 g/L shifts measured calcium by 0.02 mmol/L, in the opposite direction — so the formula adds back what albumin took away (or subtracts what it artificially added). Worked example: Measured Ca 2.6 mmol/L, albumin 20 g/L. Corrected Ca = 2.6 + 0.02 × (40 − 20) = 2.6 + 0.4 = 3.0 mmol/L — a value that looked borderline is actually significant hypercalcemia once the low albumin is accounted for. When the true value matters and albumin is markedly abnormal, an ionized calcium measured directly is more reliable than any correction formula.

Hypercalcemia: Definition & Presentation Hypercalcemia = corrected total calcium > 2.55 mmol/L (or an elevated ionized calcium). Symptoms depend on both the absolute value and the rate of rise — a slowly-developed hypercalcemia can be markedly elevated and still nearly asymptomatic, while a rapid rise to a similar level can be florid. Mild hypercalcemia is commonly asymptomatic and picked up incidentally. The classic mnemonic is "stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones" — each with a mechanism worth knowing, not just memorizing: System Findings Why Renal ("stones") Nephrolithiasis, polyuria (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), acute/chronic renal insufficiency Excess filtered calcium supersaturates urine with calcium salts; calcium also activates the calcium-sensing receptor A G-protein-coupled receptor that lets tissues directly sense extracellular calcium — expressed in the parathyroid and, importantly, along the kidney tubule in the collecting duct and thick ascending limb, which blunts the response to ADH and impairs the countercurrent gradient — the kidney literally can't concentrate urine as well. Skeletal ("bones") Bone pain/tenderness, cystic bone lesions, skeletal demineralization, spontaneous fractures Direct consequence of the resorption driving the hypercalcemia in the first place — PTH or PTH-like signaling pulling calcium out of bone faster than it's replaced. GI ("groans") Abdominal pain, pancreatitis (acute/chronic), constipation, vomiting, anorexia Calcium reduces smooth muscle excitability (constipation); high intraductal/intracellular calcium can trigger premature intra-pancreatic trypsinogen activation, precipitating pancreatitis. Cardiovascular Short QT interval, arrhythmias, hypertension Extracellular calcium speeds the plateau (phase 2) of the cardiac action potential — shortens the ST segment specifically, which shortens the QT. Neuro/psychiatric ("psychiatric overtones") Confusion, personality change, depression, apathy High extracellular calcium raises the threshold for neuronal depolarization, generally reducing excitability — the opposite direction from hypocalcemia's tetany.

Etiology: PTH-Mediated vs. PTH-Independent The cleanest way to organize the differential is by whether PTH is driving it — and a single PTH level splits the whole list in two: PTH splits the differential in two; together, primary hyperPTH and malignancy cover >90% of cases. PTH-mediated PTH-independent Primary hyperparathyroidism Hypercalcemia of malignancy Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (chronic renal failure) Vitamin D intoxication / chronic granulomatous disease Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) Medications; hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, pheochromocytoma, adrenal insufficiency, immobilization, parenteral nutrition, milk-alkali syndrome Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for >90% of cases. Malignant hypercalcemia works two ways: bony metastases releasing calcium locally (e.g. breast), or a humoral factor secreted systemically — PTHrP (lung, kidney, adult T-cell leukemia; acts on the PTH receptor), lymphokines (myeloma), prostaglandins, or vitamin D-like steroids (lymphoma). Minor causes (<10%): exogenous vitamin D; granulomatous disease (sarcoid, TB — activated macrophages make their own 1α-hydroxylase, producing calcitriol outside PTH control); immobilization with high bone turnover (Paget's, thyrotoxicosis); FHH (inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation); milk-alkali syndrome; and thiazides (reduced renal calcium excretion, usually transient). Within primary hyperparathyroidism specifically: parathyroid adenoma (80%) , parathyroid hyperplasia, parathyroid carcinoma (rare), and familial syndromes (familial isolated hyperparathyroidism, hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome, MEN syndromes).

entries.t: Telling Primary HyperPTH and FHH Apart
entries.x: Telling Primary HyperPTH and FHH Apart Case — 65F, Osteoporosis Work-Up Back pain, radius/ulna fracture at 52, ulna fracture at 61, hysterectomy at 35. Thyroid and renal function normal. Initial Ca 2.95 mmol/L, albumin 45 g/L. Repeat Ca 2.73 mmol/L, phosphate 0.69 mmol/L, PTH 14 pmol/L (ref. 1.6–6.9), 25-OH vitamin D 70 nmol/L. Correcting for her high-normal albumin: 2.73 + 0.02 × (40 − 45) = 2.63 mmol/L — still hypercalcemic, and a reminder the correction runs both directions. Elevated PTH, low-normal phosphate (PTH wastes phosphate), sufficient vitamin D: textbook primary hyperparathyroidism . Both primary hyperPTH and FHH present with hypercalcemia and a PTH that's elevated or inappropriately normal — the fractional excretion of calcium (FeCa), from a 24-hour urine collection, is what separates them: Fractional Excretion of Calcium FeCa = (Urine Ca × Serum Cr / 1000) / (Serum Ca × Urine Cr) — from a 24-hour urine collection. It answers one question: given how high the calcium is, is the kidney letting a normal amount spill into urine, or is it hanging onto calcium it shouldn't? In FHH the mutated receptor needs a higher calcium before it registers as high, so the kidney keeps reabsorbing as though calcium were normal and little reaches the urine. In primary hyperparathyroidism the sensing is intact, so more calcium escapes despite PTH's reabsorptive pull. Distinguishing FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism by renal calcium handling. Both present with hypercalcemia and a PTH that is elevated or inappropriately normal, so the calcium and PTH values alone cannot separate them. a About 20% of FHH cases fall in the 0.01–0.02 overlap zone. Interpret only once the patient has been off thiazide diuretics for 3 months, with a normal magnesium and 25-OH vitamin D > 50 nmol/L — each of these independently lowers urinary calcium and mimics the FHH pattern.

Treatment of Acute Hypercalcemia Inpatient admission is generally required if corrected Ca > 3 mmol/L. 1 Volume repletion — normal saline, 4–6 L deficit. Hypercalcemia itself causes volume depletion (the nephrogenic-DI-like polyuria above), which further impairs renal calcium clearance — rehydrating alone starts to help. 2 Forced diuresis — 4–10 L NS plus furosemide plus K⁺, only once well hydrated. Loop diuretics block the Na-K-2Cl transporter in the thick ascending limb, which (among other things) disrupts the lumen-positive gradient that normally drives passive calcium reabsorption there — more calcium is forced into urine. Never given before volume is repleted, or it just worsens the depletion. 3 IV bisphosphonate (zoledronate). Shuts down osteoclast-mediated bone resorption — the definitive fix for most causes, but takes 2–4 days to take full effect. 4 Calcitonin. Works within hours (inhibits osteoclasts and increases renal calcium excretion directly) but tachyphylaxis sets in within 48 hours — useful as a bridge while the slower bisphosphonate takes effect, not as monotherapy. 5 Prednisone 40–60 mg/day, then taper — for myeloma or vitamin D intoxication specifically. Glucocorticoids suppress the extra-renal 1α-hydroxylase activity that granulomatous tissue and some lymphomas use to overproduce calcitriol, and have direct cytotoxic/anti-cytokine effects in myeloma — this is a cause-specific step, not a general one.

Treatment of Primary Hyperparathyroidism Presentation Approach Mild, asymptomatic, age > 50 No treatment (monitor) or medical therapy — bisphosphonates, denosumab, estrogen, or cinacalcet (a calcimimetic that increases the CaSR's sensitivity to calcium, directly opposing the FHH mechanism above) Symptomatic, or meets a surgical indication below Parathyroidectomy General measures regardless of severity: adequate hydration, and avoid thiazides and lithium — both raise calcium further (thiazides reduce renal excretion as above; lithium alters the calcium-sensing receptor's set-point similarly to FHH, raising PTH). Indications for surgery: serum calcium > 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal · BMD T-score < −2.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip, or 1/3 radius · vertebral fracture · creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min · 24-hour urine calcium > 10 mmol/day with increased stone risk · nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis present · age < 50.

Hypocalcemia: Etiology by Lab Pattern Hypocalcemia results from failure to secrete PTH, failure to respond to PTH, vitamin D deficiency, failure to respond to vitamin D, or (rarely) acute complexation of calcium. In practice, phosphate is what splits these into recognizable buckets, because PTH and vitamin D pull phosphate in opposite directions: Phosphate splits PTH-axis problems from vitamin D problems; PTH then splits deficiency from resistance. Why Phosphate Splits This Way PTH wastes phosphate at the kidney (inhibiting proximal tubule reabsorption). Remove PTH (hypoparathyroidism) or make the kidney deaf to it (pseudohypoparathyroidism) and phosphate reabsorption goes unchecked — it climbs as calcium falls. Vitamin D deficiency is the mirror image: calcitriol absorbs both , so both fall, and the compensatory secondary PTH rise wastes what phosphate is left. Same low calcium, opposite phosphate. Vitamin D deficiency is more common than either PTH disorder — causes include malabsorption (it's fat-soluble), renal or liver failure (both metabolic steps live there — see the vitamin D lecture ), certain drugs (phenytoin accelerates hepatic vitamin D catabolism), rare dietary deficiency, and inadequate sun exposure (classically causing rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). Minor/other causes: hypoalbuminemia (falsely low total calcium — see corrected calcium above), hypomagnesemia (alcohol use, malabsorption), pancreatitis (calcium is saponified by fatty acids released from peripancreatic fat necrosis), tumor lysis/rhabdomyolysis/sepsis, and massive transfusion (citrate anticoagulant in banked blood chelates calcium).

Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1a is true PTH resistance — the kidney has normal or high PTH but doesn't respond, so calcium stays low and phosphate stays high, just like hypoparathyroidism, except PTH itself is elevated (appropriately trying to compensate, unsuccessfully). It carries a recognizable phenotype called Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy : round facies, short stature, and short 4th/5th metacarpal and metatarsal bones. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism has the identical Albright's phenotype but no PTH insensitivity — calcium and phosphate are normal. The two are genetically related, and the distinction comes down to a single, high-yield genetics concept: Why the Same Mutation Gives Two Different Diseases Both come from an inactivating GNAS mutation — the gene encoding G s α, the protein PTH's receptor signals through. GNAS is genomically imprinted Only one parent's copy of certain genes is active in certain tissues — the other is epigenetically silenced, whether or not it is mutated in the renal tubule: only the maternal copy works there. Maternal mutation → the kidney's only working copy is gone → PTH resistance → PHP 1a . Paternal mutation → the kidney is unaffected → normal calcium, but the Albright's phenotype still appears in non-imprinted tissues → pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism . Because G s α is shared machinery, PHP 1a often shows resistance to TSH and gonadotropins too.

Diagnosing Primary Hypoparathyroidism Diagnosis: persistent hypocalcemia with a low or inappropriately-normal PTH (it should be climbing in response to low calcium — a "normal" PTH here is actually a failure to respond appropriately). After neck surgery, hypocalcemia must persist 6 months before it's labeled permanent hypoparathyroidism — many cases from parathyroid gland stunning/devascularization recover within that window. Cause Share Post-surgical (thyroid/parathyroid/neck surgery) ~75% — the leading cause overall Non-surgical: autoimmune, infiltrative, post-radiation, functional (magnesium insufficiency or excess), metastatic, genetic ~25% combined

Symptoms of Hypocalcemia Low ionized calcium lowers the threshold for neuronal and muscle membrane depolarization — the opposite direction from hypercalcemia — which is why the clinical picture is one of hyperexcitability rather than lethargy. Timing Findings Acute, severe Tetany — perioral paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, laryngeal spasm, seizures, palpitations Acute, mild Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs (below) Chronic Emotional instability, anxiety, "brain fog," paresthesias, cataracts, dry skin, brittle nails Overtreatment Movement disorders, nephrolithiasis (from iatrogenic hypercalciuria) Two bedside signs worth knowing precisely, since they're easy to blur together: Chvostek's sign: tap the facial nerve just anterior to the ear, over the parotid gland. A positive test twitches the ipsilateral corner of the mouth (or more of the face). Sensitive but not very specific — present in a meaningful minority of normocalcemic people too. Trousseau's sign: inflate a BP cuff on the upper arm above systolic pressure and hold for ~3 minutes. Ischemia unmasks neuromuscular hyperexcitability in a hypocalcemic patient, producing carpal spasm — wrist and MCP joints flexed, fingers extended, thumb drawn into the palm (the classic "obstetrician's hand"). More specific for hypocalcemia than Chvostek's.

Treatment of Hypocalcemia Acute treatment is reserved for corrected Ca < 1.9 mmol/L with neurological symptoms (tetany, seizures, carpopedal spasm) or cardiac symptoms (prolonged QT — the mirror image of hypercalcemia's short QT, same phase-2 mechanism running in reverse). Acute Treatment Calcium gluconate : 1–2 g of 10% solution in 50 mL of 5% dextrose IV over 15–20 minutes, then 1–3 mg/kg/hr elemental calcium. Cardiac monitoring, inpatient. Gluconate rather than chloride peripherally: chloride is far more concentrated and causes tissue necrosis if it extravasates, so it is reserved for central access. Always check and correct magnesium first (or alongside). Magnesium is required for PTH to be released from the parathyroid and for PTH's receptor to signal properly at target tissue — hypocalcemia driven or worsened by hypomagnesemia will not correct with calcium alone until magnesium is repleted. Chronic Treatment Details Active vitamin D Calcitriol 0.25 mcg twice daily — monitor calcium and phosphate; target 25-OH-D > 75 nmol/L Calcium supplements 1–2 g elemental calcium daily, in divided doses Thiazide diuretics Reduce renal calcium excretion, lowering nephrolithiasis risk on replacement therapy Recombinant human PTH (rhPTH) Approved for hypoparathyroidism in the US and Europe Why Aim Low-Normal, Not Fully Normal Without PTH's phosphate-wasting, replacing calcium and active vitamin D drives both up together — and past a threshold calcium phosphate precipitates into soft tissue. Hence every part of the monitoring: keep calcium low-normal rather than fully normal, watch the calcium×phosphate product (< 4.4 mmol 2 /L 2 ), and screen directly — renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis, head MRI for basal ganglia calcification.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Framing & Relevance Thyroid disease presents as a structural problem (benign or malignant, functional or non-functional) or a functional one (hyper- or hypothyroid) — the same fork used for any gland in the approach to endocrine disease . This lecture is the functional half. Definition Prevalence Women : Men Hypothyroidism Too little thyroid hormone Up to 2% (subclinical up to 10%) 5–8 : 1 Thyrotoxicosis Too much thyroid hormone, from any source — — Hyperthyroidism Thyrotoxicosis specifically from thyroid hormone production Up to 1.5% 5 : 1 The thyrotoxicosis/hyperthyroidism distinction isn't pedantry — a thyroiditis patient is thyrotoxic but not hyperthyroid, and giving them an antithyroid drug treats a production problem they don't have.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Thyroid Function Tests TSH is the case-finding test. Order it when history, examination, an associated condition or high-risk status raises suspicion; if it is normal, you can generally stop. If it is abnormal, the free hormones tell you what kind of abnormality it is. Pattern TSH FT4 / FT3 Interpretation Normal ↔ ↔ Euthyroid Thyrotoxicosis ↓ ↑ Overt — confirm with repeat TSH plus FT4 and FT3 Subclinical hyperthyroidism ↓ ↔ Same causes as overt; see below Primary hypothyroidism ↑ ↓ The gland has failed Subclinical hypothyroidism ↑ ↔ Usually TSH < 10–20; see below Central hypothyroidism ↔ or ↓ ↓ Pituitary/hypothalamic — TSH alone will miss it Central hyperthyroidism ↔ or ↑ ↑ Rare (e.g. TSH-secreting adenoma) The Trap in the Central Patterns In both central patterns the TSH is normal or moves in the "wrong" direction, because the problem is the pituitary that produces TSH rather than the gland responding to it. A patient with a known pituitary mass or other pituitary hormone deficiencies who develops fatigue, constipation and cold intolerance therefore needs TSH and FT4 — ordering TSH alone can return a reassuring number in a genuinely hypothyroid patient. The TSH-first pathway and its four common outcomes are also drawn as an algorithm in Thyroid & Parathyroid Physiology .

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: The Diagnostic Pathway The same skeleton applies to both halves of this lecture, and the first step is not a test: 1 Is the patient stable? ABCs. Vital signs first. Thyroid disease rarely presents urgently, but when it does it is immediately dangerous — see the urgent presentations below. 2 History — symptoms, severity, risk factors. Use the clues. Severity and acuity narrow the differential as much as the symptoms themselves. 3 Physical exam — signs, severity, complications. Focused first, general if the picture is unclear. 4 Investigations, limited by what the history and exam actually found. Laboratory medicine, then imaging only where it changes management. Choosing Wisely framing worth carrying: order the least invasive test first, and only order a test that will change management — not for the learning experience, and not in anticipation of what a preceptor might want.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Thyrotoxicosis: Presentation Urgent presentations (uncommon, but do not miss): thyroid storm / haemodynamic instability, high-output heart failure, visual loss from Graves' orbitopathy, and mental-health crisis exacerbated by thyrotoxicosis. Symptoms Signs Heat intolerance · increased sweating · tremor · palpitations · hyperactivity · insomnia · emotional lability and anxiety · weight loss despite increased appetite · hyperdefecation · heart failure (edema, orthopnea, PND) Eye signs · tremor · soft, warm skin · tachycardia · increased cardiac output · heart failure Confirmation: case-find with TSH (low suggests thyrotoxicosis), then confirm with a repeat low TSH plus elevated FT4 and FT3. Many labs add the free hormones reflexively when TSH is low.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Thyrotoxicosis: Mechanism Decides Everything There are only three ways to become thyrotoxic — the gland makes too much, a damaged gland leaks what it already made, or the hormone comes from outside the body. Radioiodine uptake separates them, and the split drives the entire treatment plan: Thyrotoxicosis by mechanism. The uptake result does more than name the cause — it decides whether you suppress the gland or simply support the patient. An antithyroid drug given for thyroiditis treats production that isn't happening.

entries.t: Narrowing It Down: Clues in History & Exam
entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Narrowing It Down: Clues in History & Exam Graves' disease Toxic adenoma / MNG Thyroiditis Risk factors Female, age ~30–50, family history of autoimmune disease (esp. thyroid), iodine load Iodine deficiency → subsequent sufficiency or iodine load Recent URTI (subacute); post-partum / autoimmune Onset Acute or subacute Gradually progressive Follows the trigger Severity Often marked Mildly thyrotoxic Thyrotoxic, usually self-limiting Goiter Symmetric Asymmetric , neck mass(es) Asymmetric, symmetric or none Distinguishing Orbitopathy, dermopathy — Tenderness, odynophagia (subacute) Eye signs: which are Graves', which are just thyrotoxicosis This distinction is commonly tested and easy to blur: Any thyrotoxicosis (adrenergic, from any cause): stare (decreased blink), lid retraction , lid lag . Graves' specifically (true orbitopathy): proptosis , periorbital edema, inflammation, diplopia , and visual loss — an ocular emergency . Also Graves'-specific: dermopathy (pretibial myxedema, peau d'orange ) and thyroid acropachy (clubbing). Graves' orbitopathy is caused by increased volume of the retro-orbital connective tissue and extraocular muscles — inflammation, edema, glycosaminoglycan accumulation and increased adipocytes. The major modifiable risk factor is smoking. When to reach for a test Test Value Cost / caveats Clinical assessment (pre-test probability of Graves') Demographics, family history of autoimmunity, acuity, severity, symmetric goiter, orbitopathy ± dermopathy — often enough on its own Free TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb) Sensitive and specific for Graves'; a simple blood test Not covered by OHIP Radioiodine uptake & scan Best single test to determine the etiology of thyrotoxicosis — distinguishes Graves' (diffuse), toxic MNG/adenoma (focal) and thyroiditis (low uptake) Relatively expensive, 2-day test, contraindicated in pregnancy In practice: if the clinical picture is classic Graves' (symmetric goiter, orbitopathy, family history), you may not need either test. When the picture is not classic — an asymmetric gland, no eye signs, no family history — the uptake scan is what tells you which mechanism you're dealing with.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Subclinical Hyperthyroidism Low TSH with normal FT4 and FT3; same causes as overt disease. Rarely an artefact — assay interference can give an inaccurate TSH, so check for interfering substances and repeat TSH with free hormones. Not benign: associated with bone loss and atrial fibrillation . Treat if older and/or TSH is clearly suppressed. Monitor if younger and/or TSH is only borderline low.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Treating Thyrotoxicosis Supportive treatment is considered for everyone; whether you additionally suppress the gland depends entirely on the mechanism established above. Supportive Indication Beta blockers Palpitations, tachycardia, tremor NSAIDs Pain of subacute thyroiditis — first line Glucocorticoids Thyroiditis pain not controlled by NSAIDs Reducing hormone production Antithyroid drugs Radioactive iodine Surgery First line for Graves' — because remission is possible Toxic adenoma or TMNG ; also Graves' if no remission on drugs Rarely used Agent / extent Methimazole favoured over PTU — Total for Graves' and toxic MNG; hemithyroidectomy for a single adenoma Time to work ~4–6 weeks to euthyroidism ~6–12 weeks; ~10% need a second treatment Immediate Main drawbacks Rare but serious: agranulocytosis , liver dysfunction, drug-induced SLE; birth defects High rate of permanent hypothyroidism (it is a permanent cure); may worsen Graves' eye disease, especially in smokers; cannot be used in pregnancy Reserved for large symptomatic goiter, suspected coincident malignancy, intolerance of antithyroid drugs in pregnancy, or storm refractory to medical therapy Before You Start an Antithyroid Drug Because the serious adverse effects are haematological, hepatic and teratogenic, get a baseline CBC and liver enzymes , and a pregnancy test in anyone who could be pregnant — both to interpret later abnormalities against a baseline and because pregnancy changes the drug choice. In pregnancy the agents swap by trimester: PTU in the first trimester , because methimazole in early pregnancy is associated with a characteristic embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal and esophageal atresia); then switch to methimazole for the remainder, because PTU carries the greater hepatotoxicity risk with longer use. Counsel every patient to report fever or sore throat urgently — that is how agranulocytosis announces itself.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Hypothyroidism: Presentation Urgent presentation is myxedema coma — very rare, but characterised by obtundation and hypothermia , with hypotension, bradycardia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia and hypoventilation. Symptoms (non-specific) Signs (not sensitive) Cold intolerance · weight gain despite decreased appetite · fatigue · shortness of breath · slow mentation · apathy · constipation Cool, pale skin · bradycardia · diastolic hypertension with a narrow pulse pressure · decreased cardiac output · slow relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes Both lists are too non-specific to diagnose on clinically — which is exactly why the diagnosis rests on TSH rather than on how convincing the story sounds. When to check a TSH Because it's hard to diagnose clinically, the indications to test are broad: compatible symptoms, dyslipidemia, anemia, hyponatremia, personal or family history of autoimmune disease, susceptible populations (Down syndrome, Turner syndrome), previous thyroid disease or therapy, relevant drugs, and pregnancy. Add FT4 whenever pituitary or hypothalamic disease is suspected. Confirmation: a repeat elevated TSH with a low FT4.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Hypothyroidism: Differential Category Causes Autoimmune destruction Hashimoto's thyroiditis — by far the most common cause Drugs Lithium , amiodarone Removal or destruction Thyroid surgery, radioactive iodine, radiation Central (reduced pituitary/hypothalamic stimulation) Trauma, surgery, tumour, infiltrative disease Hashimoto's — risk factors are female sex, family history of autoimmune disease (especially thyroid) and iodine load. Symptoms are those of hypothyroidism generally: highly variable and non-specific. Signs are insensitive: goiter, bradycardia, diastolic hypertension, delayed reflex relaxation. Why Antibodies Rarely Help Here Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are sensitive for Hashimoto's but less specific, and they almost never change clinical decisions in established hypothyroidism — the treatment is levothyroxine either way. Ultrasound is likewise not sensitive, specific or required; reserve it for a nodule found on examination. Practically: ask about past thyroid treatment, consider pituitary disease if the risk is significant, and otherwise assume Hashimoto's. The one place antibodies do earn their place is subclinical disease, where anti-TPO positivity predicts progression and can tip a treatment decision.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Subclinical Hypothyroidism Elevated TSH with normal FT4 and FT3 — usually TSH < 10–20. May resolve spontaneously , especially if TSH < 10 and the patient is elderly. No evidence of benefit from treatment — the exception is pregnancy . Consider treating if TSH > 10 (high risk of progression), anti-TPO positive (higher risk of progression), or as a therapeutic trial for possible hypothyroid symptoms. How a Therapeutic Trial Ends A trial is a question, not a commitment. If levothyroxine normalises the TSH but the patient feels no different, the symptoms were not from the thyroid — the correct next step is to stop the levothyroxine and monitor for progression to overt hypothyroidism, not to escalate the dose chasing a symptom the drug has already failed to fix.

entries.p: Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction
entries.x: Treating Hypothyroidism Replacement with oral levothyroxine (L-T4) , once daily, titrated to a normal TSH. Parameter Value / rule Estimated requirement ~1.5 mcg/kg/day — weight-based Half-life 1 week Monitoring TSH every 4–6 weeks until normal Starting dose Start low and titrate up if elderly or with heart disease Why the 4–6 Week Interval Is Not Negotiable With a one-week half-life, levothyroxine takes roughly five weeks to reach a new steady state after any dose change — and TSH then needs time to re-equilibrate to that new level. A TSH drawn at two weeks is measuring a system still in transit, and will tempt you into a second dose change that the first one hadn't finished making. Change the dose, then wait. The same weight-based rule explains a common scenario in the other direction: a patient stable on levothyroxine who loses a significant amount of weight is now over-replaced on an unchanged dose, and can turn frankly thyrotoxic. The fix is to reduce the dose — and then, again, recheck at 4–6 weeks. Patient instructions that actually matter Take ≥ 1 hour before and ≥ 2 hours after eating. Separate by at least 4 hours from calcium, iron, magnesium and multivitamins — these bind it and blunt absorption. Any time of day is fine so long as it is consistent, remembered, and separated from food and supplements — bedtime often works well.

Why the Pathology Report Matters Thyroid nodules are common — 0.1% annual incidence , 10% lifetime probability . They turn up because of structural symptoms, functional symptoms, or incidentally on imaging done for something else. The diagnostic pathway — clinical risk factors, ultrasound, FNA — exists to sort out who needs an operation. The surgical pathology report is what gives the definitive diagnosis. It supplies the elements that stage the cancer, set the prognosis, and decide whether anything more needs doing. The patient this lecture is built around History: 42-year-old woman, no risk factors, no family history. A lump in the neck present and slowly enlarging over 6 months, causing some difficulty swallowing. No symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. Examination: a solitary, firm but not hard nodule, 2–3 cm, in the right lobe. No cervical adenopathy, no signs of thyrotoxicosis. Biochemistry and imaging: TSH normal. Ultrasound confirms a solitary 3.2 cm nodule, TI-RADS 3 . FNA: satisfactory specimen; diagnosis of FLUS (follicular lesion of undetermined significance). Decision: results, management options and risks discussed — she chooses a hemithyroidectomy . Everything below is what the pathologist does with what comes out. The clinical evaluation that gets you to this point — TSH-first testing, when to scan, when to biopsy — is covered in 2.1 Clinical Presentation & Evaluation of Thyroid Dysfunction . This lecture picks up at the specimen.

Normal Thyroid: Two Cell Types Normal thyroid is built from cells arranged in circles — follicles . Everything that goes wrong on this page is a departure from this picture. The three components. Follicular cells are the basic unit — they line each follicle. Colloid is stored thyroid hormone that those cells make, then resorb and break down into T4 and T3. Parafollicular (C) cells sit outside the follicles, make calcitonin, and are not identifiable on routine staining — you need immunohistochemistry to see them. Why Two Cell Types Is the Organising Fact Both cell lines can become malignant, and which one a tumour came from determines almost everything that follows: whether it takes up radioactive iodine (follicular-derived does, C-cell-derived does not), which tumour marker follows it (thyroglobulin vs calcitonin ), whether it is likely to be syndromic , and how aggressively it behaves. Capillaries run between the follicles — which is why a tumour that invades vessels can seed the bloodstream directly, and why "angioinvasion" appears on every report.

What a Nodule Can Be The thing itself. Normal thyroid on the left, the nodule on the right — distinctly different tissue, sharply demarcated from what surrounds it. "Lump, bump, tumour, mass" — they all mean the same thing here, and most are benign . A nodule can be solitary or multiple, and the patient can be: Asymptomatic , or have structural symptoms — dysphagia, hoarseness, stridor — depending on what the nodule is pressing on. Euthyroid (the usual case), or thyrotoxic if the nodule is making hormone autonomously. Etiology What it is Examples Hyperplasia An increased number of cells Nodular — multinodular goitre · Diffuse — Graves disease Inflammation Immune-mediated destruction and repair Hashimoto thyroiditis Neoplasm A clonal proliferation — may arise in normal thyroid or against the background of either of the above Benign — follicular adenoma · Malignant — the carcinomas below For each entity, the lecture works through the same six questions: prevalence, distinguishing clinical features, pathophysiology, key histological features, prognosis, and basic management. The histology is not decoration — it is how you understand the pathophysiology.

Hyperplasia: Multinodular Goitre and Graves Multinodular hyperplasia / multinodular goitre The most common cause of thyroid nodules. Prevalence 6–23% of women and 1.5–5% of men . Sporadic, or endemic in iodine-deficient regions — much less of a driver in North America than in much of the world. Nodules of varying sizes , composed of hyperplastic follicular cells with different levels of function — some more active, some less. The net result is that most patients are euthyroid , and there is no atypia . Degenerative changes are common and are much of what you see down the microscope: cystic change, haemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification. Consider surgery if it is symptomatic, if ultrasound or FNA show worrisome features, if it changes size over time, or if it is disfiguring. Multinodular goitre: enlarged, variably sized, colloid-rich follicles , with the degenerative changes that always accompany them — haemorrhage and fibrosis here. The variation in follicle size is the variation in functional activity, made visible. Graves disease (diffuse toxic hyperplasia) A common cause of hyperthyroidism — 1% of the population , F:M 8:1 . Autoimmune: antibodies bind TSH receptors , which are present on all thyroid follicular cells, stimulating both hormone production and cell proliferation. The result is a diffusely enlarged, hyperplastic, cellular gland with no atypia , with or without chronic inflammation. Hyperplastic follicle cells forming papillary projections into the lumen — but no atypia . Compare the normal follicle inset. This is the trap: papillary architecture here is a hyperplastic response, not papillary carcinoma, and the difference is in the nuclei, not the shape. Extrathyroidal manifestations: ophthalmopathy in 25–50% , pretibial myxedema in 0.5–4% . Management: control the thyrotoxic symptoms medically with adrenergic blockers , then antithyroid medication. Radioactive iodine or surgery if it cannot be controlled medically or there are compressive symptoms.

Inflammation: Hashimoto Thyroiditis Also called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis . A common cause of hypothyroidism — 1–2% of the population , F:M 4:1 . Autoimmune-mediated inflammation and destruction of the gland. Dense chronic inflammation with residual follicles lined by Hurthle cells . The triad on histology is chronic inflammation, Hurthle cells and fibrosis. Two Things That Catch People Out It can present as thyrotoxicosis. Destroying follicles releases the colloid stored inside them , so early on there may be a burst of preformed thyroid hormone and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis — before the gland fails. Same disease, opposite biochemistry, depending on when you catch it. It can present as a nodule and get operated on. The gland may be enlarged or nodular from the initial inflammation, which is exactly how a Hashimoto specimen ends up on a pathologist's bench. Later, as tissue is destroyed, the gland becomes fibrotic and small . Hurthle cell metaplasia — normal follicle cells on the left, Hurthle cells on the right at the same magnification. More pink cytoplasm, larger nuclei. This is metaplasia , not neoplasia: the same cell, changed in response to the inflammation, not a different or malignant cell. Management: thyroid replacement therapy. The clinical side is covered in 2.1 .

Neoplasms: The Classification The first question is primary or secondary — arising from cells in the thyroid, or a metastasis from elsewhere. This lecture is about the primary ones. Follicular-cell-derived tumours are the great majority — which makes sense, since follicular cells are the great majority of the gland. Read the malignant list downward: as you go, the tumours become less differentiated and more aggressive . The top two are the "differentiated thyroid cancers" that behave well and take up iodine; the bottom of the list does neither. Cell of origin Tumour Share Follicular cell Follicular adenoma — benign Incidence 3–5% Papillary thyroid carcinoma (and variants) 85–90% of thyroid cancers Follicular thyroid carcinoma 5–10% Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma < 5% Anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinoma < 5% C cell Medullary thyroid carcinoma 2% Other Lymphoma, soft tissue tumours Rare

Follicular Adenoma vs Follicular Carcinoma Follicular adenoma — benign Incidence 3–5% ; F:M 5:1 , typically in the 40s–50s . Ultrasound: solid, well-circumscribed, homogeneous. Most are non-functioning — " cold " on radioactive iodine scanning; a minority are functioning ("hot"). Cured by surgery — hemithyroidectomy, no recurrence. Frequent RAS mutations . A distinct nodule, encapsulated and well-circumscribed , clearly different from the normal thyroid it displaces. The border is the diagnosis. Well-circumscribed with a pushing border; no invasion through the capsule into adjacent normal tissue and no lymphovascular invasion . Microfollicles inside, normal follicles outside. No nuclear atypia. Uniform, small, round nuclei — and this is exactly the problem, because the carcinoma looks the same. Follicular thyroid carcinoma — malignant The lecture's own definition is the clearest one: like a follicular adenoma, but with invasion. Compare the outline with the adenoma above: this one has no clean encapsulated edge. Everything that makes it a carcinoma is happening at the border. Invasive growth into adjacent normal thyroid (focal or diffuse), and/or lymphatic or angioinvasion . Haematogenous spread — it seeds the bloodstream, so distant metastases (bone, lung) rather than neck nodes. Lacks nuclear atypia — the nuclei look benign. Frequent RAS mutations , the same as adenoma, which suggests these carcinomas are derived from adenomas . Diffusely infiltrative — tumour pushing out through the capsule into the thyroid around it. Angioinvasion — tumour inside a vessel lumen. This is the finding that makes it a carcinoma, and it is also the mechanism of its haematogenous spread. Follicular carcinoma on the left, follicular adenoma on the right. No difference in the nuclei — FNA cannot distinguish benign from malignant. The Single Most Important Point on This Page Adenoma and carcinoma are defined by architecture at the edge of the lesion , not by what the cells look like. A needle samples cells; it does not sample the capsule or the vessels around it. So a follicular lesion on FNA is an unresolvable result by design — it is not a failure of the aspirate or the cytopathologist. That is exactly why the patient at the top of this page had a hemithyroidectomy for a "FLUS" result . The operation is diagnostic as well as therapeutic: only with the whole nodule and its capsule can anyone say which of the two it was. Contrast this with papillary carcinoma below, which is de

Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma The most common primary thyroid malignancy. F:M 3:1 , typically 40–60 years . Most have a good prognosis — 93% survival at 10 years. Often multifocal. Often spreads via lymphatics to locoregional lymph nodes — and a neck node may be the initial presentation . Diagnosis is based on nuclear features. The classic type also has papillary architecture. Management: surgery, with or without radioactive iodine. Molecular: BRAF mutation, RET -PTC translocation . Papillary thyroid carcinoma — the one you will meet. Papillary architecture — fibrovascular cores lined by neoplastic epithelial cells. Present in the classic type, but architecture alone is not what makes the diagnosis. The nuclear features that do: enlarged, elongated, irregular contours , grooves , clearing , and intranuclear inclusions . Normal nuclei on the left, PTC nuclei on the right. The difference is obvious at a glance — and that is the practical point: these features are diagnostic and can be identified readily on FNA , giving good sensitivity and specificity. This is the mirror image of the follicular problem above.

The Two Aggressive Ones Anaplastic (undifferentiated) thyroid carcinoma Very aggressive disease — often lethal. A rapidly expanding neck mass in an older patient. It arises as the progression of a well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma to an undifferentiated one — the same tumour, having lost its differentiation. A large, fleshy, irregular mass with none of the organised structure of the differentiated tumours — visible before the microscope is even involved. Infiltration into the tissues of the neck often prevents adequate surgical removal. Being undifferentiated, it does not respond to radioactive iodine in most cases — consider external beam radiotherapy instead. BRAF testing is important , because a BRAF inhibitor may be an option. Extrathyroidal extension into the soft tissues of the neck, with angioinvasion. A rim of normal thyroid survives at the edge. This is why it is so often unresectable. Sheets of malignant cells with no follicle formation. "Undifferentiated" is literal — nothing here looks like thyroid any more, which is precisely why it cannot concentrate iodine. Medullary thyroid carcinoma The only one on this page that is not follicular in origin. It arises from the calcitonin-producing parafollicular (C) cells . Medullary carcinoma infiltrating the gland. Note the growth pattern named in the panel — nests, cords and trabeculae, not papillae — the architectural clue that this is not a follicular-cell tumour at all. Feature Detail Genetics Sporadic in 75% ; 25% associated with MEN 2A or 2B . RET gene point mutations — note, a point mutation , not the RET -PTC translocation of papillary carcinoma Growth Infiltrative; often multifocal. Nests, cords and trabeculae — not papillae Signature finding Amyloid deposition , which is polymerised calcitonin Immunostaining Negative for thyroid markers — it is not a thyroid follicular cell Behaviour Frequent metastasis; poorer prognosis than the differentiated cancers Follow-up Monitor serum calcitonin for recurrence — the tumour keeps making it, so it doubles as a tumour marker Nests of tumour cells separated by amorphous pink amyloid — which is calcitonin . The hormone the tumour cannot stop making is deposited in its own stroma, and it is also what you follow in the blood afterwards. Why MTC Is the One That Changes What You Do Next A quarter of these are syndromic , so a diagnosis of medullary carcinoma is a reason to think about the rest of MEN 2 — and specifically to exclude a pheochromocytoma before

entries.t: Management and What the Report Has to Say
entries.x: Management and What the Report Has to Say General thyroid cancer treatment Surgery for established (FNA-positive) or suspected cancer > 1 cm . Hemithyroidectomy for low risk; total thyroidectomy for high risk. Lymph node dissection if there is evidence of nodal disease. Postoperative radioactive iodine (I-131) for well-differentiated carcinomas at high risk of recurrence — which is why differentiation matters so much on the report. External beam radiotherapy if there is extensive extrathyroidal extension. Chemotherapy and kinase inhibitors for some advanced cancers. What goes in the report, and why each element is there Reporting element What it determines Tumour type · unifocal or multifocal · size of tumour(s) Together these decide the need for additional surgery , for RAI therapy , for external beam radiotherapy and for chemotherapy — and they set the risk of local recurrence and the prognosis Encapsulated vs non-encapsulated · capsular invasion (focal or extensive) Lymphatic invasion · angioinvasion Extrathyroidal extension Lymph node metastasis · size of largest metastasis · extranodal extension Margin status Every line is a decision, not a description. This is the point made at the very start of the lecture: the report is not a label on the specimen, it is the input to the next management step. The ATA system stratifies thyroid cancer into low, intermediate and high risk of structural disease recurrence, in patients without structurally identifiable disease after initial therapy. Read it as a gradient: extensive vascular invasion and gross extrathyroidal extension sit at the top (30–55%) ; a unifocal papillary microcarcinoma sits at the bottom (1–2%) . Thyroid , 2016. Staging, in one line The AJCC/TNM 8th edition uses age 55 as the pivot for differentiated thyroid cancer: under 55, you can only be stage I or II — stage II requiring distant metastasis. Over 55, extrathyroidal extension and the structures involved drive the stage upward. 10-year disease-specific survival: stage I 98–100% , stage II 85–90% ; and over 55, stage III 60–70% , stage IV < 50% . The Question the Lecture Ends On A patient tells you her sister has just had a hemithyroidectomy and was diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma . She asks what the prognosis is. The correct answer is that it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis — and nothing more, because you do not have the details of the report. The distractors are worth knowing individually. It is not benign — t

One-Page Summary Thyroid nodules are common , and due to hyperplasia, inflammation or neoplasia . Multinodular hyperplasia is due to different functional levels of thyroid follicular cells. Graves disease is a common cause of hyperthyroidism, secondary to stimulatory autoantibodies. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a common cause of hypothyroidism, secondary to destructive autoantibodies. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer. Most patients with well-differentiated thyroid cancers have a good prognosis . Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is an uncommon but aggressive cancer resulting from transformation of a well-differentiated cancer to an undifferentiated one. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is derived from parafollicular cells and produces calcitonin . Pathological examination of thyroid nodules provides the definitive diagnosis and the critical elements that drive management.

Learning Objectives Recognise and describe the signs, symptoms and main etiology of acute and chronic adrenal insufficiency , and describe its treatment. Recognise and describe the signs and symptoms of primary hyperaldosteronism , and describe the initial tests for it. Recognise and describe the signs and symptoms of pheochromocytoma , and describe its initial diagnostic tests. Describe an approach to the adrenal incidentaloma . Recognise and describe the presenting signs and symptoms of Cushing syndrome , and describe the screening tests for it.

entries.t: Physiology: What Is the Adrenal Gland Actually For?
entries.x: Physiology: What Is the Adrenal Gland Actually For? The lecture opens with the question, and the answer is short: to regulate the response to stress. That only helps once you pin down what stress is, because the list of things that count looks incoherent — an exam, asking someone out, surgery, sepsis, a divorce, a bereavement, being told you are terminal. The Definition That Makes the List Make Sense Stress is a disruption caused by changes in the environment which exceeds the ability to respond while staying the same. It is a homeostasis word, not an emotional one. That is why the psychological and the physiological items sit on the same list — the axis does not distinguish between them, and it cannot. It has one output. This matters clinically: it is why a patient with no cortisol reserve can be tipped into a crisis by gastroenteritis, a dental extraction, or a death in the family — and why "stress dosing" is prescribed for all of them. The normal glands — 4–10 g the pair. For an organ you cannot live without, that is very little tissue. The layers in section. The fasciculata is by far the thickest — which is why cortisol dominates adrenal output. One gland, four hormones Layer (outside → in) Product What controls it Job Zona g lomerulosa Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) Renin–angiotensin II and K + — not ACTH Salt and volume Zona f asciculata Cortisol (glucocorticoid) ACTH The stress hormone; raises blood glucose Zona r eticularis Androgens (DHEA, DHEAS) ACTH Sex-steroid precursors Medulla Catecholamines Sympathetic preganglionic fibres — it is effectively a sympathetic ganglion Fight or flight GFR from the outside in — S alt, S ugar, S ex. The one fact worth carrying out of this table is that the outermost zone is not on the ACTH circuit . The HPA axis and its rhythm Hypothalamus ( CRH ) → anterior pituitary ( ACTH ) → adrenal cortex ( cortisol ). Cortisol then feeds back negatively on both — the loop that every disease on this page breaks somewhere different. The axis, with cortisol's actual job on the left: raise blood glucose — by gluconeogenesis, by breaking muscle down for amino acids, and by inhibiting GLUT-4. Every feature of Cushing syndrome later on is one of these effects running unchecked. Cortisol is secreted in a diurnal rhythm : highest in the early morning, nadir at night. Two clinical consequences, running in opposite directions: For insufficiency: the rhythm tells you when to draw the blood — a 6–9 AM cortisol, when a healthy axis shoul

entries.t: Primary vs Secondary: Where the Lesion Sits
entries.x: Primary vs Secondary: Where the Lesion Sits Type Definition Primary (Addison's disease) Inability of the adrenal cortex to synthesise and secrete glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). Secondary (central) Impaired adrenal stimulation — abnormal ACTH and/or CRH from the pituitary or hypothalamus. Often a consequence of glucocorticoid use . The gland is intact but never gets the message. Critical illness–related Cortisol production inadequate for the metabolic demand of critical illness. The axis is not destroyed; it is outrun. Either of the first two can present for the first time as an acute adrenal insufficiency — an Addisonian crisis. The chronic and acute forms are not different diseases; the crisis is what the chronic disease does when it meets a stressor. Normal. Two separate circuits out of one gland — ACTH drives cortisol, renin–angiotensin drives aldosterone. Primary. Defect at the adrenal: cortisol and aldosterone fail; CRH and ACTH rise unopposed. Secondary. Defect above the gland: cortisol fails, aldosterone is spared. Often a consequence of steroid use. The same axis, one lesion at a time Pick a state → Normal axis feedback loop intact Primary (Addison's) the gland has failed Secondary (central) the signal has failed Cushing disease pituitary ACTH excess Adrenal Cushing ACTH-independent Exogenous steroid the commonest of all Normal axis CRH drives ACTH drives cortisol, and cortisol shuts both back down. Aldosterone comes out of the same gland but sits on a different circuit — renin and angiotensin II set it, which is why it is drawn without an arrow arriving from above. Why the two circuits matter: one lesion can take out cortisol and leave aldosterone standing. Which one it spares is the whole basis of the primary/secondary split. Primary adrenal insufficiency — Addison's disease The cortex itself is destroyed, so both zones fail: cortisol and aldosterone go together. With no cortisol to feed back, CRH and especially ACTH climb unopposed. That ACTH rise is not just a number. ACTH is cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) , the same precursor that yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone, and ACTH itself activates the melanocortin-1 receptor on melanocytes — which is why these patients pigment in the skin creases, buccal mucosa and old scars. At the bedside: hyperpigmentation, salt craving, hyperkalemia , orthostatic hypotension — all four are primary only . Secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency The lesion is above

Who Gets It, and Why Primary Secondary Peak age at diagnosis 30–50 years 50–59 years Worldwide prevalence 93–140 per million 150–280 per million Driven mostly by Autoimmune adrenalitis Exogenous steroid use Both show a female predominance . Addison's disease runs an annual incidence of about 0.6 per 100,000 and a prevalence of 4–11 per 100,000 in the US. Note that secondary insufficiency is the more common of the two, and that is almost entirely a prescribing story. Etiology of primary adrenal insufficiency The deck's own instruction is worth repeating verbatim: know the main categories and one example from each — know the principle, not all the details. Category Examples Autoimmune 80–90% in the West Isolated autoimmune adrenalitis; polyglandular autoimmune syndrome types I and II Hereditary Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (commonest, usually found in early childhood); congenital adrenal hypoplasia; familial glucocorticoid deficiency or resistance; adrenoleukodystrophy and adrenomyeloneuropathy; defective cholesterol metabolism Infectious TB and disseminated fungal infection (histoplasmosis, paracoccidioidomycosis); HIV/AIDS; syphilis; African trypanosomiasis Metastatic cancer Lung, breast, stomach and colon primaries; lymphoma Adrenal hemorrhage or infarction The acute, catastrophic route in — classically in sepsis or on anticoagulation Drugs Ketoconazole, fluconazole; rifampin, phenytoin, barbiturates About 40% of Addison's appears with a polyglandular autoimmune syndrome , so finding it obliges you to look for its company — autoimmune hypothyroidism, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, alopecia, hypogonadism. In PGA type I, adrenal insufficiency is present in 100% , autoimmune thyroid disease in 70%, type 1 diabetes in 50% and hypogonadism in 5–50%. That is why TSH belongs in the follow-up of anyone with autoimmune adrenal insufficiency. Age tells you which cause to think of. Genetic causes front-load into childhood; acquired causes accumulate with age. CAH — congenital adrenal hyperplasia; ACH — adrenal hypoplasia congenita; ALD — adrenoleukodystrophy; APS — autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome. Husebye et al., Lancet 2021;397:613–29, as shown in the lecture.

entries.t: Clinical Features: Chronic Disease vs Crisis
entries.x: Clinical Features: Chronic Disease vs Crisis Puar et al., Am J Med 2016;129:e3–9, as presented in the lecture. The chronic column is a list of complaints that could belong to almost anything — which is exactly the diagnostic problem. The three findings that should stop you are hyperpigmentation , salt craving and unexplained hyperkalemia , because none of them belong to the generic fatigue differential. The key-messages panel from the lecture. Two things follow from it: hydrocortisone goes in on suspicion, not on confirmation ; and prevention lives with the patient , not the physician — sick-day rules and an injectable at home are what stop the crisis happening at all.

entries.t: The Screening Labs — and Why Each One Moves
entries.x: The Screening Labs — and Why Each One Moves None of these makes the diagnosis. What they do is raise the question, and the pattern they form tells you which half of the axis to suspect before the cortisol comes back. Hover or tap any value for the mechanism behind it. Lab Primary (Addison's) Secondary (central) Sodium ↓ Low Two hits at once: no aldosterone means the kidney wastes sodium and the patient is genuinely volume-depleted, and no cortisol means no brake on ADH, so water is retained on top of it. Present in 85–90%. Normal or ↓ No salt wasting here — aldosterone is intact. Any fall is purely dilutional, from unrestrained ADH. The patient is usually euvolemic, not dry. Potassium ↑ High Aldosterone normally drives potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct. Without it, potassium is retained. This is the single most useful discriminator on the panel. Normal (occasionally ↑) The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system is untouched by a pituitary lesion, so potassium handling is normal. Frank hyperkalemia argues against a purely central cause. Bicarbonate / pH ↓ Both Aldosterone also drives H⁺ secretion in the collecting duct. Losing it gives a hyperkalemic, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis — the picture of a type 4 renal tubular acidosis. ↓ Mild Not a tubular acidosis — aldosterone is fine. This is the lactate and impaired free-water handling of hypotension and hypoperfusion, so it tracks how unwell the patient is. Glucose ↓ Low Cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone: it drives gluconeogenesis and opposes insulin. Remove it and fasting glucose falls. Hypoglycemia is more prominent in children and in secondary insufficiency. Calcium ↑ High Uncommon but real, and the mechanism is not fully settled. Volume depletion lowers GFR and increases proximal tubular calcium reabsorption, with a contribution from increased bone resorption. It corrects quickly on hydrocortisone — which is itself the clue. Creatinine ↑ Renal insufficiency Pre-renal. Salt wasting and vomiting drop the effective circulating volume and the kidney is simply underperfused — which is why it improves with fluids and steroid rather than with anything renal. ACTH ↑↑ High No cortisol means no negative feedback, so the corticotrophs run unopposed. The same POMC surge that raises ACTH also produces the hyperpigmentation — ACTH and MSH share a precursor, and ACTH itself activates the melanocortin-1 receptor on melanocytes. Normal or ↓ The corticotroph is the lesion. Beware the word "norma

Diagnosis: Cortisol First, ACTH Second Serum cortisol is the best blood test. It answers the only question that matters urgently — is there enough cortisol? — and it answers it straight away. ACTH is ordered afterwards , and it answers a different question: primary or secondary. Serum cortisol, drawn 6–9 AM Interpretation > 450 nmol/L Adrenal insufficiency ruled out 80–450 nmol/L Indeterminate — go to a cosyntropin stimulation test < 80 nmol/L Diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency Timing is for stable outpatients. In a symptomatic patient with a possible adrenal crisis, draw the cortisol at any time of day — and do not let the draw delay treatment. A high ACTH with a low cortisol means primary. A low or inappropriately normal ACTH means secondary. Stop estrogen at least 6 weeks before testing. It raises cortisol-binding globulin, which raises measured total cortisol and can falsely reassure you. The 250 µg cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test asks the gland directly: given a maximal signal, can you make cortisol? A rise above 450 nmol/L is normal. Specificity 95% , sensitivity 97% for primary insufficiency — but it is much weaker for secondary, because a recently damaged pituitary leaves an adrenal that has not yet atrophied and can still answer a pharmacological dose. The algorithm from the lecture. Cortisol establishes whether ; ACTH establishes where . Note the septic-shock branch on the right: in critical illness a reassuring random cortisol does not exclude insufficiency, because the demand is higher than the reference range assumes. And the instruction in red applies throughout — the cut-off varies by assay, the logic does not.

Treatment, Stress Dosing and Follow-up The adrenal crisis 1 ABCs. It is a shock state before it is an endocrine problem. 2 Send electrolytes and glucose — and, if it costs nothing, cortisol and ACTH. Worth having, because after the first dose of steroid they are uninterpretable for days. But drawing them must not delay giving anything. 3 Fluids, fast: 2–3 L of normal saline with dextrose, through two large-bore IVs. These patients are salt-depleted and hypoglycemic at the same time, which is why the fluid choice covers both. 4 Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, then 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours. Hydrocortisone is chosen because at these doses it has meaningful mineralocorticoid activity too — it replaces both arms at once. 5 Subacutely: taper fluids and steroid, add a mineralocorticoid, and find the precipitant. A crisis almost always has a trigger — infection, a missed dose, surgery, gastroenteritis that stopped the tablets going in. Fludrocortisone is added only once the hydrocortisone dose falls, because high-dose hydrocortisone is already doing that job. Rushworth, NEJM 2019, as given in the lecture — the detailed reference version of the same protocol, including paediatric dosing and the reminder to keep looking for another cause if the hypotension does not lift. Chronic replacement Drug Dose Notes Hydrocortisone 10–20 mg AM and 5–10 mg PM Split to imitate the diurnal rhythm — the bigger dose on waking Prednisone (alternative) 5–7.5 mg each morning Longer acting, so once daily Fludrocortisone (Florinef) 0.05–0.1 mg once daily The mineralocorticoid. Often not required in secondary AI — aldosterone was never lost Stress dosing — the part that prevents deaths Situation What to do Surgery (scaled to type and duration) Hydrocortisone 50–100 mg one hour before — the "on call" dose — then 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours Intercurrent illness (flu, fever) The rule of 3s: triple the dose for three days Vomiting or severe diarrhea Injection , not tablets. An oral dose that is not absorbed does not exist — this is the route into a crisis Finding the right dose: over- and under-treatment There is no blood test that tells you the replacement dose is right — a cortisol level on treatment reflects the last tablet, not the adequacy of the regimen. Dosing is titrated clinically , and the signs run in two directions: Under-treatment with glucocorticoids Over-treatment with glucocorticoids Symptoms of adrenal insufficiency returning Weight gain Constitutional symptoms — malaise, fat

Primary Hyperaldosteronism Uncontrolled, persistent overproduction of aldosterone by one or both adrenal glands , with two defining features: production is not suppressible , and it is no longer renin-dependent . It accounts for 5–10% of all hypertension — far commoner than the "rare endocrine cause" framing suggests — and it can be unilateral or bilateral , a distinction that decides the treatment entirely. When to consider it Trigger Why it points here Severe or treatment-resistant hypertension (> 3 drugs) Nothing in a standard regimen blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor — the drugs are aimed at the wrong mechanism Low K + — spontaneous, or thiazide-induced with inappropriately high urinary K + loss Aldosterone drives K + out through the urine. "Inappropriately high" is the key word: the kidney should be conserving potassium, and is not Hypertension plus an adrenal incidentaloma The mass may be the source — see the incidentaloma work-up No edema Not an indication so much as confirmation that the picture fits Only one link is broken. Aldosterone stops depending on angiotensin II (the dashed arrow), and everything else still works — including the feedback limb, which is exactly why renin ends up suppressed . High aldosterone with low renin is the signature, and it is why the ratio is the test rather than either value alone. Two Things This Diagram Explains Why there is no edema, despite all that salt retention. After the first few days of sodium retention, volume expansion and higher renal perfusion pressure trigger a natriuresis that overrides the mineralocorticoid signal — aldosterone escape . Sodium balance is re-established at a higher blood pressure but a near-normal body sodium content. The hypertension persists; the edema never arrives. Edema in a hypertensive, hypokalemic patient should push you toward the states where escape fails: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Why "secondary" hyperaldosteronism looks different. In renal artery stenosis, diuretic use or heart failure the drive comes from renin itself — aldosterone is high but renin is also high, so the ratio stays normal. That is the whole discriminating power of the ratio.

Screen, Confirm, Localise Three steps, in order, each answering a different question. Imaging first is the classic error. 1 — Screening: the aldosterone : renin ratio An elevated ratio indicates aldosterone production that is no longer renin-dependent. Measuring aldosterone alone will not do it — a high aldosterone is the appropriate response to a low volume, and plenty of hypertensive people have one. The question is whether aldosterone is high relative to the renin driving it . Pattern Aldosterone Renin Ratio Primary hyperaldosteronism ↑ ↓ suppressed ↑ raised Secondary hyperaldosteronism ↑ ↑ also high Normal Essential hypertension Normal Normal Normal Cut-offs vary between laboratories , because aldosterone and renin are measured in different units and by different assays — renin activity versus direct renin concentration , ng/dL versus pmol/L. A ratio quoted without its units and reference range is meaningless. Know the principle, not the number. The drugs that will lie to you Most antihypertensives move renin, and because renin sits in the denominator, moving it moves the ratio: Medications. Beta-blockers, central α 2 agonists and NSAIDs suppress renin → false positive . ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and dihydropyridine CCBs raise renin → false negative . And everything else. Potassium status, dietary sodium, age, renal impairment, pregnancy and renovascular hypertension all shift it too. Correct potassium to about 4.0 mmol/L and do not salt-restrict before testing — hypokalemia itself suppresses aldosterone and can hide the diagnosis. The one class that must always come off is the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and amiloride/triamterene — withdraw for 4 weeks. Verapamil slow-release, hydralazine and the α 1 blockers (prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin) are the usual substitutes if blood pressure will not tolerate a washout. 2 — Confirmation: proving it cannot be suppressed A raised ratio is a screening result, not a diagnosis. The confirmatory test asks the question directly — give a stimulus that should switch aldosterone off, and see whether it switches off. The options are a saline infusion test (2 L normal saline), fludrocortisone suppression , or a high salt load . All three work by expanding volume, which in a normal person shuts the RAAS down. A worked example from the lecture — the same patient before and after 2 L of normal saline. Reading This Result Aldosterone did not fall — it rose, 737 → 866 pmol/L, aga
