Pheochromocytoma Catecholamine-secreting tumours arising from chromaffin tissue, which exists in two places: Site of origin Name Note Adrenal medulla Pheochromocytoma Makes adrenaline as well as noradrenaline — only the medulla has the enzyme, and it needs the high local cortisol draining from the cortex to express it Sympathetic ganglia , neck to pelvis Paraganglioma Outside the gland, so noradrenaline only — no cortisol bathing it Rare: about 1 per 100,000 per year , and fewer than 0.2% of people with hypertension. Rarity is what makes it dangerous — it is never at the front of the differential. What patients notice Spell-related (paroxysmal) Chronic (sustained) The classic triad: headache, palpitations (tachycardia), sweating — with pallor Sustained hypertension Anxiety, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, blood pressure spikes Anxiety, fatigue, headache, cold hands, fever, nausea, vomiting, sweating Entirely normal between spells Orthostatic hypotension — in a hypertensive patient, an odd combination that should prompt the thought Why a Hypertensive Patient Drops Their Pressure on Standing Chronic catecholamine excess does two things at once: sustained vasoconstriction contracts the plasma volume , and the adrenergic receptors that would normally defend blood pressure on standing become desensitised . A volume-depleted patient with blunted reflexes has nothing left to respond with. The same physiology drives the surgical rule below — remove the tumour, the catecholamine drive vanishes, and an under-filled patient with down-regulated receptors can collapse. That is why alpha blockade and volume repletion come before anyone operates. Biochemistry: test the metabolites, not the hormones Adrenaline is made only where the gland expresses PNMT — the medulla — which is why an extra-adrenal paraganglioma produces noradrenaline and normetanephrine but not adrenaline or metanephrine. Fractionated plasma free metanephrines is the test to order — 99% sensitive. Note the trade-off down the table: urinary VMA is the most specific test listed and the worst one to use, because at 64% sensitivity it misses a third of cases. In a disease where a miss can be lethal, sensitivity wins. Lenders et al., JAMA 2002;287:1427–34. Why Metanephrines Beat Catecholamines Catecholamines are released episodically . If the patient is not having a spell when the blood is drawn, the level can be normal — and a rule-out test that depends on catching the tumour in the act is not a rule-out test.

The Adrenal Incidentaloma An adrenal mass found on imaging done for something else. They are common, and getting commoner as scanning does: Finding Frequency A 1–2 cm mass in adults over 50 2–3% Over the age of 70 7% Under the age of 30 Uncommon — and therefore more suspicious when found In a patient with known cancer 75% are metastases Adrenocortical carcinoma (population incidence) 5 per million Functioning: Cushing / pheochromocytoma / primary aldosteronism ~5% / ~5% / ~1% Every incidentaloma asks two independent questions , and both need answering — a mass can be hormonally active and radiologically benign, or silent and malignant. 1 — Is it functioning? Exclude overproduction of… Test Cortisol (Cushing) 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression ; 24-hour urine cortisol excretion Aldosterone (Conn syndrome) Blood pressure and electrolytes (looking for hypokalemia ); aldosterone and renin upon indication Catecholamines (pheochromocytoma) Urinary or plasma metanephrines and catecholamines 2 — Is it malignant? Unenhanced CT attenuation and size What it means ≤ 10 HU and homogeneous Benign lipid-rich adenoma — no imaging follow-up needed, irrespective of size 11–20 HU and < 4 cm Indeterminate — characterise further or re-image at 12 months ≥ 4 cm, heterogeneous or > 20 HU Relevant malignancy risk — multidisciplinary review, usually surgery The attenuation and size thresholds are added from the current European Society of Endocrinology guideline; the lecture defers the size-versus-malignancy detail to a later presentation. The lecture's own bottom line still holds: the only absolute criterion for malignancy is the presence of distant metastasis. And the rule from the section above applies here too — never biopsy an adrenal mass until pheochromocytoma has been excluded.

Cushing Syndrome: Overexposure to Glucocorticoids Recall from the physiology section what cortisol is for: raising blood glucose — gluconeogenesis, muscle catabolism for amino acids, inhibition of GLUT-4. Every feature below is one of those effects running unchecked for years. The classic habitus: central weight gain with thin extremities (muscle catabolism), a dorsal fat pad and moon face, purple striae, thin easily-bruised skin and poor wound healing. Beyond the habitus: menstrual irregularity · glucose intolerance and frank diabetes · cardiovascular disease (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, thromboembolism) · fungal infections · androgen excess (sideburns, oily skin, acne, increased libido) · neuropsychological change (lability, depression, irritability, anxiety, panic attacks) · growth retardation in children. Which signs actually move the needle Most of these features are common in people who do not have Cushing's. The likelihood ratios sort the discriminating ones from the merely associated: Sign Likelihood ratio of a positive result Ecchymoses 10 – 11.3 Osteopenia or fracture 8 – 13.8 Proximal muscle weakness 8 – 12.6 Hypertension 4.35 – 5.29 Edema 2.82 – 3.88 Striae (purple, > 1 cm) 2.72 – 2.91 Plethora 2.51 – 3.03 Hirsutism 2.21 – 2.90 General obesity / weight gain 1.75 – 3.10 Headache 1.27 – 1.57 The three at the top are the ones worth hunting for — easy bruising, osteopenia or fracture, and proximal weakness . Note where obesity sits: near the bottom. The feature everyone associates with Cushing's is one of the least discriminating, because it is so common without it. L. Nieman, Handbook of Diagnostic Endocrinology .

entries.t: Diagnosis: Three Things Go Wrong with Cortisol
entries.x: Diagnosis: Three Things Go Wrong with Cortisol Normal on the left, Cushing disease on the right. Note the y-axes are different: the normal trace tops out around 500 nmol/L and falls to nearly nothing overnight; the Cushing trace never drops below about 400. Williams Textbook of Endocrinology, 11th ed., p451. Three abnormalities, and each screening test is built to catch a different one: What is wrong The test that catches it Result suggesting Cushing Increased cortisol production 24-hour urinary excretion of cortisol Above the upper limit of normal Lack of diurnal rhythm Late-night salivary cortisol > 4 nmol/L at the time it should be at its nadir Lack of suppressibility 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression Cortisol > 50 nmol/L at 08:00–09:00 Diagnosis requires two positive screening tests. No single result is enough — each has its own false positives (shift work and depression disturb the rhythm; obesity and alcohol affect suppression). Fraser & Van Uum, CMAJ 2010. What dexamethasone is actually testing Normal response. Dexamethasone is read by the pituitary as cortisol. ACTH falls, and so does cortisol — the feedback loop works. Adrenal Cushing. ACTH is suppressed exactly as it should be — but the adrenal was never listening to it, so cortisol stays up. The test fails because the link is already cut. That is the logic of the whole test: dexamethasone is a potent synthetic glucocorticoid that the pituitary reads as cortisol, but which the cortisol assay does not detect. In a healthy axis it switches ACTH off and measured cortisol falls. It only fails to suppress when cortisol production has escaped pituitary control — either because the source is autonomous (adrenal), or because the ACTH source itself is a tumour that ignores feedback.

Then: ACTH-Dependent or Independent? Diagnosis comes first, cause second — and the branch point is a single measurement. Step 1 is diagnosing Cushing syndrome. Step 2 is the ACTH. Detectable or high ACTH → ACTH- dependent (pituitary adenoma — "Cushing disease " — or ectopic ACTH, rarely ectopic CRH). Suppressed ACTH → ACTH- independent , meaning the adrenal itself: adenoma, hyperplasia or carcinoma. Try both states in the axis simulator above. All the routes to the same syndrome. The slide asks: which cause is most common? The Answer to the Slide's Question Exogenous glucocorticoids — by a wide margin. Prescribed steroid for asthma, rheumatological or inflammatory disease is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome seen in general practice, and it is the one route on the diagram that does not involve a tumour at all. Always ask about steroids — including inhaled, topical and injected — before working anyone up. Among endogenous causes, the commonest is a pituitary corticotroph adenoma — Cushing disease — at roughly 60–80% , with adrenal causes and ectopic ACTH making up the remainder. This is also the loop back to Part 1: a patient on long-term steroid has Cushing syndrome and a suppressed axis at the same time , and stopping the drug abruptly gives them an adrenal crisis. Treatment and follow-up Surgical removal of the culprit tumour where possible. Cushing is not "cured" — it goes into remission. Recurrence is possible even after 10 years, so follow-up does not stop. Monitor clinically, and biochemically with 24-hour urine cortisol and late-night salivary cortisol — the same two properties of the hormone that made the diagnosis.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the uterus, cervix, uterine tubes, ovaries, bladder, vagina and vulva. Describe the structures that support and stabilize the uterus and vagina, and the complications when they fail. Trace the arterial supply, venous drainage and lymphatic drainage of the pelvis and perineum. Describe the nerve supply to the female pelvis and why it makes diagnosis tricky. Describe the fascial layers of the perineum and how they decide where fluid collects. Compare male and female erectile bodies and external genitalia, and their role in the sexual response. Build an approach to a 20-year-old woman with right lower quadrant pain. Dr. Martin's workshop runs for over three hours: lectures, lab videos and knowledge checks. It builds on the P1 pelvis and perineum. The embryology behind all of this (why the ovary's blood supply comes from the aorta, why the round ligament ends in the labia majora) is the next lecture, 3.7 .

entries.t: A Note on the Words Used
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: A Note on the Words Used The lecture opens by explaining its language. Sex refers to genes, chromosomes, anatomy and their products. Gender refers to the psychological, social and cultural roles a society calls masculine or feminine. Both come in more than two versions, and they combine into a person's self-identification (pronouns, language, presentation). Approach When to use it Example Person-first language One-on-one: use the person's own identification Ask for, and use, their pronouns Avoid binary shortcuts General speech "Assigned female at birth" instead of "born female"; "all sexes" instead of "both sexes"; "phenotypic" instead of "normal" development; "they" when you don't know Anatomy-first language Big general statements, when identity is unknown " Anyone with a cervix needs screening" instead of "women need screening"; "people with a prostate" instead of "men" In this course, "female" and "male" mean the assigned-female-at-birth and assigned-male-at-birth phenotypes . The same distinction comes up again in 3.8 .

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Layout Vagina → cervix → uterus → uterine tubes → ovaries. In the side view the uterus sits between the bladder in front and the rectum behind . The ovaries are lateral and posterior : you see them from behind, not from the front. From the lecture (Netter).

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Vagina A musculomembranous tube, 7–9 cm long , from the cervix to the vaginal opening in the vestibule (between the labia minora). It lies between the urethra and bladder in front and the rectum behind . Three jobs: receives the penis, carries menstrual flow, and is the birth canal. The cervix pokes into the top of the vagina, leaving a gutter around it: the fornix . It has an anterior , a posterior (the deepest) and two lateral parts. The fornices. Posterior (orange), anterior (blue) and lateral (red), all around the cervix (purple). Keep the posterior fornix in mind: it sits right against the pouch of Douglas. Why the bimanual exam works. The vagina is thin, stretchy and central, so you can feel through it: the cervix , ischial spines , sacral promontory , uterine artery pulsations , and the ovaries only when abnormal (e.g. a cyst).

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Uterus and Cervix Body (upper 2/3): fundus (the dome above the tubes), uterine ostia, isthmus. Cervix (lower 1/3): internal os → cervical canal → external os. "Os" means opening. Layer What it is Endometrium Inner mucous lining. Shed in menstruation ; where the blastocyst implants Myometrium Thick smooth muscle carrying the vessels and nerves. Hormones make it contract in menses and labour Perimetrium Outer serous coat The histology of each layer across the cycle is in 2.7 . Examining the cervix What you see through the speculum. The blades sit in the anterior and posterior fornices and open the vaginal walls. A nulliparous external os is a small pinhole . A parous os (after a vaginal birth) is a "fish mouth" slit , because it was stretched open in labour. A Pap smear scrapes surface cells off the cervix. From the lecture. Why it matters: the lecture quotes a lifetime cervical cancer risk of about 1 in 145 . Before 1940 it was the leading cause of cancer death in North American women. Deaths fell sharply once the cervix could be looked at and sampled routinely. Screening itself is a later lecture. Position: anteverted and anteflexed Two angles. Version = vagina vs cervix. Flexion = cervix vs uterine body. Normal is anteverted + anteflexed . The uterus is mobile, so retroverted or retroflexed positions (inset) are common variants. Anteverted: the cervix tips forward from the vagina. Anteflexed: the body bends forward on the cervix. Together they put the uterus on top of the bladder . That is why pregnant people need to pee so often. The top of the uterus moves around. A very full bladder can push it back toward retroversion. The position is also support : when abdominal pressure pushes down, the bladder is underneath ( Part 2 ). Shape and size across a lifetime Body : cervix ratio tracks hormones. With estrogen, the body is 2× the cervix. Without it, 1:1. Stage Body : cervix Why Newborn 2 : 1 Mom's hormones are still circulating Child 1 : 1 No hormones Puberty 2 : 1 Hormones return; still growing to adult size Adult, nulliparous 2 : 1 Adult, multiparous 3 : 1 Never shrinks fully back after pregnancy Postmenopause 1 : 1 Hormones gone again In pregnancy The uterus climbs out of the pelvis , becoming thin-walled, and reaches the costal margin by 9 months . Just before birth (month 10) it drops as the baby descends into the birth canal. Immediately postpartum it is still large and has to contract back down. Breastfeeding helps, with painful cramping. Many p

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Uterine Tubes and Ovaries (the Adnexa) Adnexa means "adjacent structures": everything lateral to the uterus. The tube, from the uterus outward: uterine (intramural) part → isthmus (narrow, thick-walled) → ampulla (widest and longest, where fertilization usually happens ) → infundibulum with its fimbriae , opening into the peritoneal cavity at the ostium. The ovary is tied to the uterus by the ligament of the ovary and to the pelvic wall by the suspensory ligament , which carries the ovarian vessels . From the lecture. Organ Jobs Uterine tube Catches the oocyte from the peritoneal cavity (the fimbriae sweep it in), is the usual site of fertilization , and carries the embryo to the uterus Ovary Develops oocytes and releases them into the peritoneal cavity , not straight into the tube; makes the reproductive hormones From sperm to implantation Sperm survive 3–5 days in the tract, so insemination usually happens before ovulation. The ovary releases the oocyte; the fimbriae draw it in. Fertilization in the ampulla. The embryo moves medially along the tube. Implantation in the endometrium 6–8 days later. Ectopic pregnancy Implantation anywhere outside the uterine body. Most common site: the uterine tube (tubal ectopic). Rarely the ovary, the cervix or the peritoneal cavity. The pregnancy can't survive, because only the uterus can provide the blood supply a placenta needs. The embryo goes looking for that blood supply anyway, so an undetected ectopic can cause severe abdominopelvic hemorrhage . It must be removed. From the lecture.

entries.t: How We Actually See It: Imaging
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: How We Actually See It: Imaging Transabdominal ultrasound , the most common and least invasive. The probe is on the belly, so the top of the image is anterior. It needs a full bladder (black = fluid) as a window. You can see the myometrium, the brighter endometrial lining and the anteverted, anteflexed position. Transvaginal ultrasound puts the probe right next to the ovary. Follicles are black circles. A mature follicle reaches about 20 mm ; after the LH surge it ruptures and releases the egg (photo, right). Hysterosalpingogram (HSG): are the tubes open? Dye (or CO 2 ) goes in through a catheter in the cervix under fluoroscopy (real-time X-ray). Top: dye fills the uterus, runs through both tubes and spills into the peritoneal cavity , so the tubes are patent. Bottom: dye fills only the uterus: blocked tubes . Tubal blockage from scarring after infection or inflammation is a major cause of infertility . From the lecture.

entries.t: Supports of the Uterus and Ovaries
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Supports of the Uterus and Ovaries The support list, colour-coded. Dynamic: urogenital diaphragm + pelvic floor. Passive: position, endopelvic fascia (cardinal and uterosacral ligaments), broad ligament, round ligament. Ovary: ligament of the ovary + suspensory ligament. Type What Dynamic (muscle) Pelvic floor and urogenital diaphragm . Both meet at the perineal body Passive Position : anteverted/anteflexed on the bladder · endopelvic fascia : cardinal and uterosacral ligaments · broad ligament · round ligament The cervix is the least mobile part of the whole tract. It is the hub the endopelvic fascia ligaments anchor to. Ligament Runs from → to Key point Cardinal (transverse cervical) Cervix and vagina → lateral pelvic wall , at the base of the broad ligament Carries the uterine vessels. Holds the uterus up by the cervix Uterosacral Cervix → mid-sacrum Stops the cervix prolapsing into the vagina. Surgical landmark: the ureter runs just lateral to it Broad A double layer of peritoneum draped over the uterus to the pelvic walls Three parts: mesometrium (uterus), mesovarium (ovary), mesosalpinx (tube; salpinx = trumpet) Round ligament of the uterus Uterotubal junction → deep ring → inguinal canal → labia majora Anchors the uterus forward. Stretches a lot in pregnancy: round ligament pain Ligament of the ovary Ovary → uterus With the round ligament, the female remnant of the gubernaculum Suspensory ligament of the ovary Ovary → lateral pelvic wall Carries the ovarian vessels (it's a "ligament" because it's covered in peritoneum) From above, as in the lab. Note the ureteric fold running under the broad ligament beside the uterosacral ligament: that is the ureter you have to protect. The broad ligament's three parts. Mesosalpinx hangs from the tube, mesovarium sticks out to hold the ovary, mesometrium flanks the uterus. The inset shows the two peritoneal layers in cross-section. Why the Round Ligament Ends in the Labia Majora In both sexes a cord called the gubernaculum tethers the gonad and pulls it down as the embryo grows. In males it drags the testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum. In females the middle of the cord gets stuck to the side of the uterus, splitting it into two: the ligament of the ovary (ovary to uterus) and the round ligament , which carries on through the inguinal canal into the labia majora, the female homologue of the scrotum . The full story is in 3.7 . Clinical: these supports are often stretched or damaged in pregnancy and

entries.t: Peritoneal Pouches and the Posterior Fornix
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Peritoneal Pouches and the Posterior Fornix The peritoneum drapes down over the bladder, dips between the bladder and the uterus, goes up and over the uterus, dips again behind it, then climbs up over the rectum. The two dips are the pouches. Vesicouterine pouch (green, between bladder and uterus): shallow. Rectouterine pouch / pouch of Douglas (red, between uterus and rectum): the deepest point of the peritoneal cavity . Fluid collects here in someone standing up. The posterior fornix sits right against the pouch of Douglas. Only a thin wall separates the peritoneal cavity from the vagina, which counts as the outside world. So you can drain fluid ( culdocentesis ) or pass a camera ( culdoscopy ) through it.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Pelvic Floor A muscular basket. Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus; purple) does most of it. Coccygeus fills in at the back. It holds the organs up and resists rises in abdominal pressure . Puborectalis slings around the anorectal junction and keeps it kinked (the anorectal flexure ). Rectum means straight, and a straight rectum would not hold. The openings: urethra, vagina (females only), rectum. Muscle From To Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) Body of the pubis, tendinous arch of the obturator fascia , ischial spine Perineal body, coccyx, anococcygeal ligament Coccygeus Ischial spine Sacrum and coccyx The urogenital hiatus is the front gap in the floor that lets the urethra and vagina through. The perineal membrane closes it from below ( Part 5 ). The pelvic walls: obturator internus (sides), piriformis (back, leaving through the greater sciatic foramen with the sacral plexus roots). The floor is levator ani + coccygeus. You contract the floor every time you cough, sneeze or bear down, to stay continent. In the lab, the floor is often thin and fatty in older donors, which is a picture of why pelvic floor weakness is so common.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Arteries of the Pelvis The internal iliac and its branches (named for their destinations; variations are common ). Pink boxes are female-only, blue box male-only. From the lecture (Netter). Branch Goes to Remember Iliolumbar, lateral sacral Back up to the lumbar region; along the sacrum Hard to see on the diagram, easy in the lab Superior gluteal Gluteal region Leaves through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis , between the lumbosacral trunk and S1 Inferior gluteal Gluteal region Greater sciatic foramen, below piriformis Internal pudendal Perineum and external genitalia Out the greater sciatic foramen, around the sacrospinous ligament, in through the lesser sciatic foramen . "Internal" because the femoral artery has an external pudendal Obturator Medial thigh With the obturator nerve through the obturator canal Umbilical Before birth, back to the placenta. After birth: superior vesical branches (roof of the bladder) Past those branches it is obliterated and forms the medial umbilical fold Uterine (female only) Uterus, cervix, tubes; the placenta in pregnancy Runs in the cardinal ligament ; crosses the ureter (below) Vaginal (female only) Vagina, lower bladder, lower ureter Usually a branch of the uterine. Male equivalent: inferior vesical (bladder, ureter, prostate, seminal vesicles) Middle rectal Rectum Anastomoses with the superior rectal (IMA) and inferior rectal (internal pudendal)

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Arteries of the Reproductive Organs The circled crossing is the one to know. The uterine artery runs medially in the cardinal ligament toward the cervix and passes over the ureter : "water under the bridge" (the artery is the bridge, urine is the water). Up top, the ovarian artery gives ovarian and tubal branches that join the uterine artery's branches, so there is plenty of collateral flow. From the lecture. Artery Source Route and targets Uterine Internal iliac In the cardinal ligament, over the ureter. Gives vaginal branches down and ascending branches that join the ovarian artery Vaginal Uterine (usually) Middle vagina Internal pudendal Internal iliac Lowest vagina. Together with the uterine and vaginal arteries it forms an anastomosis around the vagina Ovarian Abdominal aorta Retroperitoneal down to the pelvis, in the suspensory ligament . Ovarian and tubal branches join the uterine artery Two Clinical Consequences Hysterectomy: the uterine artery has to be clamped, and the ureter lies right under it. The surgeon must positively identify the ureter first so it isn't tied or cut. That is the whole point of "water under the bridge". The ovary's supply is high. Gonads develop on the posterior abdominal wall and bring their vessels (and nerves and lymphatics) with them as they descend. That is why the ovarian artery comes off the aorta near the kidneys, and why ovarian lymph drains to nodes beside the aorta (below). The uterus has a huge blood supply for a reason. Each cycle the endometrium is rebuilt with fresh blood and shed if there's no pregnancy. If an embryo implants, the vessels dilate and engorge to build and feed the placenta for the rest of the pregnancy.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Vessels of the Perineum Internal pudendal artery: it enters the perineum from behind, so it runs forward through the anal triangle in the pudendal canal . Two branches to know: the inferior rectal (anus, lower rectum; joins the rectal anastomosis) and the deep artery of the clitoris/penis ( erection ). Two veins that don't follow the arteries. Superficial dorsal vein : drains the skin to the external pudendal vein (external iliac system, via the thigh). Deep dorsal vein : drains the erectile bodies to the vesical (female) or prostatic (male) plexus, then the internal iliac. The deep dorsal vein is squeezed shut during an erection . The swollen erectile bodies press it against the tight deep fascia around them (called Buck's fascia in the penis; the clitoris has the same layer). Blood can't leave until the erection ends. More in Part 7 .

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Lymphatic Drainage Lymph runs back along the arteries . That is why the ovaries, tubes and fundus drain high, to the lumbar/pre-aortic nodes. Nodes Drain Superficial inguinal Skin of the perineum Deep inguinal Erectile bodies, external genitalia External iliac Upper vagina, cervix, lower uterine body Internal iliac Mid-upper vagina, cervix , uterine body (and male cavernous bodies) Sacral Lower vagina Lumbar / pre-aortic Ovaries, uterine tubes, fundus The chain runs superficial inguinal → deep inguinal → external iliac → common iliac → lumbar/pre-aortic → cisterna chyli → thoracic duct → back to the blood. The Lecture's Knowledge Check: Cervical Cancer Where does cervical cancer spread first? Follow the blood supply. The cervix is fed by the uterine artery , a branch of the internal iliac, so it drains to the internal iliac nodes . But the uterine artery runs out along the cardinal ligament to the lateral pelvic wall , where the external iliac nodes sit, so the cervix drains there too. In practice you check both . The general rule: nodes near a drainage path can pick up lymph even if they aren't the "textbook" group.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Sympathetic Parasympathetic Starts at Intermediolateral horn, T11/T12–L1/L2 (thoracolumbar only) S2–S4 (craniosacral only) Route Through the sympathetic chain without synapsing → lumbar splanchnic nerves → synapse in prevertebral ganglia / inferior hypogastric plexus → postsynaptic fibres to the organs Pelvic splanchnic nerves → synapse in the inferior hypogastric plexus → postsynaptic fibres to the organs Effects Uterine contraction, vasoconstriction Uterine inhibition, vasodilation The inferior hypogastric plexus is mixed : both systems run through it. And in the uterus hormones call the shots , so the autonomic effects are secondary. If the autonomic basics are rusty, the lecture points you back to the Foundations nervous-system module.

entries.t: The Pelvic Pain Line: Where Visceral Pain Goes
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Pelvic Pain Line: Where Visceral Pain Goes The red dashed line = the lower edge of the peritoneum. Above it, pain fibres ride back with the sympathetics . Below it, with the parasympathetics . The exact cut-off varies between people. So a uterus hurts in two places. Fundus pain is felt over the T11–T12 dermatomes (lower trunk, flank, back). Cervix pain is felt in the S2–S4 dermatomes (buttock, perineum, back of the thigh and leg). Above the pelvic pain line Below the pelvic pain line Organs Fundus and body of the uterus, uterine tubes, ovaries Cervix, upper vagina Pain travels with Sympathetics (via the hypogastric plexuses) Parasympathetics (pelvic splanchnic nerves) Spinal level T11–L1/L2 S2–S4 Felt in Lower trunk, flank, back Buttock, perineum, back of the thigh and leg This is the "challenge with diagnosis" in the objectives. The brain maps visceral pain onto the skin of the same spinal level, so pelvic organ pain turns up as back pain, flank pain or leg pain, and you have to think backwards from the dermatome to the organ.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Somatic Supply: the Pudendal Nerve Pudendal nerve, S2–S4. Same route as the internal pudendal artery: out the greater sciatic foramen, in the lesser. Sensory to most of the perineum, motor to the perineal muscles. Nerve Supplies Inferior rectal (pudendal branch) Crosses the ischioanal fat to the external anal sphincter , anal mucosa and perianal skin Dorsal nerve of the clitoris/penis (terminal pudendal branch) The main sensory nerve of the clitoris/penis Ilioinguinal (anterior labial/scrotal branches) Front of the labia majora / scrotum Genitofemoral (genital branch) Front of the labia majora / scrotum; motor to cremaster in males The lowest part of the vagina and rectum and the whole perineum have somatic (normal, sharp, well-localized) sensation through the pudendal nerve. Everything above has visceral sensation, which is dull and poorly localized.

entries.t: Putting the Nerves to Work: Anesthesia for Childbirth
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Putting the Nerves to Work: Anesthesia for Childbirth Each block works on a different set of fibres, so each numbs a different part of labour. From the lecture. Block Numbs Still feels Lumbar epidural / low spinal (lumbar puncture, about L3–L4) Everything from the waist down — Caudal epidural (S2–S4) The birth canal (everything below the pain line) Uterine contractions (above the pain line), so she can push actively Pudendal nerve block The lowest vagina and the perineum Contractions and the upper birth canal (cervix)

entries.t: The Diamond and Its Two Triangles
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Diamond and Its Two Triangles Diamond: pubic symphysis (front) → ischiopubic rami → ischial tuberosities → sacrotuberous ligaments → coccyx (back). A line between the ischial tuberosities splits it into the urogenital triangle (external genitalia, perineal membrane; pierced by the urethra and vagina) in front and the anal triangle (anal canal, ischioanal fat) behind. The two triangles sit in different planes : the anal canal angles backward. From the lecture.

entries.t: Fascial Layers and the Two Pouches
entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Fascial Layers and the Two Pouches From deep to superficial: pelvic floor → deep pouch → perineal membrane → superficial pouch → Colles' fascia → skin. From the lecture. Layer / space What it is and what's in it Pelvic floor Floor of the pelvis = roof of the perineum . Has the urogenital hiatus at the front Deep perineal pouch (urogenital diaphragm) Between the pelvic floor and the perineal membrane; really a region, not a space. Urethra (and vagina ) pass through. External urethral sphincter (and vaginal sphincter), deep transverse perineal muscles, dorsal neurovascular structures of the erectile tissue, bulbourethral glands (males) Perineal membrane Closes the urogenital hiatus from below. Only in the urogenital triangle; merges with the perineal body at the back Superficial perineal pouch Between the perineal membrane and Colles' fascia. Erectile bodies and their muscles , pudendal nerve branches, internal pudendal vessel branches, greater vestibular glands (females). In males it includes the scrotum and penis Colles' fascia Continuous with Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall in front (and dartos in the scrotum). Does not extend into the thighs or back into the anal triangle Where Does the Urine Go? The Lecture's Two Cases A 17-year-old with a straddle injury (swelling in the groin): the spongy urethra tears, below the perineal membrane. Urine and blood fill the superficial pouch . Colles' fascia is fused to the thighs and to the back of the membrane, and continuous with Scarpa's fascia in front, so the fluid spreads into the scrotum and penis and up the anterior abdominal wall , but never into the thighs or the anal triangle . A 26-year-old after a car crash with a pelvic fracture and free fluid on the FAST scan: the membranous urethra tears as it passes through the perineal membrane. Fluid fills the deep pouch . Its roof, the pelvic floor, has a hole in it (the urogenital hiatus ), so fluid rises up into the pelvic cavity . This stays under the peritoneum, not inside the peritoneal cavity. The same anatomy is why catheterizing , especially a male urethra with its bends, has to be done gently.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Erectile Tissue: Male vs Female Same parts, different layout. In the female, the corpus spongiosum homologue is split into the bulbs of the vestibule and the glans clitoris , with only thin bands between them. Male Female Corpora cavernosa (crura on the ischiopubic rami) Corpora cavernosa : crura on the ischiopubic rami and perineal membrane, joining to form the body of the clitoris (the only erectile tissue in the body) Bulb of the penis Bulbs of the vestibule , one on each side of the vestibule Corpus spongiosum → glans penis , around the urethra Glans clitoris , joined to the bulbs by thin bands (not part of the body) Bulbourethral glands (deep pouch) Greater vestibular glands (superficial pouch): mucus into the vestibule during arousal Penis: sexual and urinary Clitoris: sexual arousal only The superficial perineal muscles All three are supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) . Muscle Lies over Does Ischiocavernosus The crura Maintains erection : pushes blood into the erectile tissue and compresses venous outflow Bulbospongiosus Bulb of the penis / bulbs of the vestibule Helps erection. Males: expels the last urine and semen. Females: vaginal sphincter , squeezes the greater vestibular glands Superficial transverse perineal Ischial tuberosity → perineal body Support : fixes the perineal body and pelvic floor The perineal body is the fibromuscular knot in the middle of the perineum where almost everything meets: bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal, the external anal sphincter, the perineal membrane, Colles' fascia and the pelvic floor. It is the central support of the perineum.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Vulva and Vestibule The vulva (its correct name): mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris with its prepuce (hood). Inside the vestibule: external urethral orifice (about 2 cm below and behind the glans clitoris ), vaginal orifice, and the ducts of the greater vestibular glands. Part Note Mons pubis Fatty mound over the pubic symphysis, with pubic hair Labia majora Homologue of the scrotum ; where the round ligament ends Labia minora Fat-free, hairless folds that enclose the vestibule Clitoris Where the labia minora meet in front; covered by the prepuce Catheterizing a Female Patient The external urethral orifice is small and tightly closed. The catheter tip tends to slip into the larger vaginal opening just behind it. If that happens, the catheter is contaminated with vaginal flora and is no longer sterile. Throw it out and open a fresh one ; pushing a dirty catheter into the bladder invites a UTI. Male review, briefly: penis = root, body, corona and glans; its dorsal surface faces forward when flaccid. The scrotum is a fibromuscular skin sac for the testes. Its dartos muscle wrinkles the skin (thicker skin, less surface area) and works with cremaster (which lifts the testes) to keep them at the right temperature. The raphe down the middle is the seam where the folds fused in development. The membranous urethra is only about 1 cm long, as it crosses the urogenital membrane.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: The Ischioanal Fossa Wedge-shaped fat pads on each side of the anal canal. Roof: levator ani . Side: obturator internus and ischium. Middle: external anal sphincter . Contents: fat plus the inferior rectal vessels and nerves . Pudendal (Alcock's) canal: a tunnel inside the obturator internus fascia , on the side wall of the fossa. It carries the internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve , which give off the inferior rectal branches as they pass. Ischioanal fat is among the last fat to go in starvation. Without it the rectum loses support, so rectal prolapse is relatively common in starvation. Ischioanal abscess. A painful infection felt as fullness and tenderness between the anus and the ischial tuberosity . Usually from infected anal glands , or after a tear in the anal lining (gut flora and stool are right there). The two fossae connect behind the anal canal through the deep postanal space (deep to the anococcygeal ligament), so pus can spread to the other side: a horseshoe abscess . Treatment is surgical incision and drainage . From the lecture.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Rectal Vessels and Hemorrhoids Three arteries, one anastomosis: superior rectal ( IMA ), middle rectal ( internal iliac ), inferior rectal ( internal pudendal ). The veins join two systems. Superior rectal → IMV → portal . Middle and inferior rectal → internal iliac → caval . That makes the rectum a portocaval anastomosis . Hemorrhoids are varicose veins of this valveless plexus. Anything that raises the pressure in it can cause them: portal hypertension , IVC obstruction , or anything raising pelvic venous pressure, such as pregnancy (the big uterus presses on the veins). Above the pectinate line Below the pectinate line Part of the canal Upper 2/3 Lower 1/3 Embryology Hindgut endoderm Proctodeum ectoderm Nerves Autonomic (pelvic plexus) Somatic (pudendal / inferior rectal nerve) Venous plexus Internal rectal plexus External rectal plexus Hemorrhoids Internal: painless but bleed (blood on the toilet paper) External: painful, itchy, and bleed

entries.p: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
entries.x: Arousal and Erection Mechanism Triggered by Pathway Psychogenic Sounds, sights, smells, imagination Brain → sacral cord → pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) nerves. A sympathetic contribution is possible but unproven Reflexogenic Touch Sensory fibres → sacral cord → parasympathetic output (a spinal reflex) The erection pathway: S2–S4 → pelvic splanchnic nerves → inferior hypogastric plexus → pelvic plexus → prostatic plexus → cavernous nerves → through the perineal membrane to the erectile tissue. "Point and shoot." P arasympathetic = P oint (erection). S ympathetic = S hoot (ejaculation). Losing the parasympathetic input ends the erection (detumescence). Parasympathetic signal → the helicine arteries (end branches of the deep artery, from the internal pudendal) uncoil and dilate . Blood pours in and the erectile tissue engorges . The swollen bodies press the deep dorsal vein against the tight deep (Buck's) fascia, so blood can't get out . Ejaculation (or orgasm) is a sympathetic event: coordinated contraction of the reproductive tract. Detumescence: the parasympathetic drive stops, the arteries constrict again, and blood drains out through the veins. The lecture uses the male system because much less is known about the anatomy, physiology and biology of the female sexual response ; there are real gaps in the research. Erectile dysfunction Cause Treatment CNS or endocrine disorders, including low testosterone Treat the cause Nerves fail to stimulate the tissue, or vessels don't dilate Oral medication that increases blood flow to the erectile tissue (the slide shows Cialis and Viagra) Lesion of the prostatic plexus or cavernous nerves Pills can't work without the nerve signal, so surgical options : penile pump, or semi-rigid or inflatable prosthesis Why Radical Prostatectomy Causes ED The cavernous nerves run through the prostatic plexus on the surface of the prostate. Taking the prostate out for cancer very often damages them. With the parasympathetic signal cut, the arteries never get the "dilate" message, so loss of erection is a frequent result of radical prostatectomy. The sexual response cycle Stage What happens 1. Desire Wanting to take part, from outside or inside stimuli 2. Arousal Central (thoughts, fantasies) · non-genital peripheral (salivation, sweating, skin vasodilation, nipple erection) · genital (clitoral, labial and vaginal engorgement; penile erection) 3. Orgasm An altered state of consciousness; male ejaculation 4. Resolution Return to

Structure What can go wrong (from this lecture) How the pain behaves Right uterine tube Ectopic (tubal) pregnancy ; can bleed into the pouch of Douglas Above the pain line: visceral pain via sympathetics (T11–L1), lower abdomen/flank. Always check a pregnancy test Right ovary Cyst (palpable on bimanual exam only when abnormal), ovulation Above the pain line: T11–L1. Ovarian lymph and vessels run up to the aorta Right ureter A stone; injury in pelvic surgery Runs under the uterine artery and beside the uterosacral ligament Appendix, cecum, terminal ileum Appendicitis, bowel disease Gut visceral pain; RLQ once the overlying peritoneum is irritated Free fluid or blood from any of these collects in the rectouterine pouch , the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity, which is why it shows up there on ultrasound. entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: What This Lecture Covers The indifferent stage of sexual development, and the switch that sends an embryo down the female pathway. How the ovary forms, and why the egg supply is fixed at birth. The fate of the mesonephric and paramesonephric ducts in females, and how the uterus and vagina form. How the ovaries descend, and how the external genitalia differentiate. The congenital anomalies that follow when each step fails. Dr. Martin's module. The male pathway was covered in P1 with the urinary system. What goes wrong when the hormones are abnormal (CAH, androgen insensitivity) is 3.9 Disorders of Sex Development . The very first weeks of the embryo are in 2.7 .

entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: The Switch: SRY and TDF Genotype does not always decide phenotype. Hormones and tissue signals matter too. But the genetic trigger is SRY (sex-determining region of the Y), which makes TDF . TDF switches on a cascade of genes that builds a testis. No TDF → the default female pattern. From the lecture.

entries.t: The Urogenital Ridge and the Gonad
entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: The Urogenital Ridge and the Gonad Week 5. Intermediate mesoderm bulges into the urogenital ridge beside the aorta. It splits into the nephrogenic cord (kidneys) and the gonadal ridge (gonads). Urinary and genital systems grow up side by side. The gonadal ridge = thickened epithelium plus mesoderm on the medial side of the mesonephros (the temporary middle kidney). Weeks 4–6: the germ cells arrive. Primordial germ cells start in the wall of the yolk sac and crawl along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut to the gonadal ridges. No migration = no gonad : nothing else can develop without them. Meanwhile the ridge epithelium pushes finger-like primary sex cords into the mesoderm. This is the indifferent gonad , and you cannot tell a male from a female one. From the lecture.

entries.t: Two Pairs of Ducts in Everyone
entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: Two Pairs of Ducts in Everyone Week 7: both sets are present. Mesonephric (Wolffian) duct (red): part of the mesonephric kidney; becomes the male tract, fades in females. Paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct (blue): an infolded tube of epithelium; becomes the female tract, fades in males. From the lecture. Duct Kept by Removed by Female fate Mesonephric (Wolffian) Testosterone No testosterone Degenerates , leaving small remnants Paramesonephric (Müllerian) No AMH Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) Develops : tubes, uterus, cervix, upper vagina The female pattern needs the absence of two male signals: no testosterone and no AMH. That is why a problem in making or sensing those hormones shows up as a disorder of sex development in 3.9 .

entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: The Ovary Week 7 without TDF: the primary sex cords degenerate , and the surface epithelium makes new cortical cords instead. Germ cells → oogonia → (mitosis) → primary oocytes . Cortical cord cells wrap each one as follicular cells : a primordial follicle . Primary sex cords break down (in a male they would become testis cords). Surface epithelium keeps growing between the germ cells: cortical cords . Germ cells become oogonia , which divide by mitosis into primary oocytes . Cortical cord cells surround each oocyte as follicular cells . Oocyte + follicular cells = primordial follicle . The Big Difference From Males Primary oocytes arrest in prophase of meiosis I and stay there until shortly before ovulation, which can be 50 years later. No new oogonia form after birth , so the supply is fixed. Males make new sperm continuously from puberty onward. Watch the numbers between lectures. This lecture says the ovaries hold about 400,000 primordial follicles at birth . The physiology lecture's graph ( 3.3 ) shows about 2 million at birth, falling to about 400,000 by puberty , and most textbooks agree with it. The concept both lectures share: a fixed, shrinking supply with no new eggs after birth . If a question quotes a number, match it to the lecture it came from.

entries.t: What's Left of the Mesonephric (Wolffian) Duct
entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: What's Left of the Mesonephric (Wolffian) Duct No TDF (so no testosterone): the mesonephric duct and tubules fade , leaving three non-functioning remnants. They can fill with fluid and become cysts , like the Gartner's cyst on the ultrasound. From the lecture. Remnant What it would have been in a male Where it sits Epoophoron Efferent ductules and duct of the epididymis In the mesovarium Paroophoron Leftover mesonephric tubules In the mesovarium, closer to the uterus Gartner's duct Ductus deferens and ejaculatory duct Along the side wall of the uterus (in the mesometrium) and in the vaginal wall Clinical: these cysts are usually asymptomatic . When they aren't, they can cause infection, bladder dysfunction, abdominal pain, vaginal discharge or urinary incontinence. For example, an inflamed Gartner's duct cyst can press on the bladder neck .

entries.t: The Paramesonephric (Müllerian) Ducts Build the Tract
entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: The Paramesonephric (Müllerian) Ducts Build the Tract No AMH, so the ducts grow. Top ends stay separate and open into the abdomen: uterine tubes and fimbriae . Bottom ends fuse into the uterovaginal primordium : uterus, cervix and upper 1/3 of the vagina . Building the vagina. The fused ducts touch the urogenital sinus , which then sprouts the sinovaginal bulbs . These fuse into a solid vaginal plate that later hollows out. The uterine septum between the two fused ducts regresses , leaving one cavity. Step Result If it fails Cranial ends stay separate and open Uterine tubes with fimbriae — Caudal ends fuse Uterovaginal primordium → uterus, cervix, upper 1/3 vagina Bicornuate or didelphys uterus The septum between them regresses One uterine cavity Septate uterus Uterovaginal primordium contacts the UG sinus → sinovaginal bulbs → vaginal plate Lower 2/3 of the vagina — The plate's centre breaks down ( canalization ) Vaginal lumen Transverse vaginal septum The thin plate at the bottom perforates The hymen , usually open around birth Imperforate hymen

entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: Descent of the Ovaries The ovaries start on the posterior abdominal wall. As the embryo lengthens, the gubernaculum tethers them and they "descend" into the pelvis, but, unlike testes, not into the inguinal canal . Their nerves, arteries and lymph keep their high origin. The middle of the gubernaculum sticks to the uterus near the tube and splits it into the ligament of the ovary (above) and the round ligament of the uterus (below). From the lecture. Round ligament route: uterus → deep inguinal ring → inguinal canal → superficial ring → labia majora (the scrotum homologue). It is the same path the testis takes. High origin explains the adult anatomy in 3.6 : the ovarian artery comes off the aorta , and ovarian lymph drains to lumbar/pre-aortic nodes .

entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: The External Genitalia First, a note on age Term Counts from Used by Embryonic age Conception Embryology (this lecture) Gestational age First day of the last menstrual period Clinicians and ultrasound Conception is usually about 2 weeks after the period starts, so gestational age = embryonic age + 2 weeks . Weeks 4–7: both sexes look identical. About 12 weeks (embryonic): distinctly male or female. Ultrasound: sex can usually be called from 14 weeks gestational (12 embryonic), but sonographers prefer to wait for the 18–20-week anatomy scan to be sure. Indifferent stage (weeks 4–7): mesoderm around the cloacal membrane forms the genital tubercle (front; lengthens into a phallus in both sexes), the urethral (urogenital) folds either side of the urethral groove, and the labioscrotal swellings outside them. At 10 weeks the sexes still look alike. Female (estrogen, no DHT): genital tubercle → clitoris · urethral folds → labia minora · labioscrotal swellings → labia majora . The urogenital membrane breaks down around week 7 to open the vestibule . Indifferent structure Female Male Genital tubercle Clitoris (grows only a little) Penis (grows a lot) Urethral folds Labia minora : stay separate Fuse ("zip up") in the midline to enclose the penile urethra; the seam is the raphe Labioscrotal swellings Labia majora Scrotum Gubernaculum Ligament of the ovary + round ligament Pulls the testis into the scrotum

entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: Müllerian (Uterine) Anomalies The lecture's fill-in-the-blank slide; the answers are in the table below. Top left: HSG of a bicornuate uterus. Top right: septate and partially septate uteri. Bottom: uterus didelphys (two cannulas on the HSG) and a double vagina. The unicornuate uterus (one horn, one tube) is the other HSG from the knowledge check. From the lecture. Anomaly Failure of What you see Bicornuate uterus Complete fusion : caudal parts fuse, cranial parts don't Two horns, heart shape , each with its own fundus Septate uterus The septum to regress (complete or partial) One outer shape, a wall inside. Less heart-shaped on HSG because the two cavities sit close together Uterus didelphys Fusion at all : the ducts develop independently Two uteri, two cervices , one tube and ovary each (often one uterus is bigger). If the sinovaginal bulbs also form separately: a double vagina Unicornuate uterus One duct to develop at all One horn and one tube ; the tube can be patent Bicornuate and septate uteri are both linked to preterm birth. They look alike on HSG, which only shows the inside of the cavity; the outer contour (heart-shaped or not) is what separates them.

entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: Obstruction: Hematometrocolpos The MRI (lower left) shows hematometrocolpos : the uterus and vagina are distended with blood or fluid of intermediate density, pushing the bladder forward against the abdominal wall, with gassy rectum behind. The blanks are for its two causes, below. The hymen drawings show how varied a normal hymen is. From the lecture. Cause Failure of Where Transverse vaginal septum Canalization of the vaginal plate Usually at the junction of the upper 1/3 and lower 2/3 , where the uterovaginal primordium meets the part from the UG sinus Imperforate hymen The bottom of the vaginal plate to perforate The vaginal opening. The most common obstructive anomaly of the female tract Both cause vaginal atresia : the outflow tract is blocked, so menstrual blood has nowhere to go. It collects in the vagina ( colpos ) and uterus ( metra ): hemato-metro-colpos . Normal hymens vary a lot, from a small to a large opening, and usually perforate soon after birth.

entries.t: Why Do Reproductive and Urinary Defects Travel Together?
entries.p: Development of the Female Reproductive Tract
entries.x: Why Do Reproductive and Urinary Defects Travel Together? The lecture's closing question. It isn't answered in the recording; the answer is in the box. The Answer: One Duct Does Two Jobs Both systems come from the same intermediate mesoderm and grow side by side in the urogenital ridge. More specifically, the mesonephric duct sprouts the ureteric bud , which becomes the ureter and collecting system of the kidney, and it also guides the paramesonephric duct as it grows down beside it. So one faulty mesonephric duct can cost the kidney on that side and derail the Müllerian duct next to it. Renal anomalies turn up in a large share of Müllerian anomalies; renal agenesis is especially common with uterus didelphys and with a unicornuate uterus . So when you find one of these anomalies, image the kidneys . Added from outside the lecture: StatPearls, "Embryology, Wolffian Ducts"; Li et al., 2000 (renal agenesis in about 30% of Müllerian anomalies, most often with didelphys).

Learning Objectives Describe normal growth during childhood. Identify normal variants of growth in childhood. Recognize common general pediatric causes of short stature. Identify the most common endocrine causes of short stature. Identify common genetic causes of short stature. Describe the clinical features and complications of Turner syndrome. This is Dr. Gallego's second lecture of the week. The first, 3.4 Abnormalities of Puberty , already covers Turner syndrome as a cause of delayed puberty. This lecture looks at Turner as a cause of short stature. The GH axis itself is on the pituitary page , from the "too much GH" side.

Normal Growth: Three Phases Phase What drives it How fast Infancy Mostly nutrition . Thyroid hormone and bone metabolism help Fastest : about 24 cm in year 1, then 10 cm in year 2 Childhood Growth hormone is the main driver. Thyroid hormone and nutrition still matter Slow but steady: about 5–6 cm/yr (4.5–6 cm/yr from age 4 to 10). The longer this phase lasts, the taller the final height Puberty Sex steroids plus bigger, more frequent GH pulses The growth spurt: girls 8–12 cm/yr, boys 10–14 cm/yr Growth velocity by age. Remember 24 → 10 → 7–8 → 4.5–6 cm/yr. Boys have the bigger spurt. From the lecture. Measure it right. Over 2 years: standing height on a stadiometer, barefoot, heels to the board, head in the Frankfurt plane. Under 2: lying length on a measuring board. Use the age- and sex-specific chart.

entries.t: How to Evaluate Growth: Four Questions
entries.x: How to Evaluate Growth: Four Questions 1 What is the genetic potential? Calculate the mid-parental height . 2 What is the height age The age at which this child's height would sit on the 50th percentile. A 9-year-old who is as tall as an average 8-year-old has a height age of 8. The shorter the child, the younger the height age. ? 3 What is the growth velocity? This needs accurate measurements at least 1 year apart , plotted on the right chart. 4 What is the growth potential? Check the bone age A single X-ray of the left hand and wrist, compared against reference images. It shows how mature the skeleton is, and so how much growing is left before the growth plates close. . Mid-parental height The formula. The 13 cm is the average adult height difference between men and women. Add it for a boy, subtract it for a girl. The lecture's example, for a girl: mom 160 cm, dad 185 cm. (160 + 185 − 13) ÷ 2 = 166 cm . Mark it at the adult end of the chart and see whether her curve is heading there. Dr. Gallego's own warning: many referrals for short stature are children growing exactly where their parents' heights say they should. Calculate the mid-parental height before you refer. Height age and bone age Height age. Slide the child's height across to the 50th percentile line and read off the age. The lecture's 9-year-old has a height age of 8. Bone age. One X-ray of the left hand and wrist. Normal is within ± 1 year of the real age. The table on the slide is worth learning (below). Bone age Think of Why Delayed Constitutional delay, poor nutrition, chronic disease, GH deficiency (and hypothyroidism) The whole child is running on a slower clock, so growth is still "available" Normal Familial short stature , Turner syndrome The skeleton is maturing on time; the child is just built small Advanced Precocious puberty , hyperthyroidism Sex steroids (with GH) push the growth plates to mature, and close, early

When Should You Worry? Red flag Cut-off from the lecture Low growth velocity From age 4 to puberty: less than 4.5 cm/yr Crossing percentiles Crossing lines on the chart after 18 months and before puberty . Crossing is normal in the first 18 months, and upward crossing is expected in the pubertal spurt Far below genetic potential More than 2 SD below the mid-parental height Short stature (the definition) Height 2 SD or more below the mean , i.e. below the 3rd percentile The whole lecture in one slide. The first split is growth velocity . A normal growth velocity means one of the two normal variants, which are the most common causes of short stature. An abnormal growth velocity means a disease: intrauterine, nutritional, chronic illness, genetic or endocrine. From the lecture.

entries.t: Familial Short Stature vs Constitutional Delay
entries.x: Familial Short Stature vs Constitutional Delay Familial short stature (FSS) Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) Height At or below the 3rd percentile At or below the 3rd percentile (weight too) Growth velocity Normal (maybe low-normal) Normal (maybe low-normal) Puberty On time Late Bone age = chronological age Delayed , closer to the height age Family Short parents : the child tracks their target A parent who was a late bloomer Final height Short, but on the parental target Normal: they catch up late FSS: the child runs along the 3rd percentile, parallel to the lines, straight into a low parental target. Bone age matches the real age. CDGP: low all through childhood, then a late spurt carries the child up toward the normal range. The bone age is delayed, so the growing time is still there. The one-line test: bone age . On time means familial short stature. Delayed means constitutional delay. The delayed-puberty side of CDGP is covered in 3.4 .

entries.t: Small for Gestational Age, Nutrition and Chronic Illness
entries.x: Small for Gestational Age, Nutrition and Chronic Illness Cause Key points SGA Small for gestational age: born smaller than expected for how many weeks along the pregnancy was. The lecture calls it intrauterine growth restriction. (intrauterine) Ask about maternal infection, smoking, alcohol, systemic illness (e.g. type 1 diabetes), fetal malnutrition, placental insufficiency. Most SGA babies catch up by age 2. About 10% do not . That is a pathological growth pattern and an indication for GH Not enough in Mechanical problems ( cleft palate ), psychosocial deprivation, eating disorders Not absorbed Celiac disease , Crohn's disease , liver or pancreatic disease, lactose intolerance Chronic illness Chronic kidney disease , rheumatologic disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease , cystic fibrosis , asthma, malignancy, immunologic disease

Genetic Syndromes and Skeletal Dysplasias Down syndrome and Prader–Willi syndrome . PWS has two phases: a floppy, poorly feeding baby who fails to thrive, then hyperphagia and severe obesity from about age 3–5 . Noonan (think pulmonary stenosis ), Silver–Russell (severe IUGR, triangular face, big forehead), and SHOX (short forearms and shins, Madelung deformity of the wrist). Condition Remember it by Prader–Willi Microdeletion of chromosome 15 . Floppy infant with feeding trouble and FTT → hyperphagia and obesity by age 3–5. An approved GH indication Noonan Short stature + pulmonary stenosis + delayed speech/motor milestones Silver–Russell Severe IUGR and postnatal growth failure; triangular face, prominent forehead SHOX mutation Gene on the X chromosome . Short forearms and lower legs; Madelung deformity Turner syndrome One of the most common referrals for a short girl. Part 4 Skeletal dysplasias make the child disproportionate (short limbs compared with the trunk), which the other causes don't. Achondroplasia and hypochondroplasia: FGFR3. Osteogenesis imperfecta: type 1 collagen (COL1A1/COL1A2, usually dominant), with fractures, blue sclerae , easy bruising and deafness. From the lecture.

Growth Hormone Deficiency The most common endocrine cause of short stature. About 1 in 3,500–4,000 children. Caused by too little GHRH (hypothalamus) or a pituitary problem. It can be isolated or come with other pituitary hormone deficiencies . The GH axis. GHRH → GH → liver makes IGF-1 (and its binding proteins) → IGF-1 makes the growth plate grow. Most of GH's growth effect goes through IGF-1 ; only a little is direct. Where the gene breaks decides which hormones go. PIT-1 defect: lose somatotropes, lactotropes and thyrotropes, so GH + TSH + prolactin deficiency. PROP-1 sits upstream, so it also takes out the gonadotropins . Scully et al., 2002, from the lecture. Causes Type Examples Genetic Mutations in GHRH, GH-1, PIT-1, PROP-1 · GH receptor defect = GH insensitivity (Laron syndrome) · IGF-1 gene deletions or mutations · IGF-1 receptor defects · growth plate disorders Congenital structural Ectopic or hypoplastic pituitary . Usually with midline defects and multiple pituitary deficiencies Acquired Sellar/parasellar tumours (e.g. craniopharyngioma ) · cranial irradiation · head injury What congenital GH deficiency looks like When Finding At birth Normal birth weight and length . Growth in the womb depends on maternal nutrition, not GH Newborn Neonatal hypoglycemia · prolonged jaundice (especially with TSH or ACTH deficiency too) · micropenis (especially if gonadotropins are also low) After birth Severe postnatal growth failure Face and head Poorly developed nasal bridge, prominent forehead · midline defects (high or cleft palate) · irregular, late teeth · late closure of the anterior fontanelle · high-pitched voice Other Thin hair, poor nail growth Why a Newborn With No GH Gets Hypoglycemic GH and cortisol are both counter-regulatory hormones : they raise blood sugar between feeds. A newborn without GH (and often without ACTH as well, when several pituitary hormones are missing) cannot defend their glucose. That is why the lecture pairs neonatal hypoglycemia with micropenis and prolonged jaundice : together they point to the pituitary in a baby who looks normal-sized at birth. The adrenal side of this is on the adrenal page . Testing for GH deficiency A random GH is worthless. GH comes in pulses (the graph), so a low value may just be between pulses. Use IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 as the screen and provocative tests (arginine, clonidine, glucagon) to confirm. No insulin tolerance test in children : severe hypoglycemia, seizures, even deaths. The four criteria: he

Other Endocrine Causes Hypothyroidism: the lecture's case A 12-year-old girl : her height velocity has dropped, but her weight has held on the 50th percentile. She has very dry skin, fatigue, hair loss and brittle hair and nails . TSH 467 mU/L (normal 0.35–5.55): primary hypothyroidism . Slow growth with weight gain is the endocrine pattern. Also: puffy face, goiter, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, brittle hair, fatigue and a delayed bone age . Treat the thyroid and growth recovers. From the lecture; the thyroid work-up itself is in 2.1 . Too much glucocorticoid: growth stops while weight piles on (central obesity, buffalo hump, striae, hirsutism, acne). In children, true Cushing syndrome is rare. The usual cause is steroid therapy for another illness. Rickets (vitamin D deficiency or hypophosphatemic): poor growth, bowed legs. Pseudohypoparathyroidism : PTH resistance , short and obese, round face, short 4th/5th metacarpals ( "knuckle-knuckle-dimple-dimple" , Archibald's sign). More on it in 2.2 . A slip in the recording: on the audio, pseudohypoparathyroidism is described as resistance "to thyroid hormone". The slide is right: it is resistance to parathyroid hormone .

entries.t: Read the Weight Line: The Take-Home Pattern
entries.x: Read the Weight Line: The Take-Home Pattern Left, nutrition or chronic illness: the weight falls first , and height drifts down gradually after it. Right, endocrine: the weight line keeps going while height falls off sharply , so the child is relatively chubby . Look at the two lines together and you often know the category before any blood test. From the lecture. Drawn for these notes from the lecture's summary slides, which list the history, exam and investigations but don't lay out the decision. The first branch is growth velocity. The second is the weight line from the take-home slide above. The bottom row applies to every child, whichever branch they end up in.

Turner Syndrome and Growth All or part of one X is missing. 45,X in 60% · mosaic in 15% · structural X changes in 10% · other 15%. About 1 in 2,000–2,500 newborn girls. Short stature in 95–100%: the most common feature. Untreated, about 20 cm shorter than expected; mean final height 144 cm (132–154). Why they're short: some make normal GH but the bone doesn't respond properly (a mild skeletal dysplasia). Others have low GH and bone resistance . Many girls are referred for short stature alone , with none of the classic dysmorphic features. So: karyotype any short girl . Fewer, smaller GH pulses in Turner girls (left) than in controls (right), at each bone age. That is the GH-deficiency part of the story. GH treatment in Turner Approved in Canada. Start as soon as growth failure shows , often around age 4–6 . Gain: about 5–7 cm of adult height over about 8 years of treatment. Taller parents, better response. Dose: 0.35–0.375 mg/kg/week , roughly double the GH-deficiency dose.

The Rest of Turner Syndrome System Features Ovaries Complete gonadal failure in 90% (streak ovaries). Thelarche 10–15%, menarche 1% (usually mosaics), pubarche 100% (the adrenals are normal), infertility > 99% . Most need estrogen replacement to go through puberty Dysmorphic Neck webbing , short 4th metacarpals, increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus), nail dysplasia Heart Congenital heart disease, especially coarctation of the aorta Kidney Renal anomalies, e.g. horseshoe kidney Autoimmune Thyroid disease (about 10%) , type 1 diabetes, celiac disease Metabolic Metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes later Other Hearing problems · learning difficulties (non-verbal, arithmetic, visuospatial) · more ADHD Newborn Lymphedema of the hands and feet (the lymphatics are underdeveloped before birth; it improves over months), hypoplastic nails, webbed neck How Turner shows up depends on age. Newborn: dysmorphic features, heart or kidney anomaly. Child: short stature (± hypothyroidism). Teen: no or incomplete puberty, primary amenorrhea . The puberty side is in 3.4 . From the lecture.

entries.t: Putting It Together: Evaluating a Short Child
entries.x: Putting It Together: Evaluating a Short Child History and exam. The neonatal history matters (SGA, hypoglycemia, jaundice), and so do the parents' heights and pubertal timing. On exam: plot it, stage puberty, look for chronic illness, endocrine signs, dysmorphism and midline defects. Investigations. First rule out general causes: CBC, ESR, renal panel, albumin, Ca, PO 4 , celiac screen (tTG) . Then TSH and a bone age . Consider a karyotype (always in short girls) , IGF-1, and GH stimulation tests (specialist). Accurate measurement, plotted on a growth chart. Mid-parental height , from the parents' heights. Bone age to judge the growth potential. Look for general causes first (chronic illness). Endocrine causes are rare , and the child is usually small and "chubby, or at least not thin".
