Learning Objectives Recognise the clinical presentation of, describe the main diagnostic steps for, and globally discuss the management of anterior pituitary insufficiency . Recognise and describe the signs and symptoms of pituitary hormone overproduction . Describe the initial screening test for overproduction of each pituitary hormone. The lecturer's own framing is worth keeping in view: the case results and cut-off levels are illustration . What is expected is that you recognise the clinical picture and can do the initial screening — as a family physician would — not that you memorise reference ranges.

The Axes, Briefly The pituitary is not an autonomous gland. Almost everything it does is dictated from above by hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting factors delivered down the portal system, and checked from below by negative feedback from the target organ. Six hypothalamic signals, six anterior pituitary outputs. Note the one that is different: dopamine and somatostatin are inhibitory . Everything else is a releasing hormone that switches its target on; prolactin is held down by dopamine , and that single inversion explains why a stalk lesion raises prolactin while lowering everything else, and why a dopamine agonist treats a prolactinoma. The approach in one slide. Two columns of questions, asked of every pituitary patient. Note the bracket on the right: the first five deficiencies are anterior pituitary; diabetes insipidus — now called AVP deficiency — is posterior , which is why it can be present or absent independently of everything else.

entries.t: The Case, and What to Ask
entries.x: The Case, and What to Ask 53-year-old man, pituitary mass found on CT for headaches History: headache 6 months · blurring vision 3 weeks · 3 episodes of nausea and vomiting in the last 3 months · weight down 15 lb · cold intolerance. On direct questioning: decreased shaving, loss of libido. No medications, no alcohol, stopped smoking 6 months ago. Examination: 59.6 kg, 174 cm, BP 116/78, HR 62. Lean, with loss of muscle mass. Visual field defect. Minimal androgenic hair, dry skin, fine freckling around the eyes. Notice What Only Turned Up "On Asking" The patient volunteered headache and blurred vision — the mass symptoms. He did not volunteer decreased shaving or loss of libido, and those are the two that establish hypogonadism. Weight loss and cold intolerance were mentioned but easy to attribute elsewhere. This is the practical reason the lecture insists on a systematic approach: you have to go down the list of axes and ask about each one, because the endocrine symptoms are non-specific, gradual, and not what brought the patient in.

Mass Effect: The Visual Fields The optic chiasm sits directly above the pituitary. The fibres crossing in it are the nasal retinal fibres from each eye — and the nasal retina sees the temporal field. Compress the chiasm from below and you knock out both temporal fields: bitemporal hemianopia . Dysfunction of the nasal fibres of the optic nerve causes a temporal field defect. A bitemporal defect points to chiasmal compression (D) — often a pituitary adenoma. Worth drawing the fields for lesions A–C yourself. What it is actually like to have one. The full view above, the bitemporal defect below — which buildings do you miss, and which city? Patients lose the periphery on both sides and often do not notice until they walk into something. The other mass effects on the list: diplopia (lateral extension into the cavernous sinus, catching cranial nerves III, IV and VI), headaches , and pituitary apoplexy — haemorrhage into the gland, which is an emergency.

entries.t: Working Through the Axes One at a Time
entries.x: Working Through the Axes One at a Time Assess the patient by assessing each individual pituitary–target organ axis . For each: what would the deficiency look like, and what does the axis diagram predict the labs will show? 1 — Pituitary–adrenal insufficiency CRH → ACTH → cortisol. In a pituitary lesion, ACTH is low or inappropriately normal and cortisol is low. Symptoms: lassitude · weight loss · fatigue · anorexia · hypoglycaemia · decreased libido · hypotension. Note what is absent compared with primary adrenal failure: no hyperpigmentation and no hyperkalemia, because ACTH is low rather than high and aldosterone is preserved. See primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency . 2 — Pituitary–thyroid insufficiency Note the label on the TSH: "normal" or ↓ . That is the whole trap of central hypothyroidism, spelled out on the axis diagram. Symptoms: fatigue · cold intolerance · decreased appetite · constipation · dry skin · bradycardia. Our patient had cold intolerance, dry skin and a heart rate of 62 — all present, all easy to dismiss individually. 3 — Pituitary–gonadal insufficiency Same trap again: LH and FSH are "normal" or ↓ against a frankly low testosterone. Low sex steroid with unraised gonadotrophins is the abnormality. In men: infertility · decreased energy · decreased libido · hot flashes · decreased bone mineral density. In women: ovarian insufficiency · irregular or absent periods · hot flashes · vaginal atrophy. The axis itself is covered in detail in 2.6, the HPG axis . 4 — Growth hormone deficiency (adult) GHRH stimulates, somatostatin (SRIF) inhibits , GH acts largely through IGF-1 made in the liver. Because GH is pulsatile and IGF-1 is stable, IGF-1 is the practical measurement — which matters again in acromegaly below. Features in adults: changed body composition (increased fat mass, decreased lean mass) · decreased exercise capacity · impaired psychological function · increased mortality. The lecture notes there is still some discussion about these effects — adult GH deficiency is the least clear-cut item on the list, which is also why its replacement is a delayed decision. And the remaining two: prolactin deficiency (bracketed on the slide, because it is rarely clinically important outside lactation) and diabetes insipidus / AVP deficiency , which is posterior pituitary.

entries.t: The Labs — and the Trap in Them
entries.x: The Labs — and the Trap in Them The single most important line on the page. Free T4 is 5 against a floor of 10 — unambiguously low. The TSH is 4.11, comfortably inside its range. A healthy pituitary facing a free T4 of 5 would be producing a TSH in the tens. A "normal" number here is a failure to respond. The whole panel, 8–9 AM fasting Parameter Result Reference range Read as Cortisol 80 119–618 nmol/L Low — adrenal axis failed TSH 4.11 0.27–4.2 mIU/L Inappropriately normal Free T4 5 10–24 pmol/L Low — this is what makes the diagnosis Free T3 2.1–3.6 3–6.5 pmol/L Low or low-normal LH 1.5 1.5–9.0 IU/L Bottom of range — inappropriately so FSH 2.4 1.0–18.0 IU/L Inappropriately unraised Testosterone 1.2 9.1–55 nmol/L Profoundly low — gonadal axis failed Prolactin 15 2–18 µg/L Normal Growth hormone 0.1 0.01–0.61 µg/L Uninterpretable alone — GH is pulsatile IGF-1 79 115–307 µg/L Low — the usable GH measure Why TSH Fails in Secondary Disease — the Rule Behind the Trap In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid is broken and the pituitary is intact. The pituitary sees the low T4 and shouts — TSH goes up. That is why TSH is such a good screening test, and why it can be used alone. In secondary hypothyroidism the pituitary is the broken part. It cannot shout. TSH comes back low, or normal, or even mildly raised (a bioinactive form is sometimes released) — but never appropriately high. So in pituitary disease you must measure free T4 , and you interpret it directly rather than through the TSH. The same logic applies right down the panel. A gonadotrophin at the bottom of its range next to a testosterone of 1.2 is not "normal", it is inappropriate. Every axis in central disease shows the same signature: a low target hormone with an unraised trophic hormone. Primary on the left, secondary on the right, with the negative-feedback limb in red. Same low T3/T4 in both; the TSH is what separates them — ↑ in primary, ↓/normal/mildly ↑ in secondary . Clemens and van Uum, Can Fam Physician 2011. When a baseline level is not enough Axis Stimulation test needed? Cortisol Often — insulin tolerance test, ACTH (cosyntropin) test, CRH test Growth hormone Often — insulin tolerance test, glucagon Thyroid Not required Gonadal Usually not required Prolactin Not required Cortisol < 100 nmol/L confirms insufficiency; > 450 confirms sufficient function. Our patient's 80 is diagnostic without further testing. A "normal" baseline does not indicate an appropriate response to stress. A cortisol of

Cause, Imaging and Treatment Pituitary disease Hypothalamic disease Mass lesions · surgery/radiation · infiltrative diseases · infarction · genetic · empty sella syndrome Mass lesions · radiation · infiltrative diseases · trauma · infections Not a list to know in detail — but the last item on the lecture's key points is "important not to forget to look for the cause." Replacing hormones without imaging the sella treats the consequence and ignores the lesion. Imaging: in this patient, MRI showed a sellar/suprasellar mass elevating and compressing the optic chiasm and perhaps the proximal optic nerves; formal fields confirmed a subtle bitemporal hemianopia. MRI is superior to CT for the pituitary — the mass here was only found on CT incidentally. Replacement Deficiency Replacement Pituitary–adrenal insufficiency Cortisol — and the patient must be educated about stress dosing Hypothyroidism Levothyroxine — dosed and monitored on free thyroid hormone levels , not TSH Hypogonadism Testosterone — noting that testosterone itself does not restore fertility Growth hormone A delayed decision Treat the Adrenal Axis Before the Thyroid — Every Time This is the single most dangerous ordering error in the lecture. Give levothyroxine first to a patient who also has untreated adrenal insufficiency and you can precipitate an adrenal crisis. The mechanism: thyroid hormone raises the basal metabolic rate and accelerates the hepatic clearance of cortisol. In someone whose adrenal reserve is already gone, you have simultaneously increased the demand for cortisol and increased its disposal, against a supply that cannot rise. Hypothyroidism, by slowing everything down, had been partially protecting them. So: glucocorticoid first, thyroid hormone second. If you are unsure whether the adrenal axis is intact and cannot wait for the result, cover with steroid and sort it out afterwards. Details of crisis management are in the adrenal lecture . Key points Pituitary insufficiency can present at any age . It does not have to affect all hormones equally, and can be partial . Clinical recognition is the first step — you have to enquire about each hormone. Stimulation tests are often required , and deficiencies usually need treating. Do not forget to look for the cause.

Recognising It, and Proving It 26-year-old respiratory therapist, referred for possible Cushing Weight: a continuous problem from age 11; 250 lb in high school, down to 215 lb with diet and exercise, then a further gain of 10 lb after starting metformin. Over the last year: hair growth on chin, jaw, chest and lower abdomen, now shaving daily and lasering every 4–6 weeks, with no improvement on spironolactone . Increased hunger and appetite, sweats and hot flushes, puffy face, easy bruising for 5 months , easy fatigue, muscle pain and weakness — difficulty going up stairs or standing from a chair , pink striae for a year. Examination: puffy face, BP 140/90 supine and 150/100 standing, 104.5 kg with BMI 36, hirsutism and acne, pink and white abdominal striae, decreased contours of the proximal leg muscles, failed squatting test . Medications: metformin, spironolactone, an oral contraceptive. Family history: diabetes; a sister and mother with hirsutism and possible PCOS. What in That Story Actually Points at Cushing Almost all of it could be PCOS with obesity — which is exactly what the family history invites you to think. The features that carry real weight are the ones with the high likelihood ratios : ecchymoses (LR 10–11.3) , osteopenia or fracture (8–13.8) , and proximal muscle weakness (8–12.6) . Hypertension is 4.35–5.29; striae 2.72–2.91; hirsutism 2.21–2.90; and general obesity is 1.75–3.10 — near the bottom . So the discriminating findings here are the easy bruising and the failed squat , not the weight. That is why the squatting test is done: it is a bedside test of proximal myopathy, and proximal myopathy is one of the few things that separates Cushing from ordinary obesity. Spironolactone is worth noting too — it is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that also blocks several other steroid hormone receptors, which is why it is used for hirsutism. Its failure here is a small piece of evidence that the androgen excess has a bigger driver behind it. Screening: three tests, three principles Test Principle 24-hour urine cortisol Cortisol overproduction 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression Lack of normal suppression of ACTH/cortisol by steroids 11 PM / midnight plasma or salivary cortisol Lack of the normal diurnal rhythm No test has 100% sensitivity or specificity — which is why the diagnosis rests on more than one. The 1 mg DST: dexamethasone suppresses ACTH and cortisol but is not picked up by the cortisol assay. 1 mg orally at 11 PM, plasma

entries.t: Then: Where Is It Coming From?
entries.x: Then: Where Is It Coming From? Step 1 is diagnosing Cushing syndrome. Step 2 is the cause — and the branch point is a single measurement. Pituitary ACTH overproduction: ACTH up, cortisol up, CRH suppressed by the cortisol the tumour is driving. The adenoma ignores the feedback; the hypothalamus does not. ACTH result Category Causes Suppressed (normal 1.9–12 pmol/L) ACTH-independent Adrenal — adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma Normal or raised ACTH-dependent Pituitary (Cushing disease ) · ectopic ACTH production · rarely ectopic CRH Ectopic ACTH usually produces a higher ACTH than Cushing disease does — but the ranges overlap , so the number alone does not settle it. In this patient the ACTH of 46.5 against a range of 2–12 is unambiguously ACTH-dependent. All the routes to the same syndrome. The commonest cause overall remains exogenous glucocorticoid — the one arm of the diagram with no tumour in it. Among endogenous causes, a pituitary corticotroph adenoma dominates. Always ask about steroids first, then think adrenal, then pituitary. Pseudo-Cushing States Conditions with many features of Cushing syndrome that are not Cushing syndrome — hypothesised to be driven by increased neuronal CRH production. A heterogeneous group: chronic alcoholism · alcohol withdrawal · major depression · poorly controlled diabetes · obesity . This is the practical reason the 1–4× ULN urine cortisol band is ambiguous: pseudo-Cushing lives there. Above 4× ULN you are out of that territory. Imaging — and why a scan alone is not proof In 10% of healthy people a non-functioning adenoma is present on MRI or CT. A pituitary lesion on a scan is not, by itself, the answer. In Cushing disease, 80–90% are microadenomas , and in 40% nothing is visible on CT or MRI at all. CT: sensitivity 47%, specificity 74%. MRI: sensitivity 50–60%, specificity 75–98% — and more useful to the neurosurgeon. In this patient MRI raised suspicion of a 6 × 7 mm microadenoma on the right, possibly extending to the cavernous sinus. The conclusion drawn was measured: Cushing syndrome confirmed, ACTH-dependent, likely pituitary — with an incidentaloma not entirely excluded. Treatment and what happened Ketoconazole was started to reduce endogenous cortisol production while urgent transsphenoidal surgery was arranged. The tumour was far lateral, clearly visible, white and very soft, and was removed without bleeding complications. Steroids were started post-operatively — because removing the source of a long-standing co

entries.t: Prolactin: The Hormone Held Down, Not Driven Up
entries.x: Prolactin: The Hormone Held Down, Not Driven Up Made by lactotroph cells , distributed throughout the pars distalis of the pituitary. Normal < 25 µg/L in adults, and usually < 15 in men . Dopamine stimulates the D2 receptor → inhibits adenylyl cyclase → inhibits prolactin synthesis and secretion. The default state of a lactotroph is to secrete; the hypothalamus spends its time suppressing it. TRH stimulates prolactin release, and prolactin acts on the breast to increase secretory cell differentiation and milk production . Lactotroph hyperplasia occurs in pregnancy, with estrogen treatment (estrogen drives PRL gene expression), in some cases of Cushing disease, and in primary hypothyroidism . Note the red inhibitory arrow: dopamine is the brake. Everything that raises prolactin pathologically does so either by making more of it or by cutting the brake line — and that second mechanism is why a stalk lesion, or a dopamine-antagonist drug, produces hyperprolactinemia. Two Consequences of Dopamine Being Inhibitory Stalk section raises prolactin while lowering everything else. Cut or compress the pituitary stalk and every releasing hormone fails to arrive — so LH, FSH, TSH, ACTH and GH all fall. But dopamine also fails to arrive, and dopamine was the brake , so prolactin rises . A modestly raised prolactin alongside multiple deficiencies points at the stalk, not at a prolactinoma. Primary hypothyroidism raises prolactin , because the low T4 drives TRH up — and TRH stimulates lactotrophs as well as thyrotrophs. Which is why a TSH belongs in the work-up of any raised prolactin: treating the thyroid may fix the prolactin.

Prolactinomas and What They Do Most common in women, peaking in the childbearing years. In women, 95% are microadenomas (< 10 mm). Macroadenomas (> 10 mm) are more frequent in men — and those are the ones large enough to reach the optic chiasm. In both sexes: visual disturbance and headache, plus problems from the decrease of other pituitary hormones as the tumour compresses the rest of the gland. In premenopausal women Feature Detail Hypogonadism Oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea Galactorrhea 30–70% Infertility A frequent presenting complaint Defining the Terms Amenorrhea is the absence of menstrual periods . It is primary when menarche has never occurred — conventionally by age 15, or by 13 with no secondary sexual characteristics — and secondary when periods stop in someone who was previously menstruating, defined as no period for at least 3 months if cycles had been regular, or 6 months if they were irregular. Hyperprolactinemia causes the secondary form. Oligomenorrhea is the milder version: infrequent periods — cycles longer than about 35 days, or fewer than nine periods a year. Prolactin produces oligomenorrhea before it produces amenorrhea, which is why the degree of elevation tracks the severity of the menstrual disturbance. How useful is prolactin as a test in these presentations? Of patients with amenorrhea, 10–20% have hyperprolactinemia once pregnancy is excluded. Of women with nipple discharge, 14% — and 20% of those have a pituitary tumour. The mechanism, and why the level matters Prolactin inhibits GnRH → which inhibits LH (and possibly FSH) → so the gonad is never told to make sex steroid. The lab signature is no rise in LH/FSH alongside a low or falling estradiol — that is, secondary hypogonadism, exactly the pattern from Part 1. Prolactin (µg/L) Consequence < 20 Normal 20–50 Decreased progesterone only → a short luteal phase — often presenting as difficulty conceiving with apparently normal periods 50–100 Amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea > 100 Overt hypogonadism — estradiol frankly low, symptomatic A graded suppression, not an on/off switch: the higher the prolactin, the further down the axis it shuts things off. In men Decreased libido · erectile dysfunction · infertility (4% of men with infertility) · gynaecomastia · galactorrhea (rare) · osteopenia in 16 of 20 (80%) . Same lab signature: no rise in LH/FSH with a low or low-normal testosterone. Men present later and with bigger tumours, and the reason is in the symptom list: there is no menstru

Causes, and Reading the Number Physiologic Pathologic Other Stress · pregnancy · nipple stimulation · macroprolactinemia ("big prolactin") Lactotroph adenoma · decreased dopaminergic inhibition · tumours or infiltrative disease of the hypothalamus (sarcoidosis) · section of the pituitary stalk (head trauma or surgery) · drug use Idiopathic · estrogen/pregnancy · hypothyroidism · chest wall injury · chronic renal failure By anatomical location, the lecture's other cut of the same list: Hypothalamic disease — tumour, infiltrative disease, cranial radiation. Pituitary disease — prolactinoma (including as part of MEN1 ), acromegaly, pituitary stalk section, other tumours, infiltrative disease, intrasellar germinoma. Drugs — dopamine-receptor antagonists above all: chlorpromazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide , domperidone. Also methyldopa, verapamil, estrogens, cimetidine. Others — primary hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure, cirrhosis, stress. Plus macroprolactin , which is a laboratory artefact rather than a clinical problem. The degree of elevation is itself a clue. A lactotroph macroadenoma produces prolactin far above everything else; microadenomas, stalk-effect from other sellar disease, pregnancy, stress and drugs all cluster lower. A markedly raised prolactin with a large sellar mass is a prolactinoma; a modestly raised prolactin with a large mass is more likely stalk compression from a non-prolactin tumour — a distinction that changes the treatment completely. 28-year-old woman, previously healthy Irregular periods for 8 months, galactorrhea for 6 months occurring about 10× a month. Considering pregnancy. Prolactin 140 µg/L (< 23) · LH 1 IU/L (1–6) · FSH 1.7 IU/L (1–8) · Estradiol 34 pmol/L (120–650). Reading it: prolactin above 100 predicts overt hypogonadism, and that is exactly what the other three numbers show — a frankly low estradiol with LH and FSH sitting at the bottom of their ranges rather than rising to compensate. Secondary hypogonadism, driven by the prolactin. What to order: prolactin, LH and FSH, and the sex steroid (estradiol or testosterone) — plus a TSH and a pregnancy test to exclude the two commonest non-tumour causes, and a medication review for dopamine antagonists.

Treatment: Medicine Before Surgery Rationale for treating at all: Existing or impending neurologic symptoms due to the adenoma. Hypogonadism or other symptoms due to the raised prolactin. Option Detail Medical — dopamine agonists usually the first choice of therapy Cabergoline (Dostinex) · bromocriptine (Parlodel) · quinagolide (Norprolac) Surgery Removal of the hormone-producing tissue — reserved for failure of, or intolerance to, medical therapy Know This: Medical Treatment Is Preferred Over Surgery The prolactinoma is the exception among pituitary tumours. For a growth-hormone or ACTH-secreting adenoma, surgery is the primary treatment. For a prolactinoma, a dopamine agonist is first-line — including for macroadenomas . The reason is the physiology at the top of this part. Dopamine is the natural brake on the lactotroph, so a dopamine agonist is not merely suppressing a hormone: it acts on a receptor the tumour cells still express, and it shrinks the tumour as well as normalising the prolactin . Visual fields recover on tablets. No other pituitary tumour has a drug that does that. Cabergoline works somewhat better than bromocriptine — more effective at normalising prolactin, better tolerated, and dosed twice weekly rather than daily.

Acromegaly: Recognising It Recall the axis: GHRH stimulates and somatostatin inhibits GH ; GH acts largely through IGF-1 produced in the liver, which mediates growth and repair. Because GH is secreted in pulses and IGF-1 is stable in the circulation, IGF-1 is the measurable index of GH exposure — the fact the whole diagnostic pathway is built on. The full syndrome. Note the last line: increased mortality, SMR 1.72, if untreated — and note how much of the list is not about appearance. Sleep apnea, hypertension, insulin resistance, diabetes, heart failure and colonic polyps are what actually kill people with acromegaly. 34-year-old industrial technician — referred because his GP noticed large hands Past history: asthma since childhood; hypertension and type 2 diabetes, both newly diagnosed a few months ago. He volunteered almost nothing. He lives alone and rarely reflects on his own appearance, and was unaware of any change until the large hands were pointed out. On asking: reviewing old photographs, a dramatic change in appearance. Hands extremely large; work gloves now very tight. Shoe size 11 in 2000, now size 14 and tight. Increased hair growth on back and shoulders, oily sweaty skin, prominent forehead, large gaps appearing between the teeth , prominent large jaw. Skin tags under the arms, deepening voice, new snoring, increasing shortness of breath. Progressively severe right-sided headaches, worse on waking. Glucose 19 in the lab, home readings 14–20 despite metformin; polydipsia and weight loss from 290 to 264 lb. No visual change, no galactorrhea. Examination: dramatically oversized hands and feet, BP 140/90, HR 90, BMI over 30. Frontal bossing , large gaps between the teeth, large jaw. Visual fields intact, cardiovascular exam normal, mild scattered wheeze, diaphoresis and oily skin , and a positive Tinel's sign at the right wrist . Why It Takes 12 Years The lecture's own note: mean delay between first symptoms and diagnosis is 12 years. This patient is the reason. The changes are slow, and the person experiencing them is the least able to see them — he lives alone, does not study his own face, and had no idea anything had changed until someone else said so. Two things break the deadlock. Old photographs — asking the patient to compare themselves across a decade is a diagnostic manoeuvre, not small talk. And objects with sizes : gloves, rings, shoes and hats change measurably and the patient remembers the numbers. Shoe size 11 to 14 is far harder t

Diagnosis, Complications and Treatment Step Test What it asks 1 — Screening in patients with symptoms or risk factors IGF-1 Is total GH exposure raised? Age- and sex-dependent reference ranges. Note the cost to the patient 2 — Confirmation Oral glucose tolerance test — 75 g glucose, then GH every 30 minutes for 2 hours Is there normal suppression of GH? Normally glucose suppresses GH to < 1 µg/L 3 — Localisation MRI pituitary Where is the adenoma, and how big? Why Glucose Is the Confirmatory Stimulus A random GH is close to useless because secretion is pulsatile — a high value may be a normal pulse, a low value may be a trough. So the confirmatory test does not measure GH, it measures whether GH still obeys . In a normal person a glucose load suppresses GH to below 1 µg/L. A GH-secreting adenoma is autonomous and does not suppress. This is the same logic as dexamethasone in Cushing and saline in hyperaldosteronism: apply the physiological off-switch and see whether anything switches off. In this patient: IGF-1 > 1600 µg/L against a range of 115–307. GH 93.3 µg/L against 0.02–1.70. After glucose, GH fell only to 74 µg/L — against a normal of under 1. No suppression at all. Cardiovascular risk and complications Complication Frequency Hypertension 43% Left ventricular hypertrophy · cardiomyopathy — Heart failure 3–10% Diabetes mellitus 10–15% Impaired glucose tolerance A further 50% Arthropathy Common — and disabling Growth hormone is a counter-regulatory hormone that opposes insulin, which is why roughly two-thirds of patients have abnormal glucose handling once impaired tolerance is counted alongside frank diabetes. Our patient's "new" diabetes and hypertension were the disease announcing itself years before anyone looked at his hands. Treatment Goal: control tumour growth and IGF-1/GH levels. Transsphenoidal surgery — the primary treatment, unlike in prolactinoma. Medical therapy: somatostatin analogues (suppress GH production — using the axis's own inhibitory signal), and pegvisomant , a growth hormone receptor antagonist that blocks the hormone's action at the target instead of its release. Radiotherapy.

entries.t: Every Screening Test on This Page, in One Table
entries.x: Every Screening Test on This Page, in One Table Axis Suspected deficiency — screen with Suspected excess — screen with Adrenal (ACTH/cortisol) 8–9 AM serum cortisol (< 100 confirms, > 450 excludes); stimulation test if in between 24 h urine cortisol · 1 mg overnight dexamethasone · late-night salivary/plasma cortisol — then ACTH for the cause Thyroid (TSH) Free T4 — not TSH, which is unreliable in secondary disease TSH with free T4 and free T3 (TSH-oma: TSH high-normal or raised with high free hormones) Gonadal (LH/FSH) LH, FSH and the sex steroid together — low steroid with unraised gonadotrophins — Growth hormone IGF-1 ; stimulation with insulin tolerance test or glucagon IGF-1 , then oral glucose tolerance test (GH should suppress < 1 µg/L) Prolactin Rarely clinically relevant; no stimulation test required Serum prolactin — with TSH and a pregnancy test to exclude the common non-tumour causes Posterior (AVP) Assessed separately — diabetes insipidus / AVP deficiency — The pattern worth carrying: for deficiency you measure the target organ hormone, because the trophic hormone will lie to you. For excess you measure the hormone and then try to suppress it — dexamethasone for cortisol, glucose for GH — because autonomy, not concentration, is what defines the disease.

Learning Objectives List the major diagnostic criteria for PMOS (formerly PCOS). List the conditions that mimic PMOS symptoms. Outline biochemical options for distinguishing these conditions from PMOS. List the implications of a PMOS diagnosis for fertility, metabolic syndrome, diabetes risk, cancer risk and emotional health. Distinguish treatment options for PMOS: lifestyle and medications. Dr. Hashmi's interactive module: short videos on each part of the diagnostic triad, insulin resistance, treatment and a case, plus a myth-busting exercise. There is no slide deck; the module's one summary slide is rebuilt as a table at the end .

entries.t: What's in a Name: PCOS → PMOS
entries.x: What's in a Name: PCOS → PMOS The old name, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) , is still everywhere: older papers, charts, conversations. Recognize both. The name changed because the old one was wrong in three ways: Old word The problem "Poly-cystic" They aren't cysts. They're arrested antral follicles : developing eggs that stalled. They only look cystic on ultrasound "Ovary syndrome" The ovary is one target, not the only source. It involves hypothalamic GnRH , pituitary LH excess , insulin resistance and fat tissue making androgens New: "Polyendocrine Metabolic" Captures the many axes involved (HPO axis, insulin, adrenal androgens, adipokines) and the long-term cardiometabolic risk Source cited in the module: Teede HJ et al., Global Name Change Consortium, Lancet 2026;407:2329–39. Who gets it, and why More than 170 million women worldwide, up to 20% of those of reproductive age. No single cause has been found; it's best seen as several overlapping mechanisms: Mechanism What happens Ovarian dysfunction Too much ovarian stroma making testosterone HPO axis dysfunction LH ↑, FSH ↓ . The high LH:FSH balance over-stimulates the theca cells to make androgen Insulin resistance The ovaries have insulin and IGF receptors , so high insulin pushes them to make more androgen Excess fat tissue Peripheral fat converts adrenal hormones to testosterone The LH-drives-theca part is the two-cell model from 2.6 : LH makes the theca cells produce androgen, and FSH makes the granulosa cells convert it to estrogen. Tip the balance toward LH and androgen is left over.

The Diagnostic Criteria Rotterdam (2003) Androgen Excess & PCOS Society From ESHRE / ASRM AE-PCOS Society (dated 2008 in the module) Items Hyperandrogenism · oligo/anovulation · polycystic ovaries on ultrasound Hyperandrogenism · oligo/anovulation and/or polycystic ovaries · exclusion of other disorders Need 2 of 3 All 3 The module's current diagnostic triad: 1 Hyperandrogenism , on clinical exam or labs (↑ testosterone). 2 Ovulatory dysfunction : oligomenorrhea or polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound. 3 Other disorders excluded. The difference that matters: under Rotterdam, a woman with irregular cycles and polycystic ovaries but no androgen excess still counts. Under the module's triad, hyperandrogenism is required . Other sources often use Rotterdam, so know both. Drawn for these notes from the module's triad diagram and its "exclusion of other disorders" video; the module has no flowchart of its own. The exclusion step comes first on purpose: mimics like pregnancy and tumours matter more than the label. The two decisions are the other two parts of the triad.

Hyperandrogenism History Ask about Why Where the extra hair grows Upper lip, chin, underarms, groin, abdomen, back, arms. Trust the patient's own sense of what's abnormal for her When it started Lifelong hair is unlikely to be significant; new hair over the past weeks or months is concerning How fast Very rapid → think tumour. Gradual over years → fits PMOS What's normal in her family and ethnicity There's no single definition of normal hair growth; some ethnicities normally have more Acne : where, and when it started Hard-to-treat, adult-onset acne, on the chest and back as well as the face Hair loss and its pattern Androgen pattern = thinning over the vertex and front , widened part. Not focal patches Hair removal she already does Shaving, waxing and so on hide the hair you're trying to assess Be sensitive : this is uncomfortable for many patients to talk about. Exam Hirsutism. The traditional tool is the modified Ferriman–Gallwey score : 9 body areas (upper lip, chin, chest, upper and lower abdomen, arm, thigh, upper and lower back), each graded 0–4 , for a maximum of 36 . A score of 8 or more meant hirsutism, but that cut-off came from white women. The lecture suggests lower cut-offs for some Asian populations (as low as about 2), and higher ones (around 9) for women of Mediterranean or South Asian background, whose normal scores run higher. The Endocrine Society's definition is patient-centred: hirsutism is unwanted sexual hair growth, enough to cause her distress . The score is not the be-all and end-all. Acne : persisting into adulthood, beyond what's usual in her family, especially on the chest and upper back . Androgenic alopecia : diffuse thinning over the vertex and frontal scalp, a widening part. Labs: testosterone is the one Testosterone Means < 2 nmol/L Normal female range (most labs) Slightly high , e.g. 2.1–2.5 nmol/L Fits PMOS . It can also be normal > 5 nmol/L , approaching the male range (low-normal male is about 8) Too high for PMOS: think tumour DHEA (an adrenal androgen) and androstenedione exist too, but the module says not to worry about them here. All women normally make some androgen.

Ovulatory Dysfunction Oligomenorrhea is diagnosed from the history . Ask Look for Age at menarche , and the pattern after it Irregular in the first year or two is normal . Did they become regular through the late teens? Cycle length (one period to the next) through adulthood Oligomenorrhea: cycles longer than 35 days, or fewer than 9 periods a year Recent oral contraceptive use Irregular periods after stopping the pill usually weren't caused by it: the pill was hiding an irregularity that was already there Family history Irregular periods, subfertility Ultrasound: polycystic-looking ovaries (the classic "string of pearls") are follicles stuck at an early stage. They support the diagnosis, but they aren't required , and their absence doesn't rule PMOS out. They also turn up soon after menarche and in some women with perfectly normal cycles, so on their own they mean little.

Excluding the Mimics "Put on your detective hat." Anything that can cause androgen excess or irregular periods has to be ruled out before you say PMOS. Mimic Clue Test Exogenous testosterone Taking it, or exposure to a partner's topical testosterone ; supplements with hidden androgens A careful medication, supplement and social history Androgen-secreting tumour (adrenal or ovarian; also cortisol-and-androgen tumours, as in Cushing's) Rapid onset over weeks to months Testosterone markedly raised (> 5, toward the male range) → image the adrenals and ovaries Non-classic CAH Subtle; looks just like PMOS (classic CAH would have been found in childhood) 17-hydroxyprogesterone : high, because it sits upstream of the partly-blocked enzyme ( 3.9 ) Pregnancy New amenorrhea Serum β-hCG first , always Hyperprolactinemia (e.g. a prolactinoma) Galactorrhea . Prolactin switches off the gonadal axis Prolactin : > 20 = hyperprolactinemia. PMOS itself can nudge it to about 25–30; a tumour is usually far higher (90–100+) Thyroid disease The module describes thyrotoxicosis : palpitations, tremor, hair loss, rapid weight loss TSH (low, with high free T4) Just after menarche, or approaching menopause Irregularity is expected in the first 1–2 years, and in the late 40s to early 50s History; ask when the women in her family went through menopause Two notes. The video calls this mimic "hypothyroidism" but describes hyperthyroid symptoms and labs, and the module's summary slide lists hyperthyroidism ; either way, the test is a TSH. The prolactin pituitary side is in 3.2 .

entries.t: Insulin Resistance: Not a Criterion, but Almost Always There
entries.x: Insulin Resistance: Not a Criterion, but Almost Always There Insulin resistance isn't in the current criteria (new guidelines due in the next year or two may change that), but most patients with PMOS have it , and it drives much of the long-term risk. Where Look for History A gentle weight history (did the periods become irregular after weight gain?) · diabetes or prediabetes · obstructive sleep apnea (snoring, daytime sleepiness) · metabolic (fatty) liver disease · family history of type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes Exam Central, visceral fat : waist-to-hip ratio > 0.85 in women (> 0.95 in men), the "apple" shape, with ethnic variation in cut-offs · acanthosis nigricans : dark, velvety skin on the back of the neck and underarms (also groin and inner thighs) · skin tags Labs Hemoglobin A1c · lipid panel (high triglycerides) Not everyone with PMOS is overweight : a patient with a healthy BMI can still have it. And take the weight history kindly; it's a hard topic for many patients.

Myth-Busting: What to Tell Patients The module's exercise. Patients will ask you these, so here are the answers. Statement True? Women with PMOS are more prone to subfertility and early miscarriage True Women with PMOS are more likely to have metabolic syndrome (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, high lipids) True Women with PMOS are more prone to endometrial cancer True Women with PMOS are at higher risk of mood disorders True Women with PMOS cannot conceive False : harder, but very possible Women with PMOS cannot lose weight False : a balanced diet and exercise work Women with PMOS have an increased appetite and are always hungry False Eating organic or vegan helps, because food additives cause PMOS False Also more common with PMOS, from the module's wrap-up: central fat, gestational diabetes and frontal (androgenic) hair loss . Adrenal hypertrophy is not.

Treatment Everyone: lifestyle Diet: high fibre, low fat, lower carbohydrate. Exercise: at least 30 minutes, 5 days a week (the module favours muscle-based exercise). About 150 minutes a week overall. Modest weight loss is enough. Losing just 10–20 lb has let some of Dr. Hashmi's patients conceive. Be a coach, not a critic. Celebrate any weight loss, and never body-shame. It sounds obvious; the module's point is to remember it when you're running late. Then: treat whatever bothers her most Her main concern Options Watch out for Irregular periods , no pregnancy plans soon Combined oral contraceptive (COCP) : regular cycles, protects bone density, can help mood. Or cyclic progestin : a progestin-only pill for 2 weeks every 2–3 months , triggering a withdrawal bleed at least 4 times a year COCP side effects: migraines; worse mood or anxiety in some Wants to get pregnant No pill. Lifestyle and modest weight loss, then refer to OB/GYN for letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) to induce ovulation . Metformin : conflicting evidence; generally harmless but not routine. Surgery (ovarian drilling, partial resection, thermal ablation) is rare now, for refractory cases — Hirsutism Temper expectations first. Surface methods (shaving, sugaring, epilation, waxing) are fine and do not make hair grow back thicker , which is a myth. Laser : semi-permanent to permanent. Anti-androgens : spironolactone , cyproterone (alone or in the COCP Diane). The COCP itself reduces hair. Eflornithine cream (Vaniqa): slows hair growth at the follicle; not hormonal; modest Anti-androgens need contraception : they could feminize a male fetus. "Success" = shaving every few days instead of daily Hair loss (alopecia) Minoxidil (Rogaine) 5% foam on the scalp · anti-androgens · COCP · hair transplant (the most effective, but expensive and not covered) — And always: manage the risks she won't ask about Risk What to do Metabolic (diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease) Screen periodically for diabetes, BP and lipids · keep counselling on diet, at least 150 min/week of exercise and modest weight loss · raise bariatric surgery if she meets the BMI criteria: it restores cycles and fertility and lowers metabolic risk Endometrial cancer Make sure she has at least 4 withdrawal bleeds a year (COCP or cyclic progestin) · periodic pelvic ultrasound to check for endometrial thickening Why Irregular Periods Raise Endometrial Cancer Risk No ovulation means no corpus luteum, and no corpus luteum means no pr

The Case: Ms. X Story 30 years old: excess facial hair and unpredictable periods . Menarche at 12, irregular in the first year, then regular, but over the past year only about 4 periods . Dark terminal hair on the sides of the face, chin, chest and arms for 7 years; she now waxes twice a month instead of monthly (the change began a year ago). Gradual 30 lb weight gain since high school. No galactorrhea , no medications or supplements. Sedentary since college. Married 8 months ago and wants children . Family history: gestational diabetes in her mother and sister, type 2 diabetes in her father Exam BP 135/85, HR 83, BMI 30 with central fat , acanthosis nigricans on the neck and both axillae, significant hirsutism (chin, cheeks, trunk). No abdominal striae Labs β-hCG negative · testosterone 2.1 nmol/L (mildly high) · prolactin 15 (normal) · TSH 0.6 (normal) · lipids normal · fasting glucose normal Diagnosis PMOS : hyperandrogenism (clinical and lab) + oligomenorrhea + mimics excluded "But Doc, Don't I Need an Ultrasound?" No. She already meets all three parts of the triad. A pelvic ultrasound is not needed to diagnose PMOS ; that's the key teaching point of the case. Her plan: she's tearful because she hopes to conceive, so start with reassurance : conceiving is very possible, even spontaneously. If she isn't trying in the next six months or so, she needs effective contraception. Tell her cosmetic hair removal is fine and won't make it worse. Make a concrete diet and activity plan aiming for modest weight loss. Offer a COCP if she doesn't want pregnancy soon, and eflornithine cream for the hirsutism, warning her it takes time to work. Above all: stay kind .

PMOS at a Glance The module's summary slide, rebuilt as a table. Diagnosis Exclude Treat Hyperandrogenism : clinical exam or labs (↑ testosterone) + Ovulatory dysfunction : oligomenorrhea or cystic ovaries on ultrasound + Exclusion of other disorders Pregnancy Hyperprolactinemia Exogenous testosterone Testosterone-producing tumour CAH Hyperthyroidism Early menarche or menopause For androgens: surface therapies, spironolactone/cyproterone, eflornithine, minoxidil (alopecia) For ovulation: weight loss and exercise; OCPs or cyclic progesterone History highlights Exam highlights High-yield labs Risk monitoring Oligomenorrhea Hirsutism No galactorrhea Gradual onset Hirsutism Acanthosis Acne Alopecia ↑ BMI (visceral fat) β-hCG Testosterone Prolactin Endometrial cancer Diabetes · hypertension · lipids

Learning Objectives Describe the normal stages of, and the normal ages for, pubertal development in boys and girls. Define precocious puberty and delayed puberty in boys and girls, and outline their main causes. Classify disorders of precocious puberty and of delayed puberty. Interpret clinical findings and laboratory results for disorders of puberty. Summarize basic concepts of treatment for disorders of puberty. The physiology behind all of this is in 3.3, Physiology of Puberty . That page covers how the axis is switched on ( the GABA brake and the kisspeptin accelerator ) and why it switches on when it does. This lecture is about what happens when the timing goes wrong.

Normal Puberty, Briefly Puberty is the time at which a child develops secondary sexual characteristics and reproductive function. It involves four things at once: Secondary sexual characteristics: breast and testicular development, pubic hair. A growth spurt. A change in body composition: more bone mass, muscle mass, fat mass and strength. Psychosocial and psychosexual maturation. It depends on pulsatile GnRH, which drives pulsatile LH and FSH. LH acts on theca cells in the ovary and Leydig cells in the testis to make androgens . FSH acts on the ovarian follicle and the seminiferous tubules to make estradiol, inhibin and gametes . Sex steroids then feed back negatively on GnRH and the gonadotrophins. The regulators of GnRH. What starts pulsatile secretion is still not fully understood. Kisspeptin stimulates it, leptin acts on the kisspeptin neurons, glutamate excites, and GABA and NPY inhibit. 3.3 explains how these balance out. This slide adds one more brake: MKRN3 . From the lecture. MKRN3: A Genetic Brake on Puberty The slide lists MKRN3 as simply "inhibitory". There is more to it, and it ties the normal physiology to one of the diseases below. In prepubertal mice, Mkrn3 expression is high. It falls just before puberty and stays low afterwards, which is exactly what a brake that has to be released would do. In humans, loss-of-function mutations in MKRN3 cause familial central precocious puberty : the brake is missing, so the axis switches on early. The gene is imprinted , and only the copy from the father is expressed. In the original families, every affected child had inherited the mutation from their father. It sits in the Prader–Willi region of chromosome 15. Abreu et al., NEJM 2013. Added from outside the deck. Estrogen does Androgen does Breast development (thelarche) Acne; oily skin and hair; increased body odour Increase in growth rate Pubic and axillary hair (pubarche) Vaginal discharge Enlargement of the penis/clitoris; deepening of the voice Menses (menarche) Increase in growth rate Mood swings Mood swings This table is the key to working out the source of the hormone in a disorder. Breast development and menses need estrogen . Hair, acne, odour and clitoromegaly need androgen . A girl with pubic hair and no breasts has an androgen source and no estrogen source, and that points somewhere very different from a girl with breasts and no hair.

entries.t: The Normal Sequence: Girls vs Boys
entries.x: The Normal Sequence: Girls vs Boys Girls Boys First sign Thelarche (breast bud) Testicular enlargement , volume > 3 mL Sequence 1. Thelarche 2. Growth spurt (between Tanner 2 and 3) 3. Pubarche: pubic and axillary hair 4. Menarche 1. Testicular enlargement 2. Penile growth 3. Pubarche: pubic and axillary hair, body odour 4. Growth spurt (testes 10–12 mL, between Tanner 3 and 4) 5. Deepening of voice 6. Increased muscle bulk 7. Facial hair Average ages Breasts (Tanner 2): 10.3 ± 1.0 Pubic hair: 11.2 ± 1.1 Menarche: 12.7 ± 1.0 Onset of puberty: 11.5 ± 1.3 Normal range for onset 8–13 years 9–14 years Growth spurt Early , at Tanner 2–3 Late , at Tanner 3–4 Menarche comes about 2.5 years after thelarche. It is a late event in female puberty, not an early one. About 15% of girls have pubarche as their first sign , before thelarche. That is still normal. Boys start later, so they end up taller. Girls start earlier, so they end up shorter. Peak height velocity is similar in both sexes. The difference is how much growing a boy has done before his spurt starts.

Tanner Staging Tanner stages 1–5 grade breast, genital and pubic hair development separately. Stage 1 is prepubertal and stage 5 is adult. Stage 2 of breast or genital development marks the onset of puberty. Breasts. 1: prepubertal, no bud · 2: breast bud, the onset of puberty · 3: breast mound, single contour · 4: areola forms a secondary mound · 5: mature, single contour. Genitals. 1: testes ≤ 3 mL · 2: testes > 3 mL with scrotal change, the onset of puberty · 3: penile lengthening · 4: testes 10–12 mL · 5: adult, testes 20–25 mL. The Prader orchidometer. A string of graded beads compared against the testis by feel. A volume above 3 mL is the first sign of puberty in boys, so this is how you date the onset. Pubic hair, both sexes. Staged the same way, but it should not be used to mark the onset of puberty . It reflects adrenal androgen, not the gonadal axis. Why Pubic Hair Can't Date the Onset Pubic and axillary hair are made by androgen, and in children most of that androgen comes from the adrenal (adrenarche), not the gonad. The adrenal and gonadal axes run on separate switches. So a child can grow pubic hair with the HPG axis still completely off, and a child can have a failed gonad and still grow pubic hair. That is not a technicality. It is why a girl with Turner syndrome still goes through pubarche , in 100% of cases, while her breasts never develop. It is also why isolated early pubic hair is usually a benign adrenal variant rather than true precocious puberty. Both come up below.

Definition, and the Normal Variant Delayed puberty is the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 standard deviations above the population mean. In practice: Girls: no pubertal signs by age 13. Boys: no pubertal signs by age 14. There are three causes: a normal variant (constitutional delay) , primary hypogonadism , or secondary hypogonadism . Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) The typical CDGP curve. The child tracks at or below the 3rd percentile but parallel to the lines , so the growth rate is normal. Later he catches up toward the mid-parental target (MPT) . He is short because he is late, not because anything is wrong. Height at or below the 3rd percentile. Normal growth rate. Puberty typically starts between 14 and 18 . Delayed bone age. The most common cause of delayed puberty, especially in boys. Strong family history: a parent who was also late. Why a Delayed Bone Age Is Reassuring Bone age measures how far the skeleton has matured, and it tracks puberty rather than the calendar. In CDGP the whole child is simply running on a later clock. His height is appropriate for his bone age, and the growth plates are still wide open, so the growth he appears to be missing is still available . That is why these children reach a normal adult height in the end. The hard part is that constitutional delay and secondary hypogonadism look alike early on: both are prepubertal with low gonadotrophins. The things that point to CDGP are the family history, a normal growth rate, and the absence of any CNS or systemic clue. Sometimes only time separates them.

entries.t: The Split: Primary vs Secondary Hypogonadism
entries.x: The Split: Primary vs Secondary Hypogonadism The one measurement that splits delayed puberty. Sex steroids are low in both. Primary (right): the gonad has failed, so the intact pituitary is shouting and LH/FSH are high . This is also called hypergonadotropic . Secondary (left): the hypothalamus or pituitary has failed, so nobody is shouting and LH/FSH are low . This is hypogonadotropic . It is the same logic as the inappropriately normal TSH in 3.2. From the lecture. Primary hypogonadism in girls: Turner syndrome High LH/FSH. The main genetic cause is Turner syndrome . Other causes of primary ovarian failure are autoimmune, radiation, drugs and chemotherapy (e.g. cyclophosphamide), and surgery or trauma. Total or partial absence of one X. Only 60% are 45,X , with a whole X missing. 15% are mosaic (45,X/46,XX), 10% are partial losses, and 15% are other variants. About 1 in 2,000–2,500 newborn girls. Feature Frequency Short stature 95–100% , with a mean final height of 144 cm Complete gonadal failure (streak ovaries) 90% Thelarche Only 10–15% Menarche 1% (usually mosaics) Infertility > 99% Pubarche 100% , because it is adrenal Hypothyroidism 10% Dysmorphic features: neck webbing, short 4th and 5th metacarpals, increased carrying angle, nail dysplasia. Also: congenital heart disease, and renal anomalies such as a horseshoe kidney. Two Questions the Lecture Asks About Turner The most common physical feature is short stature , found in 95–100%. It is more common than webbed neck, a wide carrying angle, widely spaced nipples or short metacarpals. So a short girl with delayed puberty should have a karyotype, even with no dysmorphic features at all. What else to screen for: congenital heart disease, renal abnormalities, autoimmune disease (thyroid, celiac disease, type 1 diabetes), hearing problems, and a high risk of metabolic syndrome. Also note that 10–12% of girls with Turner carry Y-chromosome material . That matters because Y material in a dysgenetic gonad carries a risk of gonadoblastoma. It is flagged here as a reason the karyotype needs to be looked at in detail, not just as "45,X". Primary hypogonadism in boys: Klinefelter syndrome High LH/FSH. The main genetic cause is Klinefelter syndrome . Acquired causes are gonadal disease or infection, radiation, chemotherapy, surgery and trauma. Anorchia is a congenital cause. One or more extra X chromosomes. 80% are 47,XXY and 20% are 46,XY/47,XXY mosaics. About 1 in 650 newborn boys , which makes it far more com

Secondary Hypogonadism: "Think About Brain Problems" Low LH/FSH with low sex steroids. The lecture's own heading is the rule to remember: think about brain problems. Category Examples Structural CNS Trauma, infection, radiation, tumour Gonadotrophin deficiency Isolated LH/FSH deficiency, or combined with other pituitary deficiencies; congenital pituitary defects Kallmann syndrome Congenital isolated gonadotrophin deficiency with anosmia Genetic syndromes Laurence–Moon–Biedl, Prader–Willi, others Functional Chronic systemic disease; eating disorder or excessive exercise (hypothalamic amenorrhea) Hyperprolactinemia Prolactin suppresses GnRH. See 3.2 Why Kallmann Syndrome Can't Smell GnRH neurons are not born in the hypothalamus. In the embryo they arise in the olfactory placode and migrate along the developing olfactory nerves into the brain. In Kallmann syndrome that shared migration fails. The olfactory bulbs don't form properly, so there is no sense of smell, and the GnRH neurons never arrive where they are needed, so there is no puberty. That makes "can you smell?" a genuinely useful question in a teenager with delayed puberty and low gonadotrophins. The shared migration is added from outside the deck. The deck states the link to anosmia. The functional causes are the axis doing its job. 3.3 covers how GnRH activation depends on energy stores, which is where the critical metabolic mass and leptin ideas come from. An underweight, over-exercising or chronically ill child is being held back for a reason, and restoring energy balance restores the axis.

entries.t: Definition, and the Two Benign Variants
entries.x: Definition, and the Two Benign Variants Girls: onset of puberty before age 8. Boys: onset of puberty before age 9. Before calling it pathological, rule out the two variants of normal development . Each involves only one isolated sign, and neither progresses. Isolated premature thelarche Isolated premature pubarche What Isolated breast development, with very low-grade estrogenization of the vaginal mucosa Isolated pubic hair , ± mild acne, axillary hair and body odour When 6 months to 2 years 6 to 8 years , more often in girls Why Transient estrogen exposure. Minipuberty has not fully switched off (see 3.3 ) A physiological rise in adrenal androgens , i.e. early adrenarche What is absent No growth spurt and no advance in bone age , and no signs of the other hormone. This absence is what makes them variants. Outcome Often regresses spontaneously ; rarely progresses to precocious puberty Slow progression, normal final height. Associated with insulin resistance and later PCOS in girls The test that separates a variant from true precocious puberty is the growth pattern . Real puberty means real sex steroid exposure, which drives a growth spurt and advances the bone age. A breast bud or a few pubic hairs in a child growing along her usual centile is a variant until proven otherwise.

entries.t: Central or Peripheral? The Key Question
entries.x: Central or Peripheral? The Key Question Pathological precocious puberty comes in two kinds, and the gonadotrophins separate them: Central (CPP) Peripheral (PPP) Also called GnRH-dependent GnRH-independent Mechanism The normal axis switches on early . Everything is appropriate except the timing Sex steroids come from a source that bypasses the axis : a gonad or adrenal acting on its own, or a drug LH/FSH High Low , suppressed by the steroids Sex steroids High High 1 A random LH can be low even when puberty is central, because LH is released in pulses and a single sample can miss them. A GnRH (LHRH) stimulation test is the gold standard. The slide gives the random cut-off as "0.3 mIU/L", but the standard threshold is 0.3 IU/L (the same as 0.3 mIU/mL). Written in mIU/L it would be 1000× lower. Drawn for these notes: the deck makes this decision in prose across six slides. The first branch catches the benign variants. The LH branch separates a normal axis switched on early from sex steroids that are bypassing it. The bottom row is the lecture's bedside clue for boys. Why LH is the test, and why a single value can mislead. After the surge at birth, the axis is suppressed from about 6 months until puberty, when pulsatile release restarts. LH tracks the restart better than FSH. But because LH comes in pulses, one low random value can miss it. That is what the stimulation test is for. The Testicle Is the Clue in Boys LH makes Leydig cells produce testosterone, and Leydig cells live in the testes. So when the central axis is driving puberty, both testes grow: bilateral enlargement, ≥ 4 mL . When testosterone comes from somewhere else , such as the adrenal in CAH, an adrenal tumour or exogenous testosterone, you get virilization (acne, pubic hair, a longer penis, faster growth, advanced bone age) but the testes stay small, < 3 mL , because nothing is stimulating them. One more pattern: a unilaterally enlarged testis in a virilized boy suggests a Leydig cell tumour . The source is in the testis, but it is autonomous and one-sided.

The Causes Central (GnRH-dependent) Girls Boys Idiopathic Most cases . The commonest cause of precocious puberty in girls Rare: less than 50% Implication Every boy with central precocious puberty needs a careful CNS assessment. An idiopathic label in a boy has to be earned. Without a CNS abnormality: idiopathic (sporadic or familial; see MKRN3 above), or, rarely, chronic sex-steroid exposure that eventually switches the axis on. With a CNS abnormality that increases GnRH secretion: hypothalamic or pineal tumour, hydrocephalus, trauma, radiation, and congenital malformations such as a hypothalamic hamartoma or arachnoid cyst. Idiopathic CPP is not harmless if untreated. Adult height is on average 5–6 cm lower , because early estrogen closes the growth plates early. Puberty also finishes prematurely, with early menses and real psychosocial consequences. Peripheral (GnRH-independent) Source Causes Gonadal Ovarian: cysts, granulosa cell tumours · McCune–Albright syndrome (genetic) · Testicular: Leydig cell tumours (asymmetric testes) · testotoxicosis (familial male precocious puberty, genetic) Adrenal Congenital adrenal hyperplasia : autosomal recessive, with too much sex steroid, too little cortisol, ± mineralocorticoid deficiency with salt wasting · virilizing tumours · feminizing tumours · Cushing syndrome Iatrogenic Exposure to exogenous sex hormones CAH connects back to the adrenal lecture . A block in cortisol synthesis means low cortisol, so ACTH rises and keeps driving the gland, and the excess precursors are pushed down the androgen pathway. The same enzyme defect causes adrenal insufficiency and precocious virilization. McCune–Albright syndrome The classical triad: peripheral precocious puberty (multiple follicular cysts), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (the X-ray), and irregular café-au-lait patches with jagged "coast of Maine" borders (the photograph). From the lecture. A somatic activating mutation in the gene for the α-subunit of the stimulatory G protein (G s α) . The gene is GNAS ; the slide's "CNAS1" is a typo for the older name GNAS1 . The abnormal G protein keeps cAMP switched on permanently in whatever tissues carry the mutation. It is peripheral (GnRH-independent). The ovary behaves as if LH were present even though LH is suppressed. Other endocrine glands can be affected: pituitary adenoma, Cushing, thyroid. Why One Mutation Causes Three Unrelated-Looking Problems Many hormone receptors (for LH, FSH, TSH, ACTH, GHRH and MSH) signal by acti

Assessment and Treatment History Physical Investigations Timing and progression of pubertal milestones Growth pattern: any growth spurt? CNS symptoms Medications, radiation Family history: parental heights, parents' age at puberty Measure and plot height and weight Tanner stages CNS signs Dysmorphic features, skin marks (café-au-lait) Random serum LH (> 0.3 IU/L suggests CPP) Serum estradiol/testosterone Bone age (hand X-ray) TSH ± Karyotype (Turner, Klinefelter in delayed puberty) ± Pelvic ultrasound (uterine size, endometrium, ovarian volume, follicles) ± LHRH stimulation test (gold standard for precocious puberty) ± MRI head if CNS pathology suspected Two items on this list do more than they seem to. TSH is there because severe primary hypothyroidism can present with early or late puberty, and it is easy to fix. The pelvic ultrasound reads the estrogen and gonadotrophin effect directly off the organs: an enlarged uterus and thickened endometrium mean estrogen has been present for some time, and large multifollicular ovaries mean gonadotrophin or G s drive. Treating central precocious puberty: GnRH (LHRH) analogues Why Giving More GnRH Switches Puberty Off It looks backwards: you treat early activation of the GnRH axis by giving a GnRH agonist . It works because the pituitary only responds to GnRH that pulses . A long-acting analogue gives a continuous signal, and continuous stimulation down-regulates the pituitary's GnRH receptors . The pituitary becomes resistant to the child's own GnRH. Removing the pulsatile pattern stops puberty. The same physiology is on the HPG axis page : pulsatile GnRH stimulates, continuous GnRH suppresses. Delivery: a long-acting depot intramuscular injection every 12 weeks . Side effects appear minimal. The cost is about $1,200/month, covered by OHIP. Goals: (1) stop pubertal progression , including menses; (2) stop the acceleration of bone maturation and delay epiphyseal closure, to protect final height ; (3) improve psychosocial well-being . Not every child needs it. Before starting, the lecture asks you to consider: How early is the onset? Is it in keeping with the family pattern? How fast is it progressing? What is the predicted adult height? Is it below the 3rd percentile, or below the parental target? What are the psychosocial implications for the child, the parents and their peers? A girl who starts at 7½, is progressing slowly, has a mother who started early and a predicted height that is fine may reasonably be watche
