Advantages Disadvantages Non-invasive · patient autonomy and control · private, at home · inexpensive (covered by OHIP; about $350 without coverage) · technically simple, can be provided from an office and a pharmacy · same-day start · an option when the uterine cavity can't be accessed surgically Both patient and physician must commit to follow-up (up to 10% need at least one reminder) · longer treatment interval · GI side effects: diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea · 10% have delayed evacuation over days to weeks · heavy bleeding and cramps when the pregnancy passes (codeine-containing analgesia is usually prescribed) · up to 5% (typically ~3%) fail

Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) An office procedure, essentially the same as an endometrial biopsy: a cannula plus a hand-held aspirator, no electric suction and no OR . The cannulas and the aspirator. Up to 10 weeks gestation. Paracervical block with 1% lidocaine at a minimum; other sedation offered if available. Most patients, especially nulliparas , need some cervical dilatation. Transilluminate the tissue to confirm chorionic villi and a gestational sac , or do a post-procedure ultrasound to confirm an empty uterus. Failure rate 0.25%. Good for: office setting, immediate, private, local anaesthetic only, cost-effective. Not for: contraindications to local anaesthesia, a patient who can't cooperate with the exam, or very young or distressed patients who may need sedation.

Dilatation & Curettage (Suction D&C) Vacuum or suction aspiration up to and including 14+0 weeks , using a rigid cannula on an electric suction machine. It can be done under local with a cervical block, but conscious or moderate sedation is usually offered, and general anaesthetic in some hospital settings. Cervical preparation. Chemical: misoprostol orally, buccally or vaginally 1–12 h before. Osmotic: laminaria (a seaweed) or synthetic Dilapan , placed in the internal os 24 h before, which slowly absorb fluid and open the cervix (the photo shows one expanding over 24 h). Hegar dilators , sized in millimetres. Rule of thumb: dilate to about the number of weeks' gestation (a 12-week pregnancy → about 12 mm). 1 Bimanual exam : confirms size and expected gestation, and tells you whether the uterus is anteverted or retroverted so instruments go the right way and don't perforate. 2 Speculum, prep and paracervical block (lidocaine, sometimes with vasopressin and/or epinephrine to reduce blood loss). Pre-operative antibiotics are given for a therapeutic abortion. 3 Mechanical dilatation only if needed. If cervical prep was adequate, skipping it means less discomfort and less infection , because fewer instruments pass through the vagina into the uterus. 4 Suction curettage to remove all products. Sharp curettage is unnecessary in the vast majority of cases and carries a higher complication rate, including Asherman syndrome. Complications (all inside that <2% overall rate). Cervical shock: a vasovagal reaction during the block, lasting minutes. Uterine perforation: during dilatation or suction; finish the case under ultrasound or laparoscopic guidance , with the choice guided by the instrument size, the site (fundus vs laterally near the uterine arteries) and the patient's stability. From the lecture. Complication Recognize it by Do Hemorrhage More likely with uterine atony , a low implantation or a larger gestational age A repeat curettage may be needed to confirm everything is out Hematometra (post-abortal syndrome) Blood collecting in the cavity: excruciating pain, an enlarging uterus, little or no bleeding , often urinary retention Re-evacuate immediately Advantages of D&C over medical abortion: less risk than general anaesthesia (it can be done with conscious sedation), faster recovery, much less bleeding afterwards, quicker discharge without required follow-up, high patient acceptance and cost-effectiveness.

Second Trimester Surgical: D&E Medical: induction of labour How Pre-operative cervical ripening (osmotic, mechanical and/or medical), ± fetal intracardiac injection of digoxin or KCl , then decompression and removal of the uterine contents, usually under general anaesthetic. Beyond 18 weeks , serial applications of dilators Misoprostol induction, generally after intracardiac KCl or digoxin Up to Generally 25 weeks Used beyond that, and for genetic terminations Advantages Fewest complications of the second-trimester methods; much shorter from start to finish; fewer retained products Allows the pregnancy to be delivered whole for autopsy or genetic examination , and allows memory-making for families Risks General anaesthetic, uterine perforation, hemorrhage, infection (multiple instrumentations), incomplete procedure — all rising with gestational age Length (24 h or more), bleeding, and retained placenta : 5–10% need an urgent D&C or D&E anyway The lecture's own point: the greatest obstacle to safe D&E in Canada is the shrinking number of skilled practitioners . That is starting to turn around, helped by a second-trimester providers group formed during the pandemic so that clinicians know who offers what.

Compared With Continuing the Pregnancy Legal abortion is the safest outcome on the table : 0.567 deaths per 100,000, against 1.19 for miscarriage, 7.06 for live birth and 31.9 for ectopic pregnancy. Continuing a pregnancy is more than 12× more dangerous than ending it. Grimes, 2006, from the lecture.

Contraception Afterwards Ovulation can return as early as 2 weeks after a first-trimester abortion, so contraception should start immediately if wanted. Every method is appropriate : having an abortion is not a contraindication to anything. Review all of them. Timing: a pill, patch, ring or Depo-Provera can start the same day as a surgical abortion, or on the day of the day-3 bloodwork after a medical one. An IUD or implant can go in during the surgical procedure (painless under sedation), or at the two-week visit once a medical abortion is confirmed complete. Expulsion is slightly higher when an IUD is placed immediately ( 3.8% ), but still under 5%. If a method failed, offer a different one — and work out why it failed: cost, trouble swallowing or remembering pills, fear of needles, a partner who won't use condoms, or a medical reason to avoid estrogen (previous DVT, migraine with aura, smoking over half a pack a day over age 35). IUDs have their own limits, such as a uterine malformation or the cost of insertion and removal. If the procedure is done by a surgeon under general anaesthetic and the patient has completed childbearing , a tubal ligation can be offered at the same time.

Fertility and Emotions Afterwards Asherman syndrome. Left, the HSG : black filling defects inside the triangular cavity are adhesions. Right, hysteroscopy : the cavity isn't open and smooth, it's stuck together. The most common emotional reaction is relief , sometimes with transient guilt, sadness or a sense of loss. Overall, patients are content with their decision. A safe abortion carries no greater risk to fertility than a D&C for miscarriage. Asherman syndrome : adhesions form in the endometrial cavity, sometimes causing secondary amenorrhea . Risk factors are uterine curettage (about 8% of cases), repeat curettage (most often for retained products or retained placenta postpartum), and infection. The slide puts the risk at up to 30% with a third consecutive procedure . Trauma is the major cause of intrauterine adhesions; the role of infection is controversial and hard to separate out, because infected products usually mean retained products, which mean another procedure. After a single, uncomplicated first- or second-trimester procedure, the risk is very low .

The Myths, Answered The list patients will bring you. The answers are below. From the lecture. Myth The answer Abortion causes breast cancer No evidence. The only biologically plausible thread is that breastfeeding slightly lowers breast cancer risk, so not carrying a pregnancy to term means not breastfeeding — which is no different from never being pregnant, or choosing not to breastfeed It's used as birth control The decision is almost never taken lightly . Patients needing repeat abortions are often experiencing reproductive coercion , financial hardship, isolation, abuse or trafficking, or have medical contraindications to contraception (or believe the myths about it) It's illegal in Canada No. There is no federal law. (US law is a separate, shifting picture; very few patients cross the border for care here) It causes infertility No , as above Only single women have abortions 80% are unmarried, so 1 in 5 are in a committed relationship , and 60% already have children Women from religious backgrounds don't Abortion doesn't discriminate by culture, religion, ethnicity, income, relationship status or parity Products of conception are used in makeup, vaccines or unethical research Not accurate. Where tissue is used in research, it is with ethics approval and the patient's explicit, informed permission

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Learning Objectives Outline a clinical approach to both acute and chronic pelvic pain. Recognize common causes of acute and chronic pelvic pain. List a differential diagnosis for both acute and chronic pelvic pain. Outline appropriate investigations for pelvic pain. Identify treatment options for common causes of pelvic pain. Dr. Stephanie Black's 39-minute module — the first half of one deck that covers acute then chronic pelvic pain; the chronic half is 4.14 . Declared conflict: Bayer advisory board for intrauterine contraception (Mirena/Kyleena), neither of which features here. How she intends it to be used: the deck is built as clinical cases, and she explicitly prompts you to pause at each case and build a differential and an investigation plan before revealing the answer — alone or with colleagues. The case answers are given below each case on this page, so cover them if you want to work through it her way. She also teaches 4.13 .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: History and Physical Come First One bullet, deliberately. It is critical for developing the differential , and therefore for narrowing the investigations and the treatment plan. Note the third bullet. The gynecologist's role is often to rule gynecologic causes out . Patients present anywhere — primary care, walk-in, gynecology office, or the ER. Worth actually reading through once. Her instruction is to take a moment and familiarize yourself with it — and her warning is that because this is the repro block, the lecture will lead you down the gynecologic column, but you must not forget the other five when you are the one examining the patient. Figure from UpToDate on Dr. Black's slide; reproduced with permission from Howard FM, "Acute Abdominal Pain," in Primary Care for Women , Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. History of the Pain — OPQRST The standard pain history, applied here. Dr. Black's slide. Element What to ask Why it discriminates Onset What was she doing? Sudden or gradual? Her key example: woken from sleep by sudden pelvic pain vs pain starting during physical activity gives very different differentials — the second raises torsion and ruptured cyst Duration How long, and is it constant? Separates acute from chronic (see 4.14 ) Quality Sharp, stabbing, colicky, burning Colicky suggests a hollow viscus; sharp and stabbing suggests an acute vascular or rupture event Location + Radiation Where, and does it go anywhere? Shoulder tip → diaphragmatic irritation → blood in the peritoneum. Back → torsion or renal Aggravating / alleviating Rest, eating, movement, heat Worse on eating points GI; positional change points to hemoperitoneum Associated symptoms GI (constipation, diarrhea, gas) · GU (dysuria) · systemic (fever) · vaginal discharge · vaginal bleeding Each one recruits a different column of the table above Physical Exam Dr. Black's slide. Vital signs first — her reasoning: clinical instability sends you down the life-threatening path , so this is a triage step, not a formality. Overall appearance from the end of the bed — does she look genuinely sick and unwell, or fairly healthy despite the pain? A cheap and surprisingly discriminating observation. Abdomen: inspection, auscultation, palpation. Pelvic: inspection of the external genitalia, speculum inspection, and bimanual palpation — two fingers in the vagina, one hand on the abdomen, palpating the uterosacral ligament insertions , the uterus , and the adnexal regions . Don't stop at the pain histor

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 1: Katie, 25 Answer: ectopic pregnancy, likely ruptured. Dr. Black's slide. Reading This Case Five findings, each of which independently raises the diagnosis. β-hCG 2345 — she is pregnant, and condoms are a method with real typical-use failure. Sudden RLQ pain + vaginal bleeding — the classic pair. Hb 82 — she is bleeding internally ; you cannot see it. Shoulder pain — blood in the peritoneum irritating the diaphragm (see below). Tenesmus — blood pooling in the pouch of Douglas irritating the rectum. Lightheaded — hypovolemia. Put together: not just an ectopic, but a ruptured one, and she is unstable. 98% are tubal. And read the IUD footnote carefully — it is a classic exam distinction, unpacked below. The classic triad: pelvic pain + amenorrhea + vaginal bleeding. Confirmed with β-hCG + TVUS . The IUD Point, Stated Precisely Her slide footnote is worth quoting almost exactly, because the sloppy version is wrong: IUDs do NOT increase the incidence of ectopic pregnancy. What they increase is the likelihood that a pregnancy is ectopic if a pregnancy occurs with an IUD in situ. The mechanism is straightforward once stated: the IUD is very effective at preventing intrauterine implantation, so it removes intrauterine pregnancies from the denominator far more than extrauterine ones — the proportion shifts without the absolute risk rising. Practically: an IUD user with a positive pregnancy test needs an ectopic excluded urgently. Risk factors to know: pelvic infection · previous ectopic · smoking · adhesions · multiple sexual partners · IUD in situ (as qualified above). Other sites beyond the tube: ovarian, cervical, cornual, abdominal, and caesarean-section scar . And the reason this matters: ectopic pregnancy accounts for 4–10% of first-trimester deaths in pregnancy. On TVUS: an empty uterus (UT), the left ovary (L OV), and an adnexal structure separate from both — the ectopic. At laparoscopy: the distended, blood-filled tube, with free blood in the pelvis. Two distinct pain mechanisms, and both are examinable. The pelvic pain itself is visceral pain from stretching of the hollow fallopian tube — which is why it is poorly localized and colicky before rupture. The shoulder-tip pain is referred , from blood of a ruptured ectopic irritating the diaphragm : the diaphragm's phrenic innervation (C3–C5) shares dermatomes with the shoulder, so the brain misattributes the signal. Dr. Black's slide. The methotrexate criteria are the highest-yield list on this page.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 2: Sara, 17 Answer: PID. Note the discriminators from Case 1 — β-hCG negative , WBC 22 , systemic infective symptoms, and foul-smelling discharge . Dr. Black's slide. The "Chandelier Sign" Extreme cervical motion tenderness — the patient jumps toward the chandelier when the cervix is moved on bimanual exam. It signals peritoneal irritation of the upper genital tract and is a classic PID finding. Note also that Sara presented for a routine exam, not with an emergency — the diagnosis came from asking and examining. An acute infection of the UPPER genital tract — uterus, tubes, ovaries and surrounding abdominal organs. It is an ascending infection, hence sexually active women. Two named complications: tubo-ovarian abscess and Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome (perihepatic adhesions). The Definitional Point Her slide draws a line that is easy to miss: PID is specifically a community-acquired infection initiated by a sexually transmitted agent. That is what distinguishes it from pelvic infections caused by medical procedures , by pregnancy , or by other primary abdominal processes . So "pelvic infection" is not synonymous with PID, and the distinction changes both the likely organisms and the management. 4.6 covers PID in much greater depth, including the organisms, admission criteria and the 14-day rule — read the two together. Escalation for non-response: laparoscopy if the diagnosis is uncertain or she is not responding, and consideration of interventional-radiology drainage if still not responding — i.e. suspect a tubo-ovarian abscess that needs draining rather than more antibiotics.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 3: Helen, 45 Answer: ovarian torsion. Dr. Black's slide. Reading This Case — and What Rules Out the Others Onset during vigorous physical activity (stopped mid-golf-game) is the history feature she flagged in Part 1 as pointing here. Sharp, stabbing, radiating to the back , with vomiting and collapse — torsion hurts out of proportion and is strongly emetogenic. Then the exclusions: β-hCG <1 rules out ectopic; Hb 128 and stable rules out significant hemorrhage, which separates it from Case 4; temp 37.5 with no infective history makes PID unlikely. What is left is the 9 cm tender palpable mass — and a 9 cm ovary is exactly the size that torts. A surgical emergency — and the goal of the surgery is to preserve the ovary. Precipitants: intercourse, golf, vigorous exercise. The pathophysiology, which is a vicious cycle — see below. 1 The ovary rotates around both the infundibulopelvic (IP) ligament and the utero-ovarian ligament . 2 Compression of the IP ligament reduces venous outflow first, and eventually arterial inflow — because veins are thin-walled and collapse at lower pressures. 3 Arterial perfusion continues while outflow is blocked → the ovary becomes edematous and markedly enlarged . 4 That enlargement compresses the vessels further — the cycle tightens itself. 5 Ischemia → necrosis, infarction and local hemorrhage. Which is why the clock matters. At laparoscopy — the enlarged adnexal mass in situ. The delivered specimen — the sheer size is the point. An ovary this big acts "like a weighted pendulum." Untwist it, then judge whether it is salvageable — the surgery is ovary-preserving where possible. Two further points: a normal ovary can tort, just much less often ; and torsion is usually a symptom , so you must investigate the underlying ovarian mass and establish benign vs malignant. Dr. Black's slide.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 4: Lisa, 33 Answer: ruptured ovarian cyst with hemorrhage. Dr. Black's slide. Why This Isn't Case 1 — the Deliberate Near-Miss Notice how carefully this case is built to look like the ruptured ectopic: tenesmus, shoulder pain, lightheadedness, and a falling hemoglobin (110 → 78) are all Katie's findings, and for the same underlying reason — blood in the peritoneum . The one finding that separates them is β-hCG <1 : she is not pregnant, so it cannot be an ectopic. That is the whole lesson — hemoperitoneum has a characteristic presentation independent of its cause, and β-hCG is what tells you which cause you are dealing with. Two more features that fit: the LMP just over 2 weeks ago puts her right at ovulation , which is when these cysts rupture, and the pain began suddenly after intercourse — the blunt-trauma mechanism on the next slide. The postural vitals (110/70 with HR 80 lying, 86/55 with HR 112 standing) are the finding to actually copy into practice: her supine numbers look almost normal, and the instability only shows when she stands. Two mechanisms: spontaneously with ovulation, 2–3 weeks from the LMP , or secondary to blunt trauma (e.g. intercourse) if a cyst was already present . Her important caveat: significant bleeding is relatively uncommon — most ruptures bleed minimally or not at all. Lisa is the unusual case. Dr. Black's slide. Note "may repeat" the CBC — a single hemoglobin is a snapshot. Lisa's diagnosis rests on the trend , 110 falling to 78. Most often self-limited. Surgery only for ongoing bleeding or instability ; IR in selected cases. And prevent recurrence with ovulatory suppression . The Neat Ending — and a Conflict to Notice Ovulatory suppression prevents recurrence because these cysts rupture at ovulation — no ovulation, no corpus luteum cyst to rupture. It is the same "non-contraceptive benefit of a contraceptive" logic that runs through 4.10 and 4.13 . But note the clash the case sets up without stating it: Lisa is nulligravid and trying to conceive. An OCP prevents recurrence by preventing ovulation — which is precisely what she does not want. That tension, between treating the condition and respecting the patient's goal, is the same judgement Dr. Arntfield frames as "ask what her goals are" and Dr. Black frames as fertility-sparing treatment in 4.13 . Worth having an answer ready if it comes up in the small group.

Learning Objectives Describe the natural history and epidemiology of cervical cancer. Explain the role of HPV and the impact of vaccination on cervical cancer and screening. Know the eligibility for cervical screening and how samples are collected and evaluated. Summarize the rationale for the shift from cytology-based screening to primary HPV screening. Identify key cytology outcomes and the role of cytology in an HPV-based screening programme. Recognize the potential of cervical self-sampling. Dr. Cady Zeman, cytopathologist at London Health Sciences Centre. 39 minutes. She opens by flagging that the landscape is changing fast and this recording was made in summer 2025 — which is unusually honest and worth respecting when you read the numbers below.

HPV → SIL → Cancer The whole disease on one slide. Dr. Zeman's slide. 1 HPV infection , acquired during sexual contact. Most resolve on their own with no change to the epithelium at all. 2 A minority produce epithelial changes — SIL Squamous intraepithelial lesion. The current term. Older names for the same thing: CIN (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia) and dysplasia. . Most of these also resolve on their own. 3 A subset progresses to squamous cell carcinoma if untreated — typically over ten years or more . Terminology, all meaning the same thing: SIL (current) · CIN · dysplasia . Different eras, same epithelial changes. Why Cervical Cancer Is the Textbook Screening Target 1. The natural history is very well understood . 2. We can screen for precursors , not just the invasive cancer. 3. Progression is slow. Point 3 does the heavy lifting: because it takes 10+ years, a false negative on one round gets caught on the next — as long as screening happens at regular intervals . Screening is not a once-and-for-all event.

Epidemiology Canada, 1950s→1990s. Cervical cancer went from a leading cause of cancer death in women to a steadily falling one — because of screening programmes catching precursors. Further recent falls also reflect vaccination . The global picture is very different. In Canada Worldwide Most commonly diagnosed cancer 16th 4th Cause of cancer death 17th 4th The global burden is driven by very high rates in economically disadvantaged regions that lack screening programmes and vaccination access . And the Canadian success is not complete: there are still gains to be made in under-screened communities and among people facing barriers to screening — which is the argument self-sampling rests on, at the bottom of this page.

Low Risk vs High Risk Over 100 types. Cutaneous types infect skin (hand, face warts). Mucosal types are the ones that matter here, split into low risk and high risk . She is normally not a fan of memorisation, and says so — but memorise these . Low risk: HPV 6, 11 High risk: HPV 16, 18, the 30s, 45 Produces Warts and LSIL LSIL or HSIL Cancer? No — non-oncogenic Yes — oncogenic Dr. Zeman's slide. The Consequence She Wants You to Draw Because both low-risk and high-risk HPV can produce LSIL , seeing "LSIL" on a report does not tell you which type caused it — not unless HPV testing has been done. But HSIL can only come from high-risk HPV , and HSIL is the lesion that becomes cancer. HSIL is what screening exists to find.

entries.t: How Common, and Who Is at Risk
entries.x: How Common, and Who Is at Risk Dr. Zeman's slide. At least 75% of people are exposed in their lifetime — though this may fall with vaccination. Transmitted by sexual contact including intimate skin-to-skin contact . Condoms are only partially protective , because they do not cover all the skin involved. Risk factors: multiple partners · early onset of sexual activity · a high-risk partner · cigarette smoking . Why Smoking, of All Things? The suggested mechanism is that smoking interferes with immune surveillance , so the body is less able to clear an HPV infection . That gives you something concrete to offer: a patient with persistent SIL who smokes can be counselled to quit , because it may improve her chance of clearing the infection. That is a real, actionable piece of advice — not just generic smoking-cessation boilerplate.

Vaccination Three vaccines over 20 years. Available in Canada since 2006. The current schedule. Vaccine Covers Note Cervarix HPV 16, 18 The two commonest high-risk types — 70% of cervical cancers Gardasil (quadrivalent) HPV 16, 18 + 6, 11 Adds the low-risk types responsible for 90% of genital warts Gardasil 9 (nonavalent) The above + 5 more high-risk types Available since 2017 ; the one used in Canada today Group Schedule Age 9–20 1 dose — recently reduced from two Age 21–26 2 doses Age 27 and older 2 doses Immunocompromised, including people living with HIV 3 doses Two "Why" Questions Worth Being Able to Answer Why grade 7 in Ontario? Two reasons: the risk of previous HPV exposure is low at that age, and preteens mount a better immune response than older teens — independent of exposure. That better response is also why one dose now suffices under 21. Why vaccinate an adult who's already been exposed, or who has had abnormal cytology? Because there are many HPV types . The vaccine likely covers types that person hasn't met yet. That is where the benefit lies. What the data show so far: a drop in oncogenic HPV detection , a drop in cervical pre-cancer (SIL) , and a marked drop in genital warts . And now, cancer itself. She notes that 6–7 years ago she could not have said this — the progression is so slow that the evidence took time. Two key early studies ( 2020 and 2021 ) showed substantial reductions in cervical cancer in vaccinated populations . Vaccinated people are still screened. The vaccine is not perfect and does not cover every high-risk type, so SIL and cancer remain possible. Vaccination does not replace screening.

Eligibility Dr. Zeman's slide. Three conditions, and each one has a reason: Criterion Why Asymptomatic This is a screening programme. An abnormal-looking cervix or concerning symptoms needs investigation, not a Pap test. Do not let a normal screening result reassure you out of a proper work-up Ever sexually active HPV is sexually acquired , so there is nothing to find before that Age ~25 (25 in Ontario) Screening younger does not prevent cancer in that age group — progression is too slow for it to pay off. She notes the age could move later still

Collection Provider-collected is still the main route: speculum in, cervix visualised, brush or spatula to scrape cells. Aim for the transformation zone — where endocervical columnar cells undergo metaplasia into ectocervical squamous cells . It is the commonest site for dysplasia and cancer . The "don't get your sample rejected" slide. Dr. Zeman's slide. Reminder Detail Know your collection system ThinPrep (used in Ontario): do NOT leave the broom/brush in the vial — the sample will likely be rejected. SurePath : the device may be left in Lubricant Lukewarm water is preferred. If gel is needed it must be water-based, applied sparingly to the outer blades, avoiding the tip . Lubricant interferes with cellularity and specimen adequacy Labelling Two identifiers — full legal name and date of birth — plus the collection date Expiry Check the vial's expiry date before you use it. Expired vial = rejected sample Requisition Complete it before sending

The Outcomes Traditional cytology-based screening: vial → glass slide → microscope → report. What the pathologist hunts for is HPV-associated epithelial changes . Dr. Zeman's slide. NILM — 95% of screening samples. Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. Normal mature squamous cells. LSIL. The classic cell is a koilocyte — binucleated, with a perinuclear halo . HSIL. Big irregular nuclei, very high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. This is the lesion screening exists to catch. Squamous cell carcinoma. Very uncommon to see on a Pap test. The gradient of concern, with the "not sure" categories added. Dr. Zeman's slide. Result Means Clinician treats it as NILM Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. 95% of samples Normal LSIL Low grade squamous intraepithelial lesion Low grade ASC-US Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance . Differential: normal or LSIL Low grade ASC-H Atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude a high grade lesion . Differential: normal or HSIL High grade HSIL High grade squamous intraepithelial lesion High grade SqCC Squamous cell carcinoma High grade What ASC-US and ASC-H Actually Are They are the pathologist saying "I'm not certain." ASC-US means this might be normal, it might be LSIL . ASC-H means this might be normal, it might be HSIL — and because the downside of missing HSIL is so much worse, ASC-H is managed as a high grade result . Dr. Zeman's slide. The Pap test is a screening test for squamous abnormalities. It is not a good test for glandular abnormalities — but sometimes they turn up almost by accident, and they are often hard to classify. Terms you may see: AIS (adenocarcinoma in situ), atypical glandular cells , atypical endocervical cells , atypical endometrial cells . Cytology result Management under the old cytology-based programme NILM Repeat routine screening in 3 years Low grade (LSIL, ASC-US) Repeat at an interval; if persistent , refer to colposcopy High grade (ASC-H, HSIL, SqCC) Refer to colposcopy Glandular Colposcopy , sometimes with endometrial sampling

Why Change Something That Worked? Dr. Zeman's slide. 1 HPV is the cause. It makes more sense to test for the causative agent than for an intermediate step. 2 Cytology gets worse in a vaccinated population. Vaccination lowers the prevalence of SIL and cancer — and positive predictive value depends on prevalence . As prevalence falls, the PPV of cytology falls with it. The test that served for decades literally works less well now . 3 The evidence is overwhelming. From roughly 2006–2015 there was an abundance of randomised controlled trials and meta-analyses showing HPV screening outperforms cytology. HPV testing beats cytology on Meaning Sensitivity Detects more high-grade lesions Earlier detection Finds them sooner Long-term protection After a negative HPV test , far fewer high-grade lesions turn up in later rounds than after a negative cytology Negative predictive value Very high — which is what justifies the 5-year interval Cancer prevention Greater protection against cancer overall The One Catch — and Why Cytology Survives HPV testing has a lower positive predictive value . A positive HPV test does not mean you have a high grade lesion or cancer — there are more "false positives" than with cytology. So HPV screening has to be paired with a more specific test , and that test is cytology . HPV finds who might have a problem; cytology sorts out who actually does. That is the entire logic of the algorithm below.

The Algorithm The one-line version. Molecular testing for high-risk HPV first; cytology only as triage, only if high-risk HPV is present . The full pathway, from the Canadian guidelines (Zigras et al., Curr Oncol 2023;30:5652–79). She calls it a confusing diagram, which it is. Ontario switched in March 2025 , joining two other provinces; most others have plans to follow. The sample is still collected the same way — it is what the lab does first that changed. HPV result Next step Negative Return to screening in 5 years Positive for HPV 16 or 18 Reflex cytology is made up, but she goes to colposcopy regardless of the cytology result — these are the highest-risk of the high-risk types. The cytology is still informative, just not decisive Positive for another high-risk type — reflex cytology shows HSIL, ASC-H or glandular abnormality Colposcopy Positive for another high-risk type — reflex cytology NILM, ASC-US or LSIL Repeat HPV testing in 1 year At the 1-year repeat: HPV negative Return to screening in 5 years At the 1-year repeat: HPV 16/18 positive Colposcopy At the 1-year repeat: other high-risk type Reflex cytology again, and the same loop repeats — eventually she either goes to colposcopy or returns to routine screening She notes that each jurisdiction will vary this theme , particularly in how it handles high-risk types other than 16 and 18, and that the number of repeat rounds may differ. The shape — HPV first, cytology as triage, 16/18 fast-tracked to colposcopy — is the part to hold onto.

Collecting Your Own Sample No speculum required. The sample is vaginal , mostly vaginal cells with only rare cervical cells — but HPV testing is sensitive enough that this still works . The pathway differs in one important way. Self-sample result Next step HPV negative Routine screening in 5 years — same as provider-collected HPV 16 or 18 positive Directly to colposcopy. No cytology slide is made — this is a vaginal sample, not a cervical one , so there is no indication for cytology Other high-risk type She must come back for a provider-collected sample so cytology can be done, and then enters the same loop as above Why do it: it increases access for under-screened and never-screened people — exactly the group where Canada's remaining cervical cancer burden sits. It also has high acceptability in the general population. Australia has offered it to all screen-eligible people since 2022 . British Columbia included specific populations in its rollout. Where the Evidence Actually Sits — Her Honest Answer Is self-sampling as sensitive as provider sampling? As of 2025, the jury is still out. The doubts are specific: 1. Some of the original data is old. 2. Some meta-analyses showing equivalency may have included people with high viral loads , which would inflate self-collection performance. 3. Some population-based implementation studies have cast doubt. She expects forthcoming unpublished data to support equivalency , and describes her position as cautious optimism . This is a good example of a lecturer separating what we know from what we expect — worth imitating.

Summary Dr. Zeman's closing slide. Cervical cancer is preventable through vaccination and screening. HPV is the cause. Vaccination changed the screening landscape — and is a major reason for the move to primary HPV screening. Primary HPV screening is superior , especially in vaccinated populations. Self-sampling is promising but not settled. Cervical cancer could become the first major cancer we eliminate — if the tools are actually used. Her recommended resource: Cancer Care Ontario's HPV Testing Implementation Resource Hub , which is current because Ontario has just made the transition.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Learning Objectives Outline a clinical approach to both acute and chronic pelvic pain. Recognize common causes of acute and chronic pelvic pain. List a differential diagnosis for both acute and chronic pelvic pain. Outline appropriate investigations for pelvic pain. Identify treatment options for common causes of pelvic pain. Dr. Stephanie Black's 40-minute module — the second half of the deck that begins with 4.15 Acute Pelvic Pain . The general approach — the pain history (OPQRST), the physical exam, the past/social history and the investigations — is on that page and is not repeated here ; read it first. Like the acute module, this one is built as clinical cases with the answer on the slide, and she intends you to pause and build your own differential before revealing it . Two of the five cases are covered in far more depth elsewhere and are cross-linked rather than duplicated: 4.13 Endometriosis is her own separate module using the same slides, and the pathology of adenomyosis and leiomyoma is Dr. Weir's 4.12 .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
entries.x: The Approach, and the Numbers The second and third bullets are the clinical skill being taught here. Listening is an intervention , not a preamble to one. The three-part definition plus the four numbers. 40% of laparoscopies and 20% of hysterectomies for benign disease are done for this. Criterion Requirement Duration At least 6 months Location Below the umbilicus Severity Severe enough to cause functional disability or require treatment An entire slide for one statistic, which tells you how much weight she puts on it. Up to 50%. Note that "physical and sexual abuse" also appears in the differential table below under mental health, and resurfaces in Case 5 — this is not a single aside but a thread running through the lecture. Dr. Black's slide. The most important conceptual slide in the module. Dr. Black's slide. Why This Distinction Changes Management Acute pain is protective — it signals tissue damage and drives you to act, which is exactly the logic of 4.15 , where the pain points at a ruptured ectopic or a torted ovary that needs fixing now . Chronic pain serves no physiologic purpose — it is no longer a reliable report about tissue. Two consequences follow, and both are on her slides: pain intensity is often not proportional to tissue damage , so a normal laparoscopy does not mean the pain isn't real; and the therapeutic goal shifts from finding a lesion to cure toward reducing pain and restoring function — which is exactly how she frames the goal in Case 5. This also explains the uncomfortable statistic above: if 40% of laparoscopies are done for CPP, a lot of them find nothing, and the diagnostic reflex of "look inside for the lesion" is a poor fit for a pain that isn't reporting a lesion.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
entries.x: The Differential Five categories of origin. Note the last bullet again — she repeats it here rather than leaving it on the previous slide. Dr. Black's slide. Long, but the asterisks are the whole point — the footnote says they mark the most common causes of CPP, backed by substantial evidence. Those seven are extracted into the table below. Note how few of them are gynecologic. Table from UpToDate on Dr. Black's slide. Category The evidence-backed common causes Gynecologic Endometriosis · chronic pelvic inflammatory disease Urinary tract Interstitial cystitis / painful bladder syndrome Gastrointestinal Irritable bowel syndrome Musculoskeletal Pelvic floor myalgia · myofascial pain (trigger points) Neurologic Neuralgia — especially iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral or pudendal nerves The Take-Away From That Table Only two of the seven best-evidenced causes are gynecologic. Two are musculoskeletal, one urologic, one GI, one neurologic. That is a strong argument against reflexively treating chronic pelvic pain as a gynecologic problem — and it is the structural reason Case 5 ends with a multidisciplinary team rather than an operation. It also explains her own remark on that case slide: "differentiating the cause of pain may be difficult for the gynecologist." Worth also noticing the mental health block in the full table — somatization, substance use, physical and sexual abuse , depression, sleep disorders. Given the 50% abuse/trauma figure, these are not afterthoughts in the differential.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 1: Jessica, 19 Answer: primary dysmenorrhea. Dr. Black's slide. Why This Is Primary Everything in the history is consistent with a normal cycle producing pain: regular 29-day cycles , heavier flow in the first two days , and pain that lessens as the cycle goes on — i.e. the pain tracks the flow. Compare with Case 2 (the same patient six years later), where pain begins 2 days before menses and is worsening — the two features that mark it out as secondary . Dr. Weir makes the same primary-vs-secondary cut in 4.12 : primary is functional and younger, secondary is structural and acquired, and therefore commoner with age. The mechanism, and it is a proper physiological chain — unpacked below. No lab abnormalities. No abnormal physical findings. A clinical diagnosis. Which means the history is the entire test. 1 Menses is a generalized inflammatory state. 2 Prostaglandins released from endometrial sloughing at the beginning of menses induce uterine contractions . 3 When uterine pressure exceeds arterial pressure , the myometrium's own blood supply is cut off → uterine ischemia . 4 Ischemia means anaerobic metabolites accumulate , and these stimulate type C pain neurons → dysmenorrhea . Why the Two Treatments Work, and Why Each One Works The mechanism tells you both drugs directly. NSAIDs work at step 2 — they inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, so there are fewer and weaker contractions and pressure never exceeds arterial pressure. Ovulatory suppression (e.g. the OCP) works upstream of step 1: as her sub-bullet says, hormonal medications that reduce menstrual blood flow improve dysmenorrhea — less endometrium to slough means less prostaglandin released. That is the same "thin the endometrium" logic as in 4.10 and 4.13 , arriving at the same drugs from a third direction.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 2: Jessica, now 25 Answer: endometriosis. The same patient, six years on — a nice piece of teaching design, because it isolates exactly which features changed. Dr. Black's slide. This Case Is Covered in Full Elsewhere The nine endometriosis slides that follow in this deck are the same slides as Dr. Black's separate 15-minute endometriosis module , so they are not duplicated here. Go to 4.13 Endometriosis for the definition and epidemiology, the three etiologic theories, the dyspareunia approach, the physical findings, the full treatment ladder (pseudopregnancy vs pseudomenopause), the complications, and the laparoscopic appearances. The pathology is in 4.12 . The four features that changed from Case 1, and what each one signals: the pain now begins before menses (not prostaglandin-driven flow pain) · it is much worse than before (acquired, progressive) · it radiates down her left leg (disease beyond the uterus) · and there is new deep dyspareunia (deep, so masses, adhesions or endometriosis — see the deep-vs-superficial split in 4.13).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 3: Jessica, now 42 Answer: adenomyosis. The same patient again, now 42 and parous. Dr. Black's slide. Every Clause in This Case Is Doing Work Three successful pregnancies — adenomyosis is a disease of parous women; Dr. Weir's balloon model in 4.12 explains why it essentially requires a term pregnancy. Now 42 — it presents in the 4th and 5th decades . Periods less painful than before but much heavier — the endometriosis was treated, and this is a new problem dominated by bleeding rather than pain. Bleeding through her clothing despite continuous OCPs — failure of medical management, which in 4.12 is precisely the route by which adenomyosis gets diagnosed. A heavy pelvic sensation — the diffusely enlarged uterus. And no hot flashes or night sweats — that clause is there to rule out menopause as the explanation for her changing periods at 42. Note the enormous incidence range, 5–70% — a consequence of it being an incidental histological finding, so the number depends entirely on who gets a hysterectomy. Dr. Weir's figure for resected uteri is 15–30%. Tender, enlarged, boggy uterus — the three-word exam finding to memorize. Mostly a clinical diagnosis. The gross specimen: globally enlarged , thick trabeculated myometrium , with small dark haemorrhagic cystic foci — entrapped blood in ectopic endometrium that is still cycling. The full pathology, including why this produces both the bleeding and the pain, is in 4.12 . Dr. Black's slide. On ultrasound: a heterogeneous myometrium with an indistinct endometrial–myometrial junction . On MRI: the arrows mark a widened, heterogeneous junctional zone . This is the most specific imaging finding — but note her slide still says imaging is only sometimes helpful. The ladder again, ending differently from endometriosis: hysterectomy is the gold standard here , not a last resort — because the disease is the uterine wall, so there is nothing to excise short of removing the uterus. Dr. Black's slide. Adenomyosis vs Endometriosis — Side by Side The deck puts these two cases three slides apart, and the contrast is the payoff. Endometriosis (Case 2) Adenomyosis (Case 3) Where the endometrium is Outside the uterus Deep within the myometrium Typical age 20s–30s 4th–5th decades Parity Often nulliparous / infertile Parous — uncommon in nulligravids Dominant symptom Pain — dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia Menorrhagia , sometimes dysmenorrhea, heavy pelvic sensation Exam Uterosacral nodularity, fixed uterus, adnexal mass — or nothi

entries.x: Case 4: Erica, 35 Answer: fibroids. Dr. Black's slide. Two Details That Decide the Management "20-week size, mobile uterus." Mobile matters — in 4.10 Dr. Arntfield teaches that benign enlargement stays mobile while malignancy fixes the pelvic structures. And at 35 with a mobile, slowly enlarging, presumably multiple-fibroid uterus, this is not the leiomyosarcoma pattern Dr. Weir warns about in 4.12 (single dominant rapidly growing mass in a peri/postmenopausal woman). "Wishing to achieve a pregnancy." This is the constraint that makes the treatment section meaningful. It rules out hysterectomy, and — as her own slide notes further down — pregnancy after uterine artery embolization is not advised . It also rules out the ovulatory suppression that would otherwise be first line. In practice it points at myomectomy , or hysteroscopic resection if the fibroid is submucosal. Benign monoclonal tumours of uterine smooth muscle. ~50% of women over 40 have them on imaging, and not all are symptomatic . Risk factors — and note the oddity at the bottom: smoking is associated with less risk of fibroids. Not a reason to smoke; a reason to remember estrogen is the driver. Four symptom groups. Two have an important qualifier attached: AUB is commoner with submucosal fibroids, and infertility comes from fibroids that distort the uterine cavity — so in both cases it is the location , not the size, that predicts the symptom. Plus degeneration , which causes pain, bleeding or pregnancy loss. Dr. Black's slide. Location Determines Everything Subserosal — bulging outward under the serosa. Causes pressure and mass effect . Intramural — within the wall. The commonest site. Submucosal / intracavitary — protruding into the cavity. The one that bleeds and causes infertility . Pedunculated fibroids carry a risk of torsion — which links this chronic-pain lecture straight back to the surgical emergency in 4.15 . Same principle as ovarian torsion: a mass on a stalk acts as a weighted pendulum. Dr. Black's slide. Treatment The two variables are location and symptoms — not size alone. Medical options are the familiar ovulatory-suppression list. Dr. Black's slide. Submucosal → hysteroscopic resection — no abdominal incision, and it targets exactly the fibroids causing bleeding and infertility. Large and pedunculated → myomectomy or hysterectomy , by laparoscopy or laparotomy. Myomectomy is the uterus-sparing option — the relevant one for Erica. Uterine artery embolization. The hypothesis:

entries.x: Case 5: Mya, 23 Answer: myofascial pelvic pain. Dr. Black's slide. How This Case Excludes Everything Before It Read it as a systematic set of negatives. "Not associated with any time in her cycle" and "cycles are regular" — rules out dysmenorrhea, endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids, all of which are cycle-linked. Nulliparous at 23 — wrong demographic for adenomyosis and fibroids. Midline mobile uterus, no adnexal masses — no structural lesion. What remains is globally tender pelvis and pain so severe the speculum exam could not be done at all . That last detail is the finding, not a gap in the assessment. And note the functional cost, which is the definition's third criterion in action: it prevents her from working or attending school , and she is not sexually active because of the pain — five years of it, starting at 18. High resting tone in the muscles and fascia attaching to the bony pelvis — specifically levator ani and piriformis . Dr. Black's slide. The Chicken-and-Egg Point, Which Is the Real Lesson Her first bullet says myofascial pain may develop in response to pain caused by gynecologic disease — or arise independently from faulty body mechanics . So it can be both a consequence of endometriosis or fibroids and a cause of pain in its own right, which means treating the gynecologic lesion may not resolve the pain , and the pelvic floor may need treating separately. That is why "differentiating the cause of pain may be difficult for the gynecologist," and it ties back to "pain intensity is often not proportional to tissue damage" from the start of the lecture: a woman with treated endometriosis and persistent pain has not necessarily failed treatment — she may have acquired a second, muscular pain generator. Multidisciplinary is the operative word. Manual soft tissue release is "essential" — physiotherapy is core treatment, not an adjunct. Plus trigger-point local anaesthetic injection . Amitriptyline and gabapentin — neuropathic agents, not analgesics, consistent with pain that no longer reports tissue damage. And the honest framing of the goal. 1 The team: gynecologist + physiotherapist + pain treatment service + psychiatry/psychotherapy as needed. 2 Manual soft tissue release to reduce pelvic floor resting tone and tension — her slide calls this essential . 3 Local anaesthetic injection at trigger points where helpful. 4 Amitriptyline or gabapentin as pharmacological aids. 5 Psychotherapy and support — "invaluable," particularly given the h

Learning Objectives List contraceptive options and their failure rates. Counsel regarding the most effective contraceptive methods. Understand the mechanism of action of contraceptive options. Discuss emergency contraception options. Apply new knowledge to clinical case scenarios. Dr. Stephanie Black, whose fellowship was in family planning. Disclosure given in the lecture: she has had a financial arrangement with Bayer, which makes the hormonal IUDs (Mirena and Kyleena); there are no competitor products. The drugs themselves are covered in 4.4 .

Why This Conversation Matters Up to half of pregnancies are unintended (not necessarily unwanted, but unplanned). 22% of all pregnancies end in induced abortion , and half of those are in people aged 20–29. People stop methods without telling us. 42% stop without consulting anyone, 19% stop with no replacement, and 69% of those switching move to something less effective. That's why you ask about contraception often, not once. The baseline: 850 per 1,000 become pregnant within a year with no method. Also worth knowing: about 1,200 days in a reproductive lifetime when fertilization is possible. The chart to know. Ranked by effectiveness, with perfect use (middle) and typical use (right). Counsel from the typical-use column : patients use methods typically, not perfectly. SOGC, from the lecture.

Natural Family Planning Failure 12–25% , but worth knowing: it may be the only acceptable method for some patients, and it beats no method at all. Method How it works, and the catch Basal body temperature Thermometer at the bedside, taken before getting out of bed . A rise of 0.2–0.5°C marks the LH surge and ovulation. The catch: by the time it rises, ovulation has already happened Rhythm / calendar Needs a genuinely predictable cycle and a 14-day luteal phase; requires avoiding intercourse for many days Cervical mucus Clear, stretchy mucus that doesn't break between finger and thumb ( spinnbarkeit ) means the LH surge. Same catch as temperature Withdrawal Sperm can be present in pre-ejaculate, and timing errors are common Lactational amenorrhea Needs all of: <6 months postpartum , fully or nearly fully breastfeeding with no gaps over 4 hours , and no return of menses . The catch: menses returning means she already ovulated — you can miss the boat

Barrier Methods The most commonly used method worldwide , and the only one that also prevents STIs. Typical-use failure 180 per 1,000 (18%) vs 2% perfect use. Why the typical-use rate is so much worse. Note "removing the condom before ejaculation": done without the partner's knowledge, this is stealthing , a form of reproductive coercion. Oil-based lubricant breaks down latex. Material matters: latex protects against STIs; polyurethane slips and breaks more; lambskin gives no HIV protection and limited STI protection (it's porous). Nonoxynol-9 is not recommended. No added effectiveness, and it damages vaginal epithelium, increasing HIV transmission . Condom use drops when a hormonal method is added , so counsel that condoms are for STIs as well as pregnancy. Fit is a real barrier, and a solvable one. Standard condoms vary by only a couple of centimetres; companies like TheyFit/myONE ship 60 sizes to Canada with a printable sizer, so "they don't fit" is not a reason to go without. Diaphragm and cervical cap: rarely used now. The cap must be fitted to the individual and is less effective in multiparous women (the cervix changes shape after delivery). Fitting kits are almost impossible to find. The Caya is a one-size diaphragm sold over the counter, but its effectiveness is not well studied. The sponge has largely disappeared with the spermicide it needed. From the lecture.

Permanent Contraception Tubal interruption: rings, clips, cautery, salpingectomy or fimbriectomy. Ten-year failure <2% . Use contraception for a week afterwards : an ovum may already be in transit. Vasectomy beats tubal ligation on every axis : safer, more effective ( 1 per 2,000 ), cheaper, done under local without entering the abdomen. It needs a semen analysis at 3 months ; relying on it before that is the commonest cause of failure. Salpingectomy (removing the tubes) is increasingly done: it adds little time or risk, and about 30% of serous ovarian cancers may start in the fallopian tube , so it is risk-reducing. Regret is one of the most common complications , especially when young — but a young patient who understands that it is not reversible , and knows the cost of IVF or reversal, should be able to access it . Hysteroscopic occlusion (Essure) — historical. Coils placed through the cervix caused tissue to grow in and block the tubes, confirmed by HSG at 3 months , with contraception needed until then. It was voluntarily withdrawn after reports of pain and device erosion. You may still meet patients who have them, sometimes wanting them out, which is difficult because of the scarring the device is designed to cause. From the lecture.

The Medical Eligibility Criteria Four categories. 1 and 2 = generally safe. 3 = avoid unless other methods have failed or are unacceptable. 4 = absolute contraindication. There's an app for this (CDC MEC), and it's worth having. From the lecture.

Progestin-Only Methods The "mini-pill", taken at the same time every day. Failure 90 per 1,000 . In Canada: Movisse (norethindrone) and Slynd (drospirenone). Suppresses ovulation in about 50% . Depo-Provera (DMPA): 150 mg IM every 12–13 weeks (there's enough drug for 14). Failure 60 per 1,000 , better than the pill because it doesn't depend on daily use. How progestin-only methods work: thicker cervical mucus, impaired sperm motility, less tubal cilia activity (so the ovum is more likely to undergo apoptosis in transit), and, depending on the method, suppressed ovulation. Because there's no estrogen , they can be used immediately postpartum and post-abortion , and VTE risk isn't an issue. Benefits beyond contraception. Amenorrhea in about 70% by 24 months. Reduced endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, endometriosis symptoms, PMS and chronic pelvic pain, and fewer seizures (it doesn't interfere with anti-epileptics and raises the seizure threshold). The three things to counsel about. Bone density, the delay in fertility, and weight. Three Depo Myths, Corrected "You can only use it for 2 years." Not true. Bone mineral density falls in the first two years then stabilizes , the loss is reversible on stopping (up to 98% returns, even in those who used it to menopause), and the size of the drop is similar to what happens in a term pregnancy or while breastfeeding . No fractures or osteoporosis have been attributed to it. "You need bone density screening on it." Not true either. What is true: the return of fertility is delayed — an average of 9 months , longer the longer it's been used (the only reversible method where this happens). And Depo is the only contraceptive clinically proven to cause weight gain : about 7 lb in the first year , with early gain predicting more. Counsel that it's an appetite stimulant , so she can get ahead of it. The implant (Nexplanon): a single 4 cm rod of 68 mg etonogestrel in the inner upper arm (non-dominant side). Failure 1 per 2,000 (0.05%) — the same as vasectomy. It reliably inhibits ovulation into year 3. Approved in Canada in 2020 ; the FDA has since extended use to 5 years and Health Canada will likely follow. Very high satisfaction, usually lighter periods, but counsel about irregular bleeding . From the lecture.

Combined Hormonal Contraception Failure 90 per 1,000 — the same as the progestin-only pill, the patch and the ring. The progestin does the contraception (suppresses the LH surge, thickens mucus); the estrogen mainly controls bleeding. Which progestin, and why it matters. Levonorgestrel is highly androgenic (8.3) so it's a poor choice for acne; drospirenone and cyproterone have zero androgenic activity , so they help it. A piece of history from the lecture: the pill was meant to be progestin-only. The original batch was accidentally contaminated with estrogen; when they made a clean progestin-only version, women reported bloating, breast tenderness and nuisance bleeding — so the estrogen went back in. 16% of Canadian women aged 15–49 use a combined method, and about 44% of those using prescribed contraception use the pill . Continuous or extended use, skipping the hormone-free interval, is safe. Dose range: 10–35 µg of estrogen — all "low dose" compared with the original 60–70+ µg pills. No study shows 10 µg has less VTE risk than 35 µg : the risk is so low that the trial isn't feasible. The patch: changed weekly for 3 weeks, then a hormone-free week (or used continuously). Four sites. May be less effective over 90 kg — which is a counselling point, not a ban. The ring has the same failure rate but two edges: it suppresses folliculogenesis better than the pill (useful if she gets breakthrough bleeding or escape ovulation), and the local dose makes it better for peri-rectal endometriosis . Leave it in for intercourse; it can be out for up to 3 hours in 24 . The commonest complaint is increased discharge . If insertion is hard, a cardboard tampon applicator works — never a plastic one, whose teeth can scratch the slow-release surface. From the lecture. The absolute (category 4) contraindications — almost all because of the estrogen. The ones you'll actually meet in young, otherwise healthy patients: smoking >15/day over age 35 , uncontrolled hypertension , any DVT/PE history or thrombophilia , and migraine with aura (stroke risk). Most of these are fine with a progestin-only method or an IUD. From the lecture. Problem on the pill Adjustment Breakthrough bleeding Higher estrogen dose Acne or hirsutism Avoid androgenic progestins; use drospirenone or cyproterone PMDD Yaz (24/4) is the only COC approved for it Mood swings with hormone fluctuation Avoid triphasic pills; use a monophasic Depression or irritability Lower progestin potency Headaches Lower estrogen E

Copper IUD vs Hormonal IUS "Forgettable" contraception , and that's exactly why it works so well. 80% still in place at a year. The strings can be trimmed so short they can't be felt or seen — which matters for someone experiencing reproductive coercion . Canadian devices are T-shaped , so they need a normally shaped cavity. From the lecture. Copper IUD: 8 per 1,000. Copper ions cause a sterile inflammatory reaction that makes the endometrium hostile, bind sperm and impair their motility and the acrosome reaction, and accelerate ovum apoptosis. Downside: heavier, more painful periods. Upside: it doubles as EC. Hormonal IUS: 2 per 1,000. Kyleena (19.5 mg, 5 years) and Mirena (52 mg), which is also indicated for heavy menstrual bleeding . Works mainly through cervical mucus , plus decidualization, glandular atrophy, and ovulation inhibition in up to 40%. Why the Hormonal IUS Beats the Copper IUD on Failure Rate Their main mechanisms differ. The IUS works through cervical mucus , so even if it sits low in the uterus it still works. The copper IUD needs copper ions distributed throughout the cavity , so it has to be properly positioned to be fully effective. That is thought to explain much of the 2-vs-8 difference. There are very few. The ones you'll see: current pregnancy , current PID or cervicitis , and a distorted cavity (bicornuate uterus, large septum). Note that progestin-receptor-positive breast cancer rules out only the hormonal IUS — a copper IUD is still fine. None of the estrogen contraindications apply here. From the lecture.

Emergency Contraception Use it as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse. If the last period is unknown or unreliable, confirm a negative pregnancy test first: EC is not an abortifacient and does not work once pregnant . Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (Plan B): one dose, best within 72 h , usable to 5 days. It delays ovulation by affecting follicular development — so it is useless once the LH rise has begun . Available over the counter . Ulipristal acetate 30 mg (Ella): an SPRM that directly inhibits follicular rupture , so it still works during the LH rise — which makes it better than Plan B, especially on days 4–5 . Not effective after the surge. Prescription only, and often not stocked. The copper IUD is the most effective EC , works up to 7 days , and leaves her with ongoing contraception: 80% still have it at 12 months . The ranking, by day. Cu-IUD (0.01% at every time point) > ulipristal > levonorgestrel > Yuzpe. The Yuzpe method (ethinyl estradiol 100 µg + levonorgestrel 500 µg, 12 h apart, using ordinary pills) was developed here in London , but causes a lot of nausea and is now a last resort. SOGC consensus, from the lecture.

The Contraceptive CHOICE Project 7,486 participants at risk of unintended pregnancy in the Chicago area got proper counselling (30–60 minutes covering effectiveness, side effects, risks and benefits of all methods) and then their method of choice, free, for three years . Continuation at 3 years: LARCs 83–88% vs about 50% for Depo, pills, patch and ring. And the failures: under 1% for LARC across three years vs 9.4% for pill/patch/ring. The hazard ratio is 21.8 . The lesson: when cost is removed and counselling is accurate, most people choose a LARC, regardless of age or parity . The reasons they usually don't are provider bias, misinformation and cost — all three of which are on us.

The Three Cases Case The issue What fits Clarise, 18, G0 New partner, on condoms. Mother had a DVT after surgery, sister had a PE on the pill. Afraid of weight gain Strong family history of VTE in first-degree relatives → possible hereditary thrombophilia (e.g. factor V Leiden). She also names weight as a concern Avoid estrogen until thrombophilia testing. Avoid Depo (the only method proven to cause weight gain). That leaves the progestin-only pill, either IUD, or the implant — all valid Beth, 41, G2P2 Done childbearing, light regular periods, non-smoker, tired of daily pills, no drug coverage, often goes 2–3 months with nothing Cost is the barrier Copper IUD : only $30–75 and lasts 5–10 years, and her periods are already light. Or permanent contraception , which is covered by OHIP . A hormonal IUS at $350–500 up front won't work for someone who struggles with $25–30 a month Tara, 36, G6T1P1A4L1 PID two years ago, very heavy but predictable periods, 1 pack/day, cannabis and IV drug use, hep C and HIV positive, not compliant with medications, homeless, being trafficked Estrogen is absolutely contraindicated (smoking >15/day over 35). Cost, adherence and clinic attendance are all barriers, and she is at very high risk of unintended pregnancy A LARC . Despite that history there is no contraindication to an IUD : her PID was over 2 years ago, and being immunocompromised is not a barrier. A hormonal IUS also treats her heavy periods (compassionate-supply programs exist through the SOGC). Consider prophylactic STI treatment with same-day insertion after a negative pregnancy test, since she may not return for swab results

entries.t: The Summary the Lecture Ends On
entries.x: The Summary the Lecture Ends On Most women need effective contraception for most of their reproductive life. LARCs are highly acceptable and effective and should be offered preferentially, at any age and any parity. Encourage condoms as backup and for STI protection — especially here, where London has some of the highest chlamydia rates in the country. If she picks a less effective method or none, discuss emergency contraception and how to get it before she needs it. Permanent contraception needs a conversation about regret. Natural family planning beats no method , and may be the only acceptable option in some cultural or religious contexts. Every contraception discussion should also explore future fertility plans and the effect of age on fertility ( 4.2 ). Counsel with typical-use failure rates. Apps the lecturer recommends: CDC MEC (medical eligibility for any condition), IUC Expert (IUD troubleshooting and myth-busting), Health Canada STI (including treatments), and a pregnancy wheel .

Learning Objectives List the types of miscarriage, including appropriate terminology. List medical treatments for an abnormal first trimester pregnancy. Explain how to diagnose and treat ectopic pregnancy. How This Module Works — Read This First Unlike the rest of Tuesday, this is not a recorded lecture . The module is two reference documents by Dr. Laura Sovran, plus instructions. Its own guidance is worth quoting: On the spontaneous abortion document: you are not expected to memorize the ultrasound criteria — they are there as a future resource. What you are expected to take away is that there are different ways we categorize spontaneous abortions , some sense of cause , and the difference between expectant, medical and surgical management . On the ectopic document: it is preparation for the synchronous session , where you will discuss risk identification, diagnosis and management . That session is Tuesday at 3:30pm. So this page is homework for a class discussion, not a lecture to absorb passively.

Definitions and Epidemiology Spontaneous abortion (SA): a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy up to 20 weeks . Early pregnancy loss = first trimester, and it is by far the most common : 80% of SAs occur before 12 weeks . 8–20% of pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion. Ultrasound term Means Viable pregnancy Can potentially result in a live birth Non-viable pregnancy Cannot possibly result in a live birth — a failing intrauterine pregnancy or an ectopic Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) A positive pregnancy test with no pregnancy visible on ultrasound . May or may not be an undiagnosed ectopic Pregnancy of indeterminate viability An intrauterine pregnancy that doesn't yet meet criteria to be called viable PUL is the one to be careful with. It is not a reassuring result — it is an unfinished one, and an ectopic is still on the table until you have located the pregnancy.

The Five Types Two questions sort almost all of them: is the cervix open or closed? and is there still a fetal heart / are there retained products? Type Cervix Diagnosis Treatment Threatened Closed Vaginal bleeding + fetal heart present , cervix closed Expectant. No progesterone. Treat BV if found Inevitable Open Bleeding with an open cervix — tissue seen or felt through the os Expectant, medical or surgical Incomplete Open Bleeding ± pain, open cervix, products within the cervix Remove tissue at the os ; then expectant, medical or surgical Missed Closed Non-viable pregnancy ± any symptoms at all , cervix closed Expectant, medical or surgical Septic — Infected — complicates 1–2% of incomplete or threatened abortions IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + D&C Threatened Abortion Is Not Nothing It occurs in 20–25% of all pregnancies , and roughly 43% go on to miscarry . But even the ones that continue carry increased risk later in the pregnancy : Pregnancy loss 12–14% · preterm birth at 28–31 weeks: 3× · preterm birth at 32–36 weeks: 50% higher · IUGR, PPROM, abruption, perinatal death · previa, antepartum haemorrhage, manual removal of placenta, caesarean section. So "threatened abortion, went home, pregnancy continued" is a reason to watch that pregnancy more closely , not to close the file. Septic abortion kills. Complications are sepsis, ARDS, acute kidney injury, DIC and death . The organisms the CDC associates with deaths are Clostridium sordellii (toxic shock), Clostridium perfringens , and group A streptococcus (toxic shock).

Ultrasound Criteria The module explicitly says you don't need to memorize these — but you should understand the split. "Diagnostic" means you can call it non-viable now. "Suspicious" means repeat the scan. Diagnostic of a non-viable IUP Suspicious for a non-viable IUP CRL >7 mm with no fetal heartbeat CRL <7 mm with no heartbeat Mean sac diameter ≥25 mm with no embryo Mean sac diameter 16–24 mm with no embryo No embryo with heartbeat ≥2 weeks after a scan showing a sac without a yolk sac No embryo with heartbeat 7–13 days after a scan showing a sac without a yolk sac No embryo with heartbeat ≥11 days after a scan showing a sac with a yolk sac No embryo with heartbeat 7–10 days after a scan showing a sac with a yolk sac — No embryo ≥6 weeks after LMP — Enlarged yolk sac (>7 mm) ; or a small sac relative to the embryo (<5 mm difference between MSD and CRL) The pattern: the same findings, just earlier or smaller, move from "diagnostic" to "suspicious." The thresholds exist to make sure nobody terminates a wanted, viable pregnancy that was simply dated wrong.

Why It Happens Category Share Detail Abnormal karyotype 50% Trisomy 13, 16, 18, 21, 22 — 16 is the most common and is always lethal . 45,X (Turner) is the most common isolated aneuploidy . Robertsonian translocations are the commonest parental balanced translocations, and carry a repetitive risk Normal karyotype 45–55% Poorly understood — look to the maternal causes below Maternal cause Detail Infection Uncommon, poor association. Chlamydia, ?toxoplasmosis, mycoplasma, ureaplasma, HIV, syphilis, BV Chronic debilitating disease Rare — TB, carcinomatosis, celiac Endocrine Hypothyroidism (severe iodine deficiency), type 1 diabetes , rarely nutrition Drugs / environment ?Smoking, excessive caffeine (5 cups/day) , alcohol, radiation >5 rads , chemotherapy, IUD. Environmental: arsenic, lead, formaldehyde, benzene Immunologic Inherited thrombophilias Maternal surgery Usually does not cause SA. If oophorectomy before 10 weeks, supplement progesterone until 10 weeks Trauma Minimal contribution Uterine abnormality Fibroids, adhesions (Asherman's) , septum, unicornuate uterus, polyps — see 3.7 Incompetent cervix Previous cervical trauma or abnormal cervical development. Cerclage: elective at 12–16 weeks, rescue before 23 weeks The Counselling Point Half of early losses are chromosomal accidents , and of the causes that remain, trauma contributes minimally and surgery usually doesn't cause it . Patients very often believe they did something to cause the miscarriage. The evidence is mostly on your side when you tell them they didn't.

Management: The Three Options 1 Expectant management — for SA up to 13+6 . Waiting 4 weeks is safe and effective , and most complete within 2 weeks . Success at 4 weeks: 76% for missed, 91% for incomplete . 2 Medical management — for SA up to 12+6 . Two regimens, below. 3 Surgical management — D&C ± suction . 95–100% successful , ~1% serious morbidity . Consider doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h × 2 doses . Mifepristone + misoprostol Misoprostol alone Regimen Mifepristone 200 mg PO × 1 , then misoprostol 800 µg PV × 1 800 µg PV , or 600–800 µg SL/PV , up to 3 doses , minimum q3h Expulsion (3–30 days) 83.8–93.2% 67.1–75.8% Ended up needing D&C 8.8% 23.5% Canadian indication Currently approved for medical therapeutic abortion only (Mifegymiso) — so this is off-label for miscarriage Indicated for spontaneous abortion in Canada Cost $$$ $ Side effects are the same for both: bleeding, nausea, diarrhoea, fever, pain. No prophylactic antibiotics are indicated for either. Historical data for misoprostol alone: successful in 66–99% , mean 80% for missed and 92% for incomplete abortion. Availability and provider knowledge dictate use — the handout's own phrase, and an honest one. The Trade-Off in One Line Adding mifepristone roughly cuts the D&C rate from ~24% to ~9% . It costs much more and is off-label for this indication in Canada. That is the actual decision. Same two drugs as induced abortion — see 4.1 — used for a different reason.

Epidemiology and Risk Factors 2% of all pregnancies. The leading cause of early pregnancy-related death. High risk Moderate risk Low risk Previous ectopic · previous tubal surgery · tubal pathology · sterilization (tubal ligation/salpingectomy) · IUD (past, current, levonorgestrel) · IVF in the current pregnancy Previous STI · previous PID · in utero DES exposure · smoking (past and current) · previous pelvic/abdominal surgery Infertility · age >40 · age at first intercourse <18 · previous appendectomy The Thread Running Through This Look at what dominates the high and moderate columns: anything that damages the tube . Previous ectopic, tubal surgery, tubal pathology — and then previous STI and previous PID . That is the same chain you followed on 4.6 : untreated chlamydia → PID → tubal scarring → infertility and ectopic pregnancy . This page is the far end of that story. The IUD entry is a common exam trap. An IUD massively reduces your absolute risk of any pregnancy . But if you conceive with one in place, that pregnancy is more likely to be ectopic .

Where They Implant Site Share Ampulla (tube) 70% Isthmus (tube) 12% Fimbria (tube) 6% Interstitial 2% Ovarian 0.5–3% Cervical <0.1% Abdominal, caesarean scar 1 in 2000 Heterotopic (one intrauterine and one ectopic) 1 in 30,000 — but 1% with assisted reproduction The tube accounts for 80% overall , and the ampulla alone for 70%. Heterotopic pregnancy is the trap in an IVF patient: finding an intrauterine pregnancy normally reassures you — but at a 1% rate with ART, it no longer rules out a simultaneous ectopic.

Clinical Features The Classic Triad 1. Pain · 2. Amenorrhea · 3. Vaginal bleeding Uterus displaced or enlarged Orthostatic hypotension from hypovolemia — the vital sign that says she is bleeding Pelvic mass ; bulging vaginal fornix Cervical motion tenderness — the same chandelier sign as PID ( 4.6 ), which is exactly why the pregnancy test comes first Diaphragmatic irritation → shoulder tip pain — blood tracking up to irritate the diaphragm. Shoulder pain in a woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain is a red flag.

Investigations Test What you're looking for β-hCG Mean doubling time in a normal IUP is 1.4–2.1 days ; 85% of viable IUPs rise by 66% in 48 h . A slow or plateauing rise is suspicious CBC, group and screen Haemoglobin, and her Rh status — which determines whether she needs Rh immunoglobulin TVUS Above β-hCG 1500 you should see an IUP ( 99% by 3150 ). Transabdominal needs >6500 . Look for the "ring of fire" — placental blood flow around a complex adnexal mass — and for free fluid The discriminatory zone is the concept to hold. A β-hCG above ~1500 with an empty uterus is not a reassuring scan — it is a scan that should make you think ectopic .

Management Expectant Indications (all four) Prognosis Declining β-hCG and β-hCG <200 · mass <3.5 cm · no evidence of rupture · asymptomatic · no fetal heart Resolution in 50–70% . More likely if β-hCG <1000 mIU/mL . The patient must be reliable Medical — Methotrexate Methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist — it inhibits DNA synthesis , so it targets the rapidly dividing trophoblast. Indications (all four) 1. Confirmed or high clinical suspicion of ectopic · 2. Haemodynamically stable · 3. Unruptured mass — no free fluid · 4. Compliant with follow-up Absolute contraindications Relative Breastfeeding · immunodeficiency · liver disease & alcoholism · blood dyscrasias · MTX hypersensitivity · active pulmonary disease (e.g. TB) · peptic ulcer disease · hepatic/renal/haematologic dysfunction · hCG >5000 · intrauterine pregnancy Gestational sac >3.5 cm · embryonic cardiac motion Regimen Dose Monitoring Single dose MTX 50 mg/m² IM on day 1 Looking for a 15% fall in hCG from day 4 to day 7 . Plateau or rise → repeat MTX Multidose MTX 1 mg/kg IM on days 1, 3, 5, 7 hCG on MTX days; continue until hCG falls 15% from the previous measurement Side effects: GI (nausea, vomiting, stomatitis ) · transaminitis · alopecia · pneumonitis · bone marrow depression · neutropenia. β-hCG is the most important predictor of treatment failure. hCG <5000: 92% success. >5000: 4× more likely to fail. 15–20% need a second dose of 50 mg/m² IM. Washout period: 3–6 months of contraception recommended afterwards — methotrexate is a folate antagonist and therefore teratogenic. Do not skip this in counselling. Surgical Salpingectomy (remove the tube) vs salpingostomy (open it, remove the pregnancy, leave the tube). Indications for surgery 1. Haemodynamic instability · 2. Previous ectopic in the same tube · 3. Ruptured mass · 4. Patient request, or unable to follow up · 5. Methotrexate contraindications · 6. Known tubal disease How to Actually Choose Unstable or ruptured → surgery. No debate. Stable, unruptured, low hCG, reliable follow-up → methotrexate. Declining hCG already below 200, asymptomatic → you can watch. Notice that "compliant with follow-up" appears in both the expectant and medical lists . Both strategies depend entirely on her coming back — and the consequence of not coming back is rupture. That makes it a clinical criterion, not an administrative one.

Rh Immunoglobulin Don't Forget This One Positive β-hCG + vaginal bleeding + Rh negative = give Rh immunoglobulin (WinRho, RhoGAM). It prevents Rh isoimmunization , which protects her future pregnancies . It does nothing for the current one — which is exactly why it is easy to forget in the middle of managing a miscarriage or an ectopic.

The Original Documents Both reference documents, as provided.
