The spontaneous abortion document is the one whose highlighted section the module flags as clinically relevant for obstetricians, gynecologists, family physicians and emergency physicians — a resource for clerkship rather than something to memorize now. Spontaneous abortion — page 1 of 2. Definitions, types, ultrasound criteria, etiology. Page 2 carries the management section, reproduced above. Ectopic pregnancy — the whole document on one page. This is your prep sheet for the synchronous session.

Learning Objectives Define endometriosis. Describe clinical symptoms and physical exam findings. Outline an approach to discussion of dyspareunia. Apply treatments for endometriosis. Describe clinical outcomes of endometriosis. Dr. Stephanie Black's 15-minute module. She states at the outset that she is not covering the pathology — that is Dr. Weir's 4.12 , and the two modules are designed to be read together. This one is purely clinical. Her declared conflict of interest: Bayer advisory board re: intrauterine contraception. She also teaches 4.14 and 4.15 , where endometriosis reappears as a cause of chronic pelvic pain.

entries.t: The Case, and Why It Isn't Primary Dysmenorrhea
entries.x: The Case, and Why It Isn't Primary Dysmenorrhea Five features, each doing work. Dr. Black's slide. The Discriminator She Spells Out Primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandin-mediated pain that occurs with menstruation. What marks Jessica out is that her pain begins two days before menses and is worst in those two days and the first day after onset. Add mid-cycle pain , which is also common in endometriosis, and the picture shifts. Two more red flags in the history: the pain is new and worsening against a background of lifelong painful periods, and it radiates down her leg , which points to disease involving or irritating structures beyond the uterus. Primary dysmenorrhea Endometriosis Timing of pain With menstruation Starts before menses; worst in the first 24–48 h Mechanism Prostaglandin-mediated Inflammation (incompletely understood) Course Stable; typically declines with age New or progressively worsening Mid-cycle pain No Common Deep dyspareunia No Common

Definition and Epidemiology Endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Same three theories as in 4.12 — and note the parenthesis that undermines the first one. Dr. Black's slide. 1–7% of the population. 7% of first-degree relatives will report a family member with it — there is a familial component worth asking about. 5–33% of infertile women — see the box below, because this number is routinely misread. Why Retrograde Menstruation Can't Be the Whole Answer Her own objection, and it is a good piece of reasoning to be able to reproduce: most women have some degree of retrograde menstruation with every cycle, and most women do not have endometriosis. So the theory is not sufficient on its own — something about the host must permit the refluxed tissue to implant, establish a supply and keep cycling. And retrograde flow cannot explain disease above the diaphragm at all, which is what haematogenous or lymphatic spread is there to account for. Coelomic metaplasia — peritoneal cells converting to endometrial tissue — is the third theory. Where It Is Found Commonly in the pelvis: around the rectosigmoid colon , in the cul-de-sac (between uterus and rectum), on the bladder flap , in the ovarian fossa , and on the uterosacral ligaments . But she is clear it can be almost anywhere — including the diaphragm , and rarely the lungs . Catamenial Pneumothorax — Verified Outside the Deck Her striking example: in rare cases with endometriosis in the lung, a woman can collapse a lung with every period . This is real and has a name — catamenial pneumothorax , defined as a spontaneous, recurrent pneumothorax occurring from 24 hours before to 72 hours after the onset of menstruation . It is the commonest manifestation of thoracic endometriosis syndrome , and accounts for up to ~25% of spontaneous pneumothoraces in women who go to surgery, with thoracic endometriosis pathologically proven in about 65% of those cases. It is characteristically right-sided , and the proposed reason is elegant: refluxed endometrial cells track up the right paracolic gutter to the subdiaphragmatic space, with the hepatic ligaments acting as a barrier on that side, then air passes through congenital diaphragmatic fenestrations or defects created by the implants. Other manifestations of the syndrome: catamenial haemothorax, catamenial haemoptysis, catamenial chest pain, pulmonary nodules, diaphragmatic hernia . Not on the slides — checked against the AME Surgical Journal literature review of thorac

entries.t: Pain, Severity, and the Diagnostic Delay
entries.x: Pain, Severity, and the Diagnostic Delay Two bolded lines, both of which change how you practise. Dr. Black's slide. The Two Directions the Mismatch Runs Direction one: a patient with debilitating pain affecting her quality of life, her productivity at work or school and her relationships, who has very little clinical disease on examination. Direction two: a woman investigated for infertility who is found to have stage IV endometriosis with a frozen pelvis and disease everywhere — with no or very little pain . Neither the exam nor the imaging tells you how much she hurts, so the pain has to be taken at face value. And the corollary she wants you to carry: many of these women have already seen several physicians and been told it is normal. They are frustrated by the time they get a diagnosis. Treating "just dysmenorrhea" as a safe default is how that happens.

Approaching Dyspareunia Objective 3, and the part of this lecture that generalizes furthest beyond endometriosis. The red line is the whole point: she will not raise it unless you do. Dr. Black's slide. 1 Ask, in a non-judgmental and normalizing way. Her exact two-step wording is worth memorizing because it doesn't presume anything: "Have you ever had penetrative sexual activity?" and, if yes, "Do you experience pain with sexual activity?" 2 Consider putting it on the intake questionnaire. Some patients will disclose on paper what they won't volunteer in the room. 3 Then split deep from superficial — that single question sorts the differential, because the two groups of causes sit at different depths. Type Where it hurts Think about Superficial Pain with penetration , at the entrance Vulvodynia Chronic vulvar pain without an identifiable cause on examination. · atrophy · vulvar skin conditions (see 4.11 — lichen sclerosus and lichen planus both cause dyspareunia) · vaginismus Involuntary reflex spasm of the pelvic floor muscles on attempted penetration. Deep Pain on deep penetration Endometriosis · masses · adhesions · musculoskeletal causes

Physical Findings Four bullets, and the last one is capitalized for a reason. Dr. Black's slide. Nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments or cul-de-sac — palpable nodules or plaque-like structures. This is the same finding Dr. Weir's case had in the rectovaginal septum. A fixed, immobile uterus in severe cases — tethered by adhesions. Adnexal masses — an endometrioma , a collection of old blood within the ovary itself. Often nothing. Her words: the most common exam finding in endometriosis is no finding at all .

Treatment Medical first, surgery selectively, hysterectomy last. Dr. Black's slide. Why Contraceptives Treat Endometriosis The logic is one sentence: anything hormonal that suppresses ovulation and thins the endometrium, lightening menstrual periods, also suppresses the growth of the endometriotic lesions — because those lesions are endometrial tissue responding to the same hormones. So the drugs used are largely the contraceptives, prescribed for their non-contraceptive benefit. That is the same principle Dr. Arntfield applies to AUB in 4.10 . The two strategies, named by the physiological state they imitate. Dr. Black's slide. Strategy Agents Notes Pseudopregnancy first line OCP · NuvaRing · Evra patch · Depo-Provera · hormonal IUS · Visanne Visanne (dienogest) is a progestin-only pill specifically targeted at endometriosis — the same agent that appears on the AUB slide in 4.10 Pseudomenopause usually second line Danazol — a testosterone derivative Lupron / Zoladex — injectable GnRH agonists , monthly or 3-monthly Very effective , but danazol's testosterone-like side effects are sometimes intolerable , and GnRH agonists produce a menopausal state. Hence second line despite the efficacy One Agent She Names That Isn't on the Slide She mentions in passing an oral agent for pseudomenopause — Orilissa (elagolix) . Worth getting the class right, because it differs from Lupron and Zoladex: elagolix is an oral, non-peptide GnRH antagonist , not an agonist. It produces dose-dependent estrogen suppression — partial at lower doses, nearly complete at higher ones — which is the practical advantage: you can titrate how much of a menopausal state you induce, and being an antagonist it does not cause the initial gonadotropin flare an agonist does. It is approved for moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain , and bone mineral density loss is the dose- and duration-limiting concern , which is why the labelled durations are capped. Not on the deck. The drug class and the dose-dependent suppression mechanism are confirmed from the PubMed-indexed clinical evaluation of elagolix; the specific labelled regimens (150 mg once daily, up to 24 months; 200 mg twice daily, up to 6 months) come from secondary review sources rather than a primary document I could open, so treat the numbers as lower-confidence than the class. Where Surgery Fits Lesions can be excised or ablated at laparoscopy — sometimes with a CO 2 laser to laser away the deposits. But lesions come back after

entries.t: Complications — and the Infertility Statistic Everyone Misreads
entries.x: Complications — and the Infertility Statistic Everyone Misreads Read the starred note before the first bullet. Dr. Black's slide. The Direction of the Association The slide says endometriosis is present in 5–33% of infertile women , which is easy to turn into "endometriosis causes infertility a third of the time." Her correction is explicit: endometriosis does not necessarily cause infertility — it is more common in women who are already infertile. Most women with endometriosis conceive without difficulty. The statistic is a product of where you look : take an already-infertile population, go looking for endometriosis, and you will find it more often than in the general population. When it does cause infertility, the mechanism is tubal occlusion from scarring . Worth holding this next to 4.12 , where Dr. Weir gives infertility in 30–40% of endometriosis and names it as one of the three lesions associated with infertility. The two are not in conflict — Dr. Weir is describing surgical/pathology specimens, i.e. women with disease severe enough to be resected, whereas Dr. Black is describing the whole clinical population including mild and asymptomatic disease. If asked for a number, give the source's number; if asked to counsel a newly diagnosed patient, Dr. Black's framing is the honest one. The more common complications, in her ranking: chronic pain and dyspareunia — with the reminder attached that patients will not volunteer the second one.

entries.t: What It Looks Like at Laparoscopy
entries.x: What It Looks Like at Laparoscopy Four appearances, all endometriosis. Top left — "powder burn" lesion on the pelvic sidewall peritoneum: dark, reminiscent of gunpowder. Top right — white scarring and lesions , also on the sidewall toward the ovarian fossa. Bottom left — "blueberry" lesion : a collection of blood and endometriosis just beneath the peritoneum, raised and blueberry-coloured. Bottom right — simply blood and hemosiderin scattered in the pelvis. Dr. Black's slide. The Fifth Appearance, Not Shown — and Why It Matters She adds one that isn't on the slide: endometriosis can appear vesicular , and this is more common in younger women . A young patient may have only clear vesicles , with none of the classic powder-burn or pigmented findings. So an operator expecting powder burns can look at a pelvis full of disease in a 20-year-old and call it normal. Pair this with "severity doesn't correlate with pain" and you have the two reasons this diagnosis gets missed. A peritoneal window in the cul-de-sac — a pseudo-opening that does not extend deep into the peritoneum. Orientation: uterus anteriorly (above), rectum posteriorly (below), the patient's left ovary to the side. An endometrioma — this dark cystic structure taking up the entire left ovary . The leaking material is old blood and endometriosis tissue , with the consistency of chocolate fondue , which is where "chocolate cyst" comes from. The right ovary is completely normal . Diagnosis at Laparoscopy Any one of these appearances is diagnostic of endometriosis — the appearance is classic enough to make the call in the operating room. For a definitive diagnosis, any of them can be excised and sent to pathology , which is where 4.12 's "any 2 of 3 features" rule takes over. Note the consequence of pairing the two lectures: a visual diagnosis is available at laparoscopy, but a histological one may fail in long-standing burned-out disease that no longer contains endometrial tissue.

Learning Objectives Explain how fertilization occurs. Describe the optimal time for intercourse to achieve a pregnancy. Outline an approach to infertility for a family physician. Outline general causes of infertility, including prevalence. Describe an approach to a sensitive assessment of fertility concerns. Describe populations who require early referral for fertility concerns. Outline how pelvic infection or pain affects fertility. Dr. Krista Cameron's module. It's built as reading and interactive activities rather than a recorded talk, so these notes follow the module itself. The cycle it rests on is in 3.3 , and PMOS has its own page at 3.10 .

Sperm Transport 72 days from the start of spermatogenesis to the tail of the epididymis. The head is a nucleus capped by the acrosome , a bag of proteolytic enzymes it will need to get through the zona. Sperm reach the tube within about 5 minutes. Note how few of the 300 million make it. Capacitation then happens in the tube . Step What happens Ejaculation Active sperm rapidly enter the uterus ; the seminal plasma stays in the vagina . Contractions of the female tract help sperm into the cervical mucus Transport Sperm can be at the site of fertilization within 5 minutes Capacitation (in the tube) Three changes: ability to bind the zona pellucida · capacity to undergo the acrosome reaction · hypermobility Two Things to Reassure Patients About "It all fell out when I stood up." That is seminal fluid . The sperm are already gone from the vagina and into the uterus. "Should I lie down for 30 minutes after?" No. Sperm reach the fallopian tube within about five minutes.

Egg Pick-Up and Fertilization Pick-up. The egg and its cumulus mass stick to the ovary's surface and the fimbriae sweep over and collect it . Transport then needs ciliary motion, muscular contractions and tubal fluid . Variations happen: an ectopic pregnancy, or one tube retrieving an egg from the opposite ovary. The zona pellucida does two jobs: it carries species-specific ligands for sperm binding, and after the first sperm makes contact it undergoes the zona reaction , becoming impenetrable and preventing polyspermy . The oocyte is viable for about 12–24 hours after ovulation. Sperm survive up to 5 days , but their fertilizing capacity probably lasts 2–3 days . Fertilization happens in the ampulla , and may not be entirely random: there is evidence sperm are attracted to the egg. The sequence, with its timings. Binding to the zona for about a minute → the acrosome reaction , mediated by acrosin (a trypsin-like protein on the sperm's inner membrane) → membrane fusion , making a zygote → the cortical reaction and metabolic activation of the oocyte → meiosis completes at about 3 hours , releasing the second polar body → sperm and egg chromosomes join, restoring the diploid number → DNA synthesis begins 9–10 hours after insemination. From the module.

Definitions and Numbers When to assess, and how common it is. <35: after 1 year. ≥35: after 6 months. Infertility affects 10–15% of couples, about 1–2 in every 10. Most couples conceive. 85% by one year, 93% by two. This is the number that frames the whole conversation. Question Answer What is infertility? Regular, unprotected intercourse for a year without pregnancy. Frequency matters : if partners are apart for long stretches, or can't time intercourse around ovulation, the one-year rule means less Primary vs secondary? Primary : she has never been pregnant. Secondary : she has had a previous pregnancy (not necessarily a live birth). A partner's children from another relationship don't change it — that's still primary Who gets worked up early? ≥35 → after 6 months (egg quantity and quality decline). Known problems → immediately : e.g. irregular cycles from PCOS, because without ovulation they won't conceive

Age Infertility roughly doubles from the early 20s to the early 30s : 7% at 20–24 vs 15% at 30–34 , and the chance of remaining childless climbs steeply after 35. Miscarriage risk by age: 10–15% under 35, about 1 in 4 at 35–39, and close to 60% over 40 — mostly from aneuploid embryos . Fertility starts to decline around 30 and the decline accelerates. Both curves — falling fertility and rising miscarriage — are driven by the same thing: the age of the eggs.

The Standard Infertility Work-Up Test When What it answers Blood work Days 2–4 (day 1 = first day of bleeding) FSH, LH, estradiol, prolactin, TSH . Is the brain signalling the ovaries properly? Is prolactin or thyroid the problem? Sonohysterogram (+ ExEm foam) Days 6–12 : lining is thin after the period, and there's no pregnancy yet Saline opens the cavity to look for polyps and fibroids ; the foam shows whether the tubes are open ; the ovaries are checked and follicles counted for egg reserve Day 21 progesterone About a week before the expected period Did she actually ovulate? After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum and makes progesterone. Even regular cycles aren't always ovulatory Semen analysis Any time The male half — see below Infectious disease screening Both partners Required by law in Ontario before using assisted reproductive technology. Best done at the fertility clinic: family doctors often miss tests like HTLV-1 and -2 AMH Any time in the cycle Egg reserve , not natural fertility Why FSH, LH and Estradiol Are Always Ordered Together On day 2–4 everything should be low . If estradiol comes back at 500 , that's far too high for early cycle: a dominant follicle is already growing, so the patient isn't where you think she is in her cycle. That matters because an FSH of 30 alone looks like diminished ovarian reserve or premature ovarian insufficiency. But if estradiol is also 500, the sample simply wasn't taken at the start of the cycle, and that FSH may be completely normal. LH is checked because it should be low at baseline; in PCOS it can already be high (up to about 18) , which is why home ovulation strips are so hard to interpret in PCOS. Progesterone isn't part of day-3 bloods, unless the cycle phase is unknown or an ultrasound shows a complex cyst that might be a corpus luteum. Normal sonohysterogram. The dark oval is the cavity, opened with saline so its shape can be seen. An endometrial polyp in the cavity — typically treated surgically. Normal ovary vs polycystic ovary. Black circles are follicles (the antral count estimates reserve). On the right, the classic "string of pearls" : more than 20 follicles around the edge. HSG when the sonohysterogram is inconclusive: dye and X-ray. Left to right: both tubes patent , a hydrosalpinx , and one blocked tube . Below it, the cycle graph that explains the timing of every test above.

Confirming Ovulation, and Timing Intercourse Method How it works Practical? Mid-luteal progesterone About 7 days before the expected period ; a high level means ovulation happened Yes — the standard LH urine strips Two lines always appear; a true surge is when both lines are equally dark . Ovulation follows in about 36 hours Yes , and the surge day is the best day for intercourse Ultrasound monitoring A mature follicle, its collapse, free fluid, then a corpus luteum Accurate but needs daily scans Cervical mucus Two consecutive days of clear, stretchy mucus Varies a lot between people Basal body temperature A rise after ovulation Hard to measure and track accurately The fertile window. Pregnancy rates peak around cycle days 13–14 (most 28-day cycles surge on day 14), and the single best timing is about 2 days BEFORE ovulation , with rates dropping quickly afterwards. That is why the LH surge day is the day to aim for. Below: AMH 15–28 is normal ; >28 suggests PCOS , <15 suggests diminished ovarian reserve . From the module. What AMH does and doesn't tell you. It's made by granulosa cells of small follicles that aren't yet FSH-responsive, so it measures reserve . It does not predict natural fertility , even though patients panic about a low number. Its real use is guiding medication doses for IVF or egg-freezing.

entries.t: When Is a Cycle Actually Irregular?
entries.x: When Is a Cycle Actually Irregular? It depends on how long it's been since menarche. 1–3 years post-menarche: abnormal if <21 or >45 days . 3 years to perimenopause: abnormal if <21 days, >35 days, or fewer than 8 cycles a year . After the first year , any cycle over 90 days is abnormal. Primary amenorrhea : no period by 15 , or more than 3 years after thelarche , needs assessment (see 3.4 ). In the first year after menarche , irregular cycles are normal : the HPO axis is still immature.

PCOS: The Commonest Ovulatory Disorder About half of this fertility practice. It is a diagnosis of exclusion , lifelong, with no cure . Counsel on the symptoms: acne, excess hair, oily skin, hair loss, irregular cycles, infertility, weight gain, insulin resistance, mood changes. And the long-term risks: cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, endometrial hyperplasia or cancer , and infertility. Best management is preventing weight gain through lifestyle and regular exercise. For fertility: ovulation induction , usually a pill that grows a follicle, sometimes with an injection (Ovidrel) to trigger release . The point is that PCOS patients usually need help to ovulate . A 5–10% weight loss can restart spontaneous ovulation — a genuinely motivating number for patients. The full diagnostic work-up, including the mimics, is 3.10 PMOS .

Endometriosis Revised ASRM staging. For fertility, group it: I–II (minimal/mild) = superficial plaques, no significant adhesions. III–IV (moderate/severe) = ovarian involvement, deep disease, dense adhesions ("kissing ovaries", a "frozen pelvis"). Affects 30–50% of infertile women (with better imaging, this clinic suspects closer to 80%). Gold standard: laparoscopy with biopsy. In practice most diagnoses are made on symptoms and response to treatment (combined pill or a progestin such as Visanne). Advanced ultrasound with pelvic mapping is increasingly useful. Staging does not correlate with symptoms. Minimal disease can be debilitating; severe disease can be silent. Theory Idea Sampson's retrograde menstruation The most cited: menstrual tissue flows backwards through the tubes Embryonic rest Misplaced embryonic Müllerian duct cells proliferate in the abdomen Coelomic metaplasia Peritoneal cells, embryologically similar to endometrium, transform into it Halban's Lymphatic and vascular spread (lesions are found even in brain and lung) No single theory explains it; most researchers favour a multifactorial model : retrograde menstruation plus immune dysfunction, genetic susceptibility and environmental factors. Why Endometriosis Causes Infertility — Four Ways at Once Toxic fluid: the peritoneal fluid contains embryotoxic factors . Poor implantation: implantation rates are lower. Impaired follicles: ovarian reserve is often diminished and the eggs retrieved behave worse. Tubal transport: the pelvis sits in a chronic pro-inflammatory state that extends into the tubes, so sperm and egg have a harder time meeting. Add them up and you see why it fills the infertility clinic. Treating it Approach Not trying to conceive Hormonal suppression (it's estrogen-sensitive): combined pill, progestin-only pill, Visanne, progesterone IUD or implant, Depo-Provera. Second line: Orilissa or Lupron , which induce a chemical menopause Trying to conceive, stage I–II Suppression isn't possible. Laparoscopic ablation or excision may improve spontaneous pregnancy rates for up to 9 months after surgery Trying to conceive, stage III–IV IVF , which bypasses the toxic pelvic environment (implantation rates are still reduced) Endometriomas Avoid surgery in anyone wanting future fertility: it costs ovarian reserve. Operate only for severe symptoms, after careful risk–benefit counselling

Male Factor: Half of It Female 41% · male 24% · both 24% · unexplained 11%. Altogether that is 50% female and 50% male , which is why both partners must be investigated . Too often only the woman is referred, when a simple semen analysis would have found it. WHO reference values come from the lowest 5th percentile of fertile men (over 303,000 samples, 15 countries, partners who conceived within 12 months). Don't memorize the numbers — know that the test is essential. Cause Detail Idiopathic The most common : no clear explanation Varicocele Second most common : enlarged scrotal veins impairing sperm production and quality Exogenous steroids Common in men using anabolic steroids. Testosterone acts as a male contraceptive : it suppresses the brain's drive, so spermatogenesis stops. Result: zero sperm on analysis Erectile / ejaculatory dysfunction Often linked to cardiovascular disease or hypertension . Ask about sexual function Infections Past genital infections can obstruct the tract Genetic Klinefelter syndrome , Y chromosome microdeletions Radiation and chemotherapy Damage testicular tissue Lifestyle Marijuana, smoking, hot tubs 1 Semen analysis first : count, motility, morphology. 2 If abnormal, hormones : LH, testosterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (which can pick up non-classical CAH ). 3 If extremely abnormal, consider a karyotype . 4 Counsel about more than fertility: an abnormal semen analysis is associated with an increased lifetime cancer risk and earlier mortality . Male aging matters less than female aging, but it isn't nothing: semen volume, motility and morphology decline while concentration stays stable, and there are more new autosomal dominant mutations and higher rates of schizophrenia and autism in offspring. Male age is not associated with aneuploidy or sex chromosome abnormalities.

Recurrent Pregnancy Loss Two or more losses — consecutive or not, including biochemical pregnancies . Two losses is enough to warrant a work-up. Fewer than 5% of couples have two consecutive losses, and fewer than 1% have three or more. Cause Share What to do Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome 5–20% Diagnosed by three specific antibodies . If criteria are met, treat with heparin and aspirin from the first positive pregnancy test . This reduces loss , which is why ruling it in or out matters Uterine anomalies 10–15% Septate, unicornuate or bicornuate uterus, or intrauterine polyps (see 3.7 ) Endocrine — Thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, poorly controlled diabetes Chronic endometritis — A low-grade infection of the cavity; two weeks of antibiotics improves outcomes Genetic ~5% of couples A balanced reciprocal translocation in one partner produces unbalanced embryos, so karyotype both partners The work-up: endocrine bloodwork, ultrasound of the cavity (usually sonohysterogram), karyotypes of both partners, and an endometrial biopsy. Even so, about 50% have no identifiable cause , which is frustrating for everyone.

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Learning Objectives Develop an approach to asking relevant family and genetic history. List ethnicities (and conditions) requiring specific fetal screening. Identify red flags and indications for Prenatal Genetics referral. Describe the timing and process of fetal genetic screening. Define non-invasive prenatal testing. Define invasive prenatal testing. Define preimplantation genetic screening and diagnosis. Assess your own and future patients' values and beliefs about genetic testing and actions. This is Dr. Maha Saleh's asynchronous module, 50 minutes in three parts. She is a clinical geneticist at LHSC who does general and prenatal genetics, and she declares no conflicts of interest. The three parts are primary prevention (12 min), non-invasive screening (14 min) and invasive testing (19 min), and this page follows that order. It builds on the pedigree and inheritance material from Foundations. It also sits beside 4.2 for IVF and 4.9 for pregnancy loss.

entries.t: The Big Picture: Two Kinds of Prevention
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: The Big Picture: Two Kinds of Prevention Primary prevention happens before pregnancy. Refer early , because genetic testing takes time. Dr. Saleh's slide. Primary prevention Secondary prevention When Preconception During an ongoing pregnancy What Personal and family history, ethnicity, carrier screening, healthy habits Prenatal screening (non-invasive) → diagnosis (invasive) Goal Spot red flags and refer in time to test Give information and management options Folic acid 0.8–1 mg/day , from 3 months before conception through the 1st trimester , to reduce NTD risk. Avoid smoking (low birth weight), alcohol (FAS), drugs (teratogens), and saunas or heat stress. The map for the rest of the module. Non-invasive tests are screens; invasive tests are diagnostic.

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Part 1 — The Family History Take a three-generation pedigree , which you drew in Foundations. Use the standard symbols: circles for females, squares for males, shading for affected individuals and an arrow for the proband . A pregnancy of unknown sex is drawn as a diamond, and a miscarriage or termination as a small triangle. Record ethnicity on both sides . The Southwestern Ontario family-history form. It shows the couple, the pregnancy and both sets of grandparents, with a red-flag checklist underneath. Dr. Saleh's slide. What to ask about. What prompts a referral to Genetics. Red flag What it makes you think of Consanguinity (first cousins? second?) Autosomal recessive disease Developmental delay or autism , especially in males Fragile X and other X-linked conditions Birth defects (heart defect, cleft palate, extra digits) Chromosomal or syndromic cause ≥3 miscarriages or infertility A balanced translocation in a parent Male infertility (CBAVD) Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens points to cystic fibrosis Early heart disease or sudden death Hereditary cardiac conditions Neonatal death , known genetic diagnosis, ethnicity Specific recessive disease or carrier screening

entries.t: Fragile X and the FMR1 Spectrum
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Fragile X and the FMR1 Spectrum Dr. Saleh's example pedigree. Mostly affected boys , carrier women with early menopause, and an older man with tremor. The repeat grows each time it passes down. Dr. Saleh's slide. Three Presentations, One Gene Fragile X is the most common single-gene cause of developmental delay in boys . The inheritance is X-linked. The gene is FMR1 , and the mutation is a CGG triplet-repeat expansion . The repeat size decides which condition you see: The repeat ranges. Dr. Saleh's slide. CGG repeats Category Clinical picture 6–44 Normal — 45–54 Intermediate — 55–200 Premutation Women: POI , with raised FSH and menopause before 40 of no other known cause. Men: FXTAS , a late-onset tremor and cerebellar ataxia that is often misdiagnosed as Parkinson's . >200 Full mutation Fragile X syndrome : developmental delay, large head, long face, prominent forehead and chin, protruding ears, joint laxity, and large testes after puberty. Why the POI History Matters in Preconception Counselling A woman with unexplained POI before 40 may be a premutation carrier. If she conceives before her ovaries fail, the repeat can expand to a full mutation in her child, and a son will have fragile X syndrome. So early menopause in a female relative counts as a red flag , even though it doesn't sound like a genetics question.

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Ethnicity-Based Carrier Screening Carriers are healthy because they have one working copy. The problem arises when two carriers have a child, who then has a 1 in 4 chance of being affected (autosomal recessive). Ancestry Screen for Carrier frequency How European (or personal or family history, or clinical features of CF) Cystic fibrosis ~1 in 24 (spoken) Recurrent mutation analysis Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Asian, African Thalassemia and hemoglobinopathies — Check MCV <80 fL , then Hb electrophoresis . Always start with the mother and test the partner only if she is a carrier. Ashkenazi Jewish Tay-Sachs , Canavan , familial dysautonomia (and the rest of the SickKids AJ panel) 1/30 · 1/37 · 1/32 Blood sent to the SickKids lab French-Canadian (Bas-St-Laurent, Gaspésie, New Brunswick) Tay-Sachs 1/14 Carrier screening Anabaptist (Amish, Old Order Mennonite) Community-specific panels — LHSC requisition. Local midwives know it well. CF : offer it to European couples. Thalassemia : the Old World belt. Start with the mother. The full SickKids Ashkenazi Jewish panel . Tay-Sachs is the most common, at ~1 in 29–30. French-Canadians carry Tay-Sachs too , at an even higher rate of 1/14. This one is specific to London : the LHSC carrier panels for the Amish (Milverton) and Old Order Mennonite communities. Many couples know about the rare, severe conditions in their community and choose screening. Dr. Saleh's slide.

entries.t: Part 2 — Why Offer Prenatal Screening (and Why Not)
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Part 2 — Why Offer Prenatal Screening (and Why Not) Screening is offered, always optional , and couples can opt out. For: reassurance (more than 97% of pregnancies are normal), plus anticipatory guidance, delivery planning, further testing, fetal surgery, or termination before 24 weeks . Against: anxiety, uncertain results, false positives. "Knowledge is not necessarily power." Her Example She describes a mother with an abnormal screen or an uncertain ultrasound who spent the rest of the pregnancy overwhelmed, and then delivered a healthy baby. That is the cost of a false positive, and it belongs in the counselling before the test, not after.

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Nuchal Translucency 11w0d – 13w6d , a narrow window. >3.5 mm is abnormal. Dr. Saleh's slide. A trained sonographer measures the fluid behind the fetal neck. Excess fluid reflects trouble with the heart or lymphatics , and that is why the associations are: Aneuploidy: T21, T13 (Patau), T18 (Edwards), and 45,X (Turner) . Turner fetuses can become frankly hydropic . Congenital heart defects. Single-gene causes: Noonan syndrome , skeletal dysplasias. Turner syndrome Noonan syndrome Cause Chromosomal: 45,X , or mosaics (45,X/46,XX; 45,X/46,XY), or isochromosome Xq Single-gene , several genes, autosomal dominant Karyotype Abnormal Normal Sex Female Males and females Features Short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries (delayed puberty, infertility), visual-perceptual difficulties. Cognition usually normal. Looks like Turner. Congenital heart disease and cardiomyopathy. Runs in families? No Yes The slides illustrate both syndromes with photographs of affected children. They are left off this page and their features are listed in the table above instead.

entries.t: Multiple Marker Screening, the Anatomy Scan and Soft Markers
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Multiple Marker Screening, the Anatomy Scan and Soft Markers Placental and fetal-liver biomarkers in the mother's blood , combined with maternal age , give a calculated risk for T21 (± T18) , reported against a cut-off of about 1 in 200. Choose based on gestational age, ultrasound access , and early result vs detection rate. eFTS = NT + 1st-trimester markers. MSS = serum only, at 16–20 weeks. eFTS (enhanced first-trimester screen) MSS (maternal serum screen) Components NT + 1st-trimester serum markers Serum only (triple or quad) Timing 11–13 wk 16–20 wk Performance Best of the serum screens: highest detection, lowest false positives Lower detection Use when Default No ultrasound access , or presenting after 14 weeks and past the NT window Anatomy scan at 18–20 weeks : a head-to-toe check of brain, heart, hands, feet and genitalia. Soft markers matter mainly when the serum screen is also abnormal .

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: NIPT As placental cells turn over by apoptosis, they release cell-free DNA into the mother's blood. NIPT measures whether there is too much chromosome 21, 13 or 18 and checks X and Y . Dr. Saleh's slide. OHIP-funded indications. A previous trisomy qualifies at any age, even a 20-year-old. The Ontario pathway: screen everyone, give NIPT to the high-risk group, and confirm any positive with a diagnostic test. NIPT has the highest detection, the lowest false-positive rate and the earliest timing, and it also costs the most. Dr. Saleh's slide (JOGC 2017). Test Cost T21 detection False positive When NT alone ~$100 69–75% 5–8.1% 11–13 wk FTS ~$100 75–85% 3–9% 11–13 wk eFTS ~$100 85–90% 3–6% 11–13 wk NIPT ~$600 (she says ~$550 privately) 99% <1% ≥9 wk What NIPT Cannot Do NIPT screens only the common aneuploidies (T21, T13, T18) and the sex-chromosome aneuploidies . It is still a screen , so a positive result needs CVS or amniocentesis to confirm it. It says nothing about single-gene conditions such as NF1, Noonan syndrome or Huntington's. That point is exactly what the module's knowledge check tests ( below ). Because it tests only the mother's blood, there is no miscarriage risk .

entries.t: Part 3 — Invasive Testing: CVS and Amniocentesis
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Part 3 — Invasive Testing: CVS and Amniocentesis Invasive testing gives a definitive diagnosis . It can detect aneuploidy and other chromosomal imbalances, or provide fetal DNA for single-gene testing when the family mutation is known (for example, Marfan syndrome in a parent). Maternal-fetal medicine specialists perform both procedures under ultrasound guidance. Which test is chosen depends on how small the change is and how fast the answer is needed . A karyotype sees changes above ~5 Mb. A microarray sees missing or extra segments down to the kb range. Single-gene methods (QF-PCR, MLPA, sequencing) resolve down to a single base. Dr. Saleh's slide. CVS samples the placenta (chorionic villi). Amniocentesis samples amniocytes , fetal skin cells shed into the fluid. Dr. Saleh's slide. See the note on the miscarriage figures below the table. CVS Amniocentesis Samples Placenta (villi) Amniotic fluid (fetal cells) When 11–13 wk , the same window as the NT scan 15–20 wk (usually from 16) Miscarriage risk Higher: "1/400 or ~1%" on the slide, "1%" spoken Lower: "1/800 or ~0.5%" on the slide; some centres quote 1/1000 Maternal cell contamination Yes , because villi contain maternal tissue No Confined placental mosaicism Yes . Rarely, the placenta carries a change the fetus doesn't. No, because it samples the fetus, not the placenta Advantage Earlier answer Truly representative of the fetus Discrepancy in the source: the slide's "1/400 or ~1%" is internally inconsistent, since 1/400 is 0.25%, and the same goes for "1/800 or ~0.5%". For exams, remember the relationship: CVS carries a higher loss risk than amniocentesis . Dr. Saleh's spoken figures are about 1% for CVS and 1/1000 at some centres for amnio.

entries.t: Timelines: Why the Clock Drives the Choice
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Timelines: Why the Clock Drives the Choice Anomalies found at 18 weeks leave about 6 weeks before the 24-week limit. Dr. Saleh's slide. Test Turnaround NIPT ~10 days Microarray (on CVS or amnio) ~2 weeks Single-gene test ~3 weeks minimum Work Backwards from What the Family Wants The questions are: what are we suspecting, how long does each test take, and what will the family do with the answer ? The answer might mean termination (which must happen before 24 weeks), NICU planning, or palliation and taking the baby home. If NIPT would take 10 days and a positive would still need an amnio plus 2 more weeks, it can make more sense to go straight to amniocentesis .

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Values, Beliefs and Ethics Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice. Dr. Saleh's slide. Culture, personal and religious beliefs , plus personal and family experience with genetic diagnoses, all shape choices. A family that has already had two trisomies may not want a third. Never assume. She has seen religious Amish, Mennonite and Muslim couples choose termination, and couples told the fetus had T13 or T18 who declined all testing and carried to term. Religion does not predict the decision. Offer all options to everyone , regardless of background. Never judge.

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT) PGT means testing IVF embryos before transfer and implanting only unaffected ones. Her example is a couple with Huntington's disease in the family: autosomal dominant, a 50% risk in every pregnancy, progressive and untreatable, so they are unwilling to take the chance. The technique was first developed in the late 1980s , when PCR was used to determine the sex of embryos in carriers of X-linked disorders. Requires IVF ± ICSI . DNA can come from a polar body , one blastomere (cleavage stage), or 5–10 trophectoderm cells (blastocyst). Biopsy on day 3–5 . She recommends the trophectoderm at the blastocyst stage. Testing methods: PCR or multiplex PCR for single genes, and FISH or microarray for translocations and de novo aneuploidy. Cost: the first IVF cycle is funded, but the PGT itself is not and costs about $6,000–15,000 . Caveat: the few cells biopsied may not represent the whole embryo. Trophectoderm becomes placenta. So she recommends confirming with invasive testing once the pregnancy is established.

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Case: Doris A 29-year-old with an omphalocele and bilateral cleft lip and palate on the 18-week scan. Dr. Saleh's slide. 1 Multiple midline defects point to aneuploidy, most likely trisomy 13. 2 Options: NIPT (a screen, 10 days) or amniocentesis (diagnostic). She is at 18 weeks, past the CVS window. A positive NIPT would still need an amnio, which adds 2 more weeks before the 24-week limit. So it depends on whether the couple wants a definitive answer and whether it would change management. They choose amniocentesis. 3 QF-PCR gives a rapid answer: an extra 13. Because it is abnormal, it reflexes to a karyotype , and two weeks later: 46,XX,t(13;21)(q10;q10),+13 . The count is 46, but extra chromosome 13 material is fused onto a 21 in a Robertsonian translocation (both are acrocentric, with no meaningful p arm). This is a translocation trisomy 13. Doris: 45,XX,der(13;21)(q10;q10) . She is a balanced carrier with 45 chromosomes and no missing or extra material. Why Test the Parents Here but Not for Classic Trisomy 13 Free trisomy 13, with three separate copies, comes from nondisjunction, and testing usually stops there. A translocation trisomy can be inherited from a balanced carrier parent , so both parents are tested. Balanced carriers often present with recurrent miscarriage , because unbalanced conceptions are lost. That is why ≥3 miscarriages is a red flag in Part 1. Dr. Saleh's slide. For this pregnancy For future pregnancies For the wider family Continue or terminate (the answer came before 24 weeks ). If continuing, choose conservative or aggressive management at delivery, from holding the baby and making memories to NICU care. High recurrence risk. Options are PGT with IVF, or NIPT from 9 weeks followed by early invasive testing. A daughter has a 50% chance of being a balanced carrier . Doris's siblings may be carriers too and need counselling and testing (cascade testing). "Lethal" Is the Wrong Word Trisomy 13 and 18 are often called lethal, but not every affected baby dies at birth . Technology can sustain life for long periods, and she has a 3-year-old patient with trisomy 13. Families understand "lethal" in different ways, and a lethal diagnosis does not automatically mean no intervention .

entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Summary Offer prenatal screening to every pregnancy , after a full discussion of risks and benefits. Couples can opt in or out . Every couple has a 2–3% chance of a baby with a congenital anomaly regardless of screening . Screening can reassure, but it never guarantees.

entries.t: Check Yourself: the Module's Knowledge Check
entries.p: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
entries.x: Check Yourself: the Module's Knowledge Check Alice is 29 with NF1 , confirmed by a molecular test that found her pathogenic mutation. She knows it is dominant, with a 50% recurrence risk. She is now pregnant and wants prenatal diagnosis. 1. Which test should be offered to confirm the baby's status? A. Enhanced first-trimester screen B. NIPT for NF1 C. Amniocentesis D. Detailed anatomy ultrasound for features of NF1 Why Amniocentesis provides fetal DNA to test for her known familial mutation . eFTS and NIPT screen only for aneuploidy, not single-gene conditions . NF1 has no known prenatal ultrasound findings . 2. When can that test be offered? A. First week of life B. Any time after 10 weeks of gestation C. First trimester, 11–13 weeks D. 15–20 weeks of gestation Why Amniocentesis is done at 15–20 weeks . Option C, 11–13 weeks, is the window for eFTS and CVS. CVS would also work for a known mutation, but it wasn't offered as an option here. Discrepancy in the source: the module's feedback says NIPT is done "after 10 weeks", but the slides and lecture say after 9 weeks .

Learning Objectives Describe the pharmacological principles underlying the clinical uses of estrogens, progestins and androgens. Describe the basic components of combined contraceptive products and their routes of delivery. Compare combined products with emergency contraception, progestin-only and long-acting progestin contraception. Identify the benefits, risks, side effects and contraindications of contraceptive preparations. Explain how selective estrogen and progesterone receptor modulators are used in breast cancer and endometriosis. Describe the pharmacological uses of androgen agonists and antagonists. Explain how NSAIDs and tranexamic acid are used to treat menstrual symptoms. Dr. Fabiana Caetano Crowley's module, deliberately the pharmacology counterpart to Dr. Black's clinical lecture ( 4.3 ) — expect overlap, and use it to consolidate. The module also assigns a review article on hormone replacement therapy: Lobo RA, "Hormone-replacement therapy: current thinking", Nat Rev Endocrinol 2017;13:220–31.

Why the Axis Is Druggable Two concepts. Pulsatility and a temporal pattern . Disrupt either and ovulation fails — which is a disease when it happens by accident and a drug when you do it on purpose. Three strategies, one map. Note where each drug class acts: GnRH agonists/antagonists at the pituitary, aromatase inhibitors on androgen→estrogen conversion, 5α-reductase inhibitors on testosterone→DHT, and receptor antagonists at the target tissue. Strategy Used for Disrupt the HPO axis Preventing pregnancy Oppose overgrowth of hormone-dependent tissue Breast, endometrial, prostate and other reproductive cancers Replace low hormone levels Menopause, hypogonadism, ovarian dysgenesis

Physiology First: Estrogen and Progesterone Estrogen does far more than reproduction: bone density, HDL over LDL , vasodilation, coagulation factor synthesis (and fibrinolysis), angiotensinogen, neuroprotection. Every one of those reappears later as a side effect. Progesterone slows GnRH frequency , builds secretory endometrium, maintains pregnancy, quiets the myometrium — and affects glucose and aldosterone , which is where several progestin side effects come from. Four estrogen-directed classes: agonists, SERMs , antagonists and aromatase inhibitors . Two progesterone-directed classes: agonists ( progestins ) and SPRMs . Simpler than the estrogen side. Both hormones work through nuclear receptors (ERα/ERβ, PR-A/PR-B) that regulate gene transcription . Hold on to that: it's the whole explanation for how SERMs can be agonists in one tissue and antagonists in another.

Mechanism The pattern the drugs destroy. First half: frequent, small LH pulses, rising estradiol. Mid-cycle: sustained estrogen flips negative feedback to positive → LH surge → ovulation. Second half: progesterone makes LH pulses less frequent but larger . Two levels. Central: continuous supraphysiologic hormone suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH. Local: poor follicle and endometrial development, altered tubal peristalsis, and thick cervical mucus. Combined Progestin-only Ovulation suppressed? Consistently Only about 50% of cycles — except DMPA , which reliably suppresses it So what makes it work? Central suppression plus local effects Mostly the local effects : cervical mucus, endometrium, tubal transport Missed dose More forgiving Over 3 hours late → backup method . The local effects start reverting, and you can't know whether she ovulated This is the practical consequence. The mini-pill's effect depends on a local action that wears off, so it is much less forgiving than the combined pill. From the lecture.

What's Actually in Them Ethinyl estradiol (mestranol is metabolized to it), 10–50 µg . Hepatic metabolism via CYP enzymes plus enterohepatic recirculation . Four families, by what they're derived from. Pregnanes from progesterone; estranes and gonanes from testosterone ; fourth-generation (drospirenone) from spironolactone . Why the Family Tells You the Side Effects A progestin's structure decides not just how well it binds the progesterone receptor but how much it hits the other steroid receptors . Pregnanes (progesterone-like) are the most selective progestationally. Estranes (testosterone-like) are the most androgenic → acne, oily scalp, facial hair, weight gain. Gonanes are androgenic but less so. Drospirenone is anti-androgenic (good for acne) but has mineralocorticoid activity → fluid and salt retention and a risk of hyperkalemia . All of it is dose-dependent , which is why the same progestin appears with different profiles at different doses. So pick the progestin for the goal: acne → anti-androgenic; opposing estrogen in menopause → high progestational activity. The cross-selectivity table. Some progestins also hit glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors, which is where the glucose and fluid effects come from. Route changes pharmacokinetics. Patch and ring bypass first-pass metabolism , so plasma levels can be higher for the same dose. Pills lose on adherence; patches irritate skin and are affected by weight; rings are invasive and can cause discharge or dryness. Progestin-only options, each with its own trade-off. Mini-pill : adherence, and the 3-hour window. LNG-IUS : invasive, costly up front, small perforation risk — but excellent adherence for 3–10 years. DMPA injection : the one that truly suppresses ovulation (highest progestational activity, closest in structure to progesterone), at the cost of weight gain, bone loss and irregular bleeding . Implant (etonogestrel) . From the lecture.

Side Effects, Predicted From Physiology Estrogen side effects are its physiology, unwanted. Breast proliferation → tenderness . Vasodilation → headache . RAAS effects → fluid retention and edema . Plus nausea and bloating. Progestin side effects follow the receptor it hits. HPO suppression → less endogenous estrogen → low libido, low mood, bone loss . Androgenic → acne, facial hair, oily scalp, weight gain . Mineralocorticoid → fluid retention, hyperkalemia . Plus breakthrough bleeding , commoner with progestin-only. Not for memorizing. The point of this table is that androgenic activity varies with both the progestin and its dose , and the products at the bottom (drospirenone-containing) are the anti-androgenic ones — which come with fluid retention instead. RxFiles, from the lecture.

The Serious Risks In the endometrium they oppose each other. Estrogen alone → proliferation → endometrial cancer risk ; the progestin protects . This is why estrogen-only preparations are never used as contraceptives . In breast they act together , both driving proliferation → increased breast cancer risk , for combined and progestin-only preparations. Net effect across cancers: combined contraceptives are associated with a decreased risk of ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancer. Liver and metabolism. The two hormones pull lipids in opposite directions, so the net is a slight rise in triglycerides . Estrogen's effect on bile means gallstones , making gallbladder disease a relative contraindication. Why VTE. Estrogen raises factors VII, VIII, IX and X and lowers anticoagulant factors. The progestin type modifies it: anti-androgenic progestins (drospirenone, cyproterone) carry a higher reported thrombosis risk . The honest summary. Combined > progestin-only > no method for VTE risk, and substantially less than pregnancy . Whether patch or ring is worse than pills is inconclusive . Progestin-only is safe , with the injection as the exception. Contraindications , with the relative ones underlined on the slide. Hypertension is relative ; undiagnosed abnormal bleeding must be worked up first . Many of these still allow a progestin-only method, since the problem is usually the estrogen — including for smokers over 35 . And the benefits, from 50+ years of use. Fewer ovarian cysts, less ovarian and endometrial cancer, less PID, better dysmenorrhea and endometriosis, lighter and more predictable periods (or none), better acne and PMS. And don't forget the risks of pregnancy itself , which are higher than the risks of the pill. From the lecture. Drug interactions to remember: smoking alters estrogen clearance through CYP enzymes, and carbamazepine , rifampin and aprepitant can lower estrogen levels enough to matter. Common antibiotics do not.

How Tissue Selectivity Works The mechanism. Hormone binds → receptor changes shape → dimer binds a response element → co-activators or co-repressors are recruited → transcription changes. The worked example. Bone expresses co-factors X and Y; breast only Y. A SERM that recruits only X is a partial agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast (it binds, recruits nothing, and blocks estrogen). Same drug, opposite effect. Three things decide the outcome: which receptor isoform the ligand prefers , what shape it forces the receptor into , and which co-factors that tissue happens to express . The table to know. Both are antagonists in breast (so both treat estrogen-dependent breast cancer) and agonists in bone (so both help osteoporosis). The difference is the endometrium : tamoxifen is a partial agonist there → endometrial cancer risk ; raloxifene is an antagonist → no such risk . Both still raise VTE risk . Clomiphene: blocking a brake. It antagonizes estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary , removing estrogen's negative feedback, so GnRH, LH and FSH rise and a follicle develops. You induce ovulation by inhibiting an inhibition. Pure antagonists exist too: fulvestrant binds, blocks and degrades the estrogen receptor, shutting signalling down completely; it's used in advanced breast cancer, including tumours resistant to tamoxifen. Aromatase inhibitors take a different route: less androgen→estrogen conversion means less estrogen to begin with.

entries.t: SPRMs: From Fibroids to Emergency Contraception
entries.x: SPRMs: From Fibroids to Emergency Contraception A spectrum, not a switch. From progesterone and levonorgestrel (agonist) through ulipristal to mifepristone (mostly antagonist). Anti-proliferative effects on the endometrium make them useful for fibroids, endometriosis and abnormal bleeding . Drug What it does Mifepristone Mostly anti-progestin and anti-glucocorticoid . Blocking endometrial PR lowers hCG support and detaches the pregnancy → termination (see 4.1 ). The anti-glucocorticoid action makes it useful in Cushing syndrome Ulipristal acetate A partial agonist used for emergency contraception and fibroids Why the windows differ. Levonorgestrel only delays ovulation , so it fails once the LH surge starts (≤ 72 h). Ulipristal also directly inhibits follicular rupture and thins the endometrium, so it still works during the LH rise — up to 120 h . The head-to-head. Ulipristal beats levonorgestrel at every interval, and the gap matters most in the later windows. Glasier et al., Lancet 2010. Neither is an abortifacient. Once a pregnancy is established, they don't work. The clinical side of emergency contraception, including the copper IUD, is in 4.3 .

Androgens One hormone, three fates. 5α-reductase → DHT for external genitalia and hair follicles; testosterone itself for Wolffian structures, muscle and erythropoiesis; aromatase → estradiol for bone and libido. Compare with 3.9 . Three classes. Agonists for hypogonadism and female-to-male transition. Receptor antagonists (flutamide) for metastatic prostate cancer and severe hirsutism. 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride) for BPH and alopecia. Side effects of antagonists: lower libido, erectile dysfunction . Aromatase inhibitors appear here too, treating breast cancer, endometriosis and gynecomastia — and, as seen in 4.2 , inducing ovulation (letrozole).

NSAIDs and Tranexamic Acid Dysmenorrhea is a prostaglandin problem. Endometrial prostaglandins drive the painful contractions, so blocking COX-1 and COX-2 relieves the pain — and, by causing vasoconstriction, also reduces bleeding . Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue that blocks plasminogen's fibrin-binding site, so clots aren't dissolved . It doesn't stop clots forming — which is exactly why a history of thrombosis is a contraindication . NSAIDs Tranexamic acid Does Inhibit COX → fewer prostaglandins → less pain and less bleeding . Most women get moderate to excellent pain relief Antifibrinolytic : prevents clot breakdown, so more effective than NSAIDs at reducing blood loss Side effects GI upset (prostaglandins protect gastric mucosa), renal damage (they maintain renal perfusion) Headache in up to 60% , backache, cramps, GI distress Avoid if Renal failure, gastritis or peptic ulcer, coagulation disorders (COX makes thromboxane, a platelet aggregator) History of thromboembolic events Note Both are symptomatic : they treat the bleeding and pain, not the underlying cause. Tranexamic acid is usually taken for a few days, or only on heavy days

entries.t: The Whole Module on One Slide
entries.x: The Whole Module on One Slide The map. Three hormones, each with agonists, antagonists and modulators, each with its own clinical use. If you can rebuild this diagram from memory, you have the module. From the lecture. Core concept The point Contraceptive components Ethinyl estradiol plus one of many progestins. Effects and side effects depend on dose and progestin type Delivery systems Combined: pill, patch, ring. Progestin-only: mini-pill, injection, IUS, implant Adverse effects Shared: nausea, bloating, breast tenderness, headache. Hormone-specific: VTE with estrogen , breakthrough bleeding with progestin , weight gain proven only for DMPA and the implant Modulators Tissue-specific because of receptor isoforms and co-factors; can be agonist, partial agonist or antagonist in different tissues Ulipristal An SPRM that delays ovulation and inhibits follicular rupture , so it works later than levonorgestrel — but not once pregnancy is established Androgens FDA uses: replacement (testosterone esters), BPH ( finasteride ), prostate cancer ( flutamide ). Non-FDA: hirsutism, alopecia. ADRs: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction

entries.t: Week 4 · Family Planning, Infections & Early Pregnancy
entries.p: Week 4 · Family Planning, Infections & Early Pregnancy
entries.x: > Week 4 Monday is ending a pregnancy, starting one, preventing one, and the drugs behind all of it. Tuesday turns to what comes through the clinic door: discharge, sexually transmitted infection, cervical screening, and the two early-pregnancy emergencies. Thursday is bleeding and pain — abnormal uterine bleeding and the vulva, then the same four benign lesions twice over, once under the microscope and once at the bedside, finishing with acute and chronic pelvic pain. Friday is prenatal genetic screening, from the family history before conception to amniocentesis. The physiology they rest on — the menstrual cycle and the HPO axis — is in 3.3 and 2.6 . 4.1 Abortion in Canada The law and access across Canada, medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol, surgical options (MVA, D&C, D&E), complications, the risk compared with pregnancy, contraception after, fertility and the myths → 4.2 Fertilization & Infertility How fertilization happens and the fertile window, the definition and prevalence of infertility, causes in both partners, the family physician's work-up, and who needs early referral → 4.3 Contraception Typical vs perfect use failure rates, the tiers of effectiveness, how each method works, LARCs, the estrogen contraindications, and emergency contraception → 4.4 Drugs Used in Gynecology Estrogen and progesterone pharmacology, contraceptive products and their side effects and risks, SERMs and SPRMs, androgen agonists and antagonists, and the other drugs used in gynecology → 4.5 Vaginal Discharge Why estrogen makes discharge, how it changes across the cycle, the assessment with pH, whiff test and wet mount, and the four causes — BV, candida, trichomoniasis and atrophic vaginitis → 4.6 Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infection Chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis, hepatitis B serology and HIV, then pelvic inflammatory disease in depth — why it isn't always an STI, when to admit, and the 14-day rule → 4.7 Public Health and STIs STBBIs, the rising local and provincial numbers, antimicrobial resistance in gonorrhea, risk factors, your legal duty to report, and why reducing stigma is itself a transmission-control measure → 4.8 Cervical Cancer Screening HPV and its low- and high-risk types, the vaccines and schedules, cytology outcomes from NILM to HSIL, and Ontario's March 2025 switch to primary HPV screening with its algorithm → 4.9 Early Pregnancy Complications Spontaneous abortion — the five types, the causes, and expectant vs medical vs surgical ma

Learning Objectives Build a differential diagnosis for structural causes of AUB & pelvic pain based on knowledge of anatomy and pathology. Narrow the differential diagnosis based on age, common reasons & clues in history & physical examination. Compose an oral narrative which explains to patients the reasons for AUB & pelvic pain. Dr. Michele Weir's 42-minute module, delivered in three parts, plus her written handout Benign Uterine Lesions & Endometriosis (revised July 2022) — both are sources for this page. She is an anatomical pathologist at LHSC University Campus subspecializing in gynecologic pathology, and she says outright that this module is preparation for the two-hour small group — that's the DSSG: Pathology of Pelvis & Perineum, Thursday 3:30pm , with four case scenarios to look at beforehand . Objective 3 is unusual and worth noticing: each lesion gets a "What to tell your patient" slide, which is examinable in a way pure pathology isn't. She refers explicitly back to Dr. Arntfield's 4.10 , and her resources are mypathologist.ca (for explaining pathology reports to patients) and Choosing Wisely Canada .

entries.t: The Framework She Reuses Three Times
entries.x: The Framework She Reuses Three Times Every case runs through the same structure, and she loops back to the same two differential slides each time. Learn the framework once and the three cases become variations. Case 1 — Alexa, 40. Note the exam finding does all the work: a 2 cm fleshy cervical mass . Is she stable? Check the vitals first. Her emphasis — when someone is bleeding, that comes before the history. Looking down the speculum. Acetic acid (vinegar) highlights the transformation zone as the white ring; the arrow marks where the cervical os should be, and something is sitting in it instead. Courtesy of Dr. M. Rebel, on Dr. Weir's slide. The same ABC…N list as 4.10 , with the greyed-out entries eliminated by one exam finding . This slide is objective 2. The single most useful slide in the deck. Structural on the left, functional on the right; benign structural = PALE . The asterisks mark the ones that can appear at the cervical os . How One Finding Collapses a Long List Her reasoning, step by step: a 40-year-old has a long differential for AUB. But a mass at the os means there is a structural lesion , and coagulopathy, DUB, endocrine causes, exogenous hormones and infection do not present as a mass at the os. That leaves anatomic, baby and neoplasia — and within the benign anatomic group, adenomyosis and endometritis don't form mass lesions either . Final differential: polyp, leiomyoma, malignancy, baby . Four items from twelve, on the strength of one speculum exam. The step between clinic and diagnosis. Tissue you can see with your eyes goes into formalin . The specimen here has a stalk and a head — and the head is hemorrhagic because it was being traumatized sitting in the cervix , which is also why Alexa was spotting daily. Dr. Weir's slide.

Endometrial Polyp Definition — general: a growth which projects above a mucosal surface (you get them anywhere there is mucosa — she references GI polyps). Specific: a benign overgrowth of endometrium , driven by hormone-dependent growth — associated with estrogen and with tamoxifen . Her Homework Question, Answered She sets this explicitly: why does tamoxifen, an anti-estrogen drug used for breast cancer, stimulate endometrial growth? Because tamoxifen is a SERM Selective estrogen receptor modulator — a drug that acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist in some tissues and an agonist in others. , not a pure anti-estrogen. It is an ER antagonist in breast tissue but a partial estrogen agonist in the endometrium . The tissue-specific switch comes down to which co-regulators get recruited to the receptor : in breast cancer cells tamoxifen recruits co-repressors (NCoR, SMRT) to ER target promoters, whereas in the endometrium it recruits co-activators , so the same drug-receptor complex turns transcription off in one tissue and on in the other. There is also a dose-of-estrogen effect: premenopausally, when estrogen is high, tamoxifen behaves as an antagonist even in the endometrium; postmenopausally, when estrogen is low, it behaves as an agonist. Polyps are the commonest endometrial change in tamoxifen users, reported at 13–30% prevalence . Verified outside the deck — the deck only names the association. Source: the review of estrogen and progesterone receptor expression in endometrial polyps of tamoxifen-exposed postmenopausal women in PMC (PMC3915668) and the Oncology Letters review of molecular mechanisms of tamoxifen-associated endometrial changes. 25% of women , commoner over 40 , asymptomatic in many . Three symptoms: AUB (commonest), infertility , and pain if it protrudes through the os . Pedunculated (has a stalk) vs sessile (no stalk, rises directly from the endometrium). Note the cystic areas in the sessile one — those are the dilated glands you will see on histology. The three components of a polyp, all labelled here: endometrial glands (the white lumens lined by epithelium), fibrous endometrial stroma (the blue-staining supporting tissue), and thick-walled blood vessels . Two things to link up: the dilated glands are what made the gross specimen look cystic, and the vessels come right up to the surface — which is the mechanism by which a traumatized polyp bleeds. Dr. Weir's slide. Level Findings Gross Single in 80% , multiple in 20% · pedunculated

Leiomyoma Her framing: "fibroid" is the silly term; the pathology term is leiomyoma — leio- smooth, myoma muscle. A benign smooth muscle neoplasm . The Point She Makes Three Ways Leiomyoma is NOT pre-malignant and NOT a precursor to malignancy. It does not turn into leiomyosarcoma. Her slide says it three times because students reliably get it wrong. Her "what is it?" slide. Solid, well circumscribed, whorled — and the reason it is so sharply demarcated is week 6 of Foundations: a slowly growing tumour compresses the surrounding normal tissue gradually , producing a clean pushing border rather than an infiltrating one. Dr. Weir's slide. Commonest neoplasm in women. Estrogen responsive — grows in pregnancy, shrinks after menopause or oophorectomy. That hormone dependence is the basis for medical management. Asymptomatic in many. When symptomatic: AUB is #1 , then infertility and pregnancy problems, pain, and mass effect . Mass effect, mechanically: the fibroid and therefore the uterus gets large enough to push forward onto the bladder (urinary frequency) or backward onto the bowel (constipation) — so the patient may present with GU or GI complaints rather than gynecologic ones. Read the caution sign as a rule, not a footnote — see the box below. The three sites plus two others. The prompt at the bottom left is the actual task: what symptoms follow from each location? Site Where exactly Consequence Intramural In the myometrial wall — commonest Bulk, mass effect, bleeding Submucosal In the myometrium beneath the endometrial surface Bleeds most — and may grow above the mucosa, develop a stalk and mimic an endometrial polyp , even prolapsing through the cervical os (i.e. it could have been Alexa's lesion) Subserosal In the myometrium under the serosa; can be pedunculated Mass effect outward; often an incidental finding Cervical / lower uterine segment As named Can obstruct or present at the os Broad ligament / uterine ligaments Outside the uterus proper Palpable on pelvic exam and easily mistaken for an adnexal mass The One Thing Not to Get Wrong Leiomyoma does not become sarcoma — but leiomyosarcoma exists and presents differently. The pattern she wants you to recognize: a peri- or postmenopausal woman with a single dominant uterine mass that is growing rapidly . Fibroids are usually multiple and are supposed to shrink after menopause, so this is the wrong picture in the wrong age group. Her instruction, verbatim in substance: do not put that patient on hormon

The Dysmenorrhea Differential Layer this over the AUB differential. Primary = functional , younger (late teens/20s, then declines). Secondary = structural and acquired , and therefore commoner with aging — because these lesions take reproductive years to develop. Secondary is PALE + endometriosis . Dr. Weir's slide. With no exam findings in a 40-year-old, the AUB list is long again. Combining the two differentials, the things causing bleeding and pain are PALE, DUB, and baby . In the case, β-hCG is negative, ultrasound shows diffuse but non-specific changes, and an endometrial biopsy excludes hyperplasia and cancer. She fails the pill, keeps bleeding and hurting, and opts for hysterectomy — which is exactly how adenomyosis is usually diagnosed.

Adenomyosis Definition: endometrial tissue deep in the myometrium. Non-neoplastic. Present in 15–30% of resected uteri (she says "about a third" out loud). Cause unknown, but ?parity-related — uncommon in nulligravids . Two findings in one specimen. Upper left: a small nodule poking through the serosa — an incidental subserosal leiomyoma , and not the cause of her bleeding. Centre: the myometrium replaced by a diffuse process with an almost "chicken-wire" appearance — pale-centred areas outlined as if highlighted. That is adenomyosis. Dr. Weir's slide. The balloon analogy, and the best explanation on the page. In pregnancy the endometrial lining is stretched like an inflating balloon. After delivery the myometrium contracts down hard, but the endometrial lining does not come back evenly — it folds irregularly, leaving endometrial pouches trapped out in the wall . Some stay connected to the cavity and some don't. Her own comparison: analogous to colonic diverticular disease. This is also why it needs a pregnancy past ~20 weeks and is uncommon in nulligravids. Dr. Weir's slide. Diffusely enlarged uterus, thick trabeculated myometrium, and cystic-looking areas that are entrapped blood . The mechanism slide. Bleeding because there is simply more endometrial tissue . Pain because entrapped blood irritates muscle and the myometrium contracts against it. Why It Hurts and Why the Uterus Enlarges The key insight is that ectopic endometrium keeps cycling even though it is buried in muscle. Cyclical bleeding in an enclosed space releases prostaglandins and inflammatory mediators , which are highly irritating to muscle . The myometrium responds by contracting — which is the pain — and, since it is doing that work every cycle for years, it undergoes smooth muscle hypertrophy , which is why the uterus becomes diffusely enlarged. Patients may describe gushing or very heavy bleeding when cystic areas rupture. Microscopic: endometrial tissue (stroma and/or glands) deep in the myometrium, usually >¼ of the wall thickness , with smooth muscle hypertrophy . Clinical picture: pre- or perimenopausal , abnormal bleeding, pain (menstrual and pelvic), enlarged uterus. The examinable point. You cannot diagnose adenomyosis on an endometrial biopsy — the glands are too deep for the pipelle to reach. Imaging confirms it in some patients but not all. So the typical route is: work-up negative → presumed dysfunctional bleeding → fails medical management → hysterectomy → found incidentall

Endometriosis Adele, 35. Note what is absent : no AUB at all. Three findings point one way. Dr. Weir's slide. The History That Makes the Diagnosis Pelvic pain prior to the onset of the period — she calls this "very unusual in patients without this entity." That, plus new worsening dysmenorrhea and one year of infertility , is the classic triad. Then the exam confirms it: a very painful pelvic exam , palpable nodules in the rectovaginal septum , and a fixed uterus — normally the uterus is somewhat mobile on its ligaments, and here it is tethered in the pelvis by adhesions. Laparoscopy. A white puckered adhesion and pigmented "powder burns." The biopsy. Endometrial glands and stroma — outside the uterus. That is the definition. Hold the three side by side: polyp = endometrium above the surface · adenomyosis = endometrium in the uterine wall · endometriosis = endometrium outside the uterus. Dr. Weir's slide. Why It Happens — Three Theories She teaches these because patients ask "why do I have this?" — which is objective 3. Dr. Weir's slide. 1 Implantation. Retrograde menses happens in every woman — shed endometrium travels out along the tubes into the peritoneum. In most people the host clears it. In some it implants but sits quiescent without cycling. In endometriosis the host permits the implant to establish a blood supply and to cycle. The surgical variant of the same theory: entering the endometrial cavity at caesarean section can implant endometrium in the C-section scar . 2 Metaplasia. The peritoneum "switches personality" to endometrial tissue — plausible because the Müllerian and peritoneal tissues share an embryological origin . 3 Vascular or lymphatic spread. Her point: this is the only way to explain endometriosis above the diaphragm , in lung or lymph nodes. Clinical Her mnemonic for the order: gravity pulls endometrial tissue down. 1 Ovaries → 2 Uterine ligaments → 3 Rectovaginal septum → 4 Pelvic peritoneum. Adele's nodules were in #3. But it can be anywhere — cervix, tubes, vagina, skin (umbilicus, surgical scars), omentum, lymph nodes, ureter, bladder, lung. Dr. Weir's slide. Feature Detail Frequency 10% of women aged 20–40 Pain Acquired — menstrual, pelvic, and back Infertility 30–40% Other symptoms Dyspareunia , dysuria , dyschezia (painful defecation), irregular bleeding Spectrum Asymptomatic to severely symptomatic — same wide range as adenomyosis Gross and Microscopic — Read Them as a Timeline Early → late in three pictures. Blueberry les

entries.t: Her Own Quiz, and the Take-Home
entries.x: Her Own Quiz, and the Take-Home Worth committing to memory, because she asks it directly. Dr. Weir's slide. Lesion Infertility? Mechanism Endometriosis Yes — 30–40% Dense adhesions binding tubes and ovaries Endometrial polyp Yes If large enough, there is no room for implantation Leiomyoma Yes A mass lesion in the endometrial cavity once it reaches a certain size; also miscarriage and interference with fetal position Adenomyosis No — and note it is also uncommon in nulligravids , i.e. it tends to require a prior pregnancy These are common benign uterine lesions with important clinical sequelae: AUB, pain, infertility, mass effect. Exclude structural reasons for AUB and pain before assigning anything functional. Use age, common reasons and clues to narrow the differential. Recognize the role of the pathologist in the diagnosis — and always send the tissue.

Learning Objectives Identify common STIs in Canada, including relevant age groups. Describe patterns of global disease burden with regard to STIs. Identify and list risk factors for STIs. Review the role of public health in responding to STIs, and the role of physicians in reporting. Outline population-level interventions that reduce the burden of STIs. Dr. Alex Summers, Associate Medical Officer of Health at the Middlesex-London Health Unit. 20 minutes, recorded September 2021. This is the deliberate step out of the individual patient encounter that 4.6 covers, and into the population view.

STI vs STBBI Dr. Summers' slide. STBBI covers infections that are sexually transmitted or transmitted through blood: HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, HPV and more. You will increasingly hear STBBI rather than STI. Why Group Them? Because the risk factors overlap heavily , the stigma is similar , and case and contact management is approached the same way . Grouping them makes the public health response coherent.

Middlesex-London Reported STBBIs in Middlesex-London, 2005–2018 . Dr. Summers' slide. Chlamydia dwarfs everything else — and has climbed steadily over 15 years. Gonorrhea is climbing , especially in the most recent years. Syphilis is rising fastest relative to its own history. Syphilis in Ontario. Rare a decade ago; climbing steeply in the last 3–5 years . Syphilis in Middlesex-London, 1990–2019. Absolute numbers: <20 a year in the mid-1990s , now north of 120 and pushing 200 . Why Were the Early 1990s So Quiet? Bacterial STI rates were very low in the early 1990s , and the explanation offered is behaviour change following the HIV epidemic — condoms were used readily because of fear. As that fear receded, barrier use fell, and the bacterial STIs came back.
