In his closing remarks he names the modern version of the same mechanism: effective contraception and HIV prevention with PrEP mean fewer people feel they need a condom, so bacterial STI transmission keeps rising . Chlamydia — rising locally and provincially. Gonorrhea — an even more notable recent climb. HIV is the exception — it has been fairly stable. There was a local spike above the provincial average a few years earlier, driven predominantly among people who inject drugs . Bringing it down took focused work on access to care and support with treatment , because an undetectable viral load means no transmission . Dr. Summers' slide. Caption warning: the auto-transcript renders "STI" variously as "babies," "guys," "Saudis," "setbacks," "acids," "FBI" and "eyes," and "syphilis rates climb" as "the crime that is happening." The figures above are read off the slides.

Global Burden and Resistance More than 1 million STIs acquired every day worldwide. An estimated 376 million new infections a year with one of four: chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, trichomoniasis (WHO data). The gonorrhea escalator. Penicillin and tetracyclines → resistance in the 1980s → fluoroquinolones in the 1990s → resistance again → third-generation cephalosporins since the mid-2000s. We have gone from a tablet to an injection, and there is not much runway left.

The List From the Canadian STI guidelines . The second half. Risk factor The reasoning Sexually active youth under 25 Emphasised hardest. STIs circulate readily in this group — it shows in the chlamydia and gonorrhea numbers New partner, or >2 partners in a year More partners → higher probability of exposure Serial monogamy The subtle one. One partner at a time, but a series of them — and these patients often never get re-screened between partners No contraception, or only non-barrier methods An IUD, the pill or Depo-Provera is great at preventing pregnancy and useless at preventing STIs Alcohol and other substances with sex The conversation about condoms and contraception simply doesn't happen Unsafe practices, blood exchange Higher transmission probability, especially HIV where blood is involved Sex work, survival sex, street involvement More partners plus power dynamics that reduce barrier use Anonymous partnering No knowledge of a partner's history; no chance to ask about screening Sexual assault or abuse; previous STI A previous STI predicts a future one The Actual Point of the List His framing: almost everybody falls into one of these categories at some point. Sex is common, normal and part of the human experience — which means everybody is at risk at some point in their life . That is why the public health approach is not abstinence . It is reducing risk , and screening people with new or changing partners regardless of how they present . You will not remember all these risk factors — you are meant to remember the conclusion.

Reportable Diseases A legal obligation on clinicians, labs, institutions and governments. Chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C are all reportable. Three reasons it matters. 1 Surveillance. Reporting is how anyone knows whether syphilis is rising or falling, and it carries risk factor information with it. 2 It empowers public health action. Individual-level data enables case and contact management — the same contact tracing everyone learned about during COVID, which public health has been doing for STIs for decades. It also triggers the legislative authority of the Medical Officer of Health . 3 It fulfills Canada's obligations under the International Health Regulations . What that looks like in practice: a syphilis report lets the health unit follow up with that individual, confirm they are treated , and identify, test and treat their contacts . It also lets a Medical Officer of Health say something more useful than "the whole community is at risk" — in London, that rising syphilis was concentrated among men who have sex with men, and among workers in the sex industry , which is what lets outreach be targeted.

The Pan-Canadian Framework The vision: a Canada where STBBIs are rare, with the goal of reducing STBBIs in Canada by 2030 . Dr. Summers' slide. Principle What it means Prevention Population level: sexual health promotion embedded in primary, secondary and post-secondary curricula — not just STIs but healthy sexuality and consent . Individual level: asking patients about condoms, and making sure condoms are actually available Testing Identifies people so they can be treated, and identifies their contacts so transmission stops. For HIV especially: find it, treat it, undetectable viral load = no transmission Initiation of care and treatment Requires access to primary care . Without it, diagnosis achieves nothing Ongoing care and support Particularly for HIV, hepatitis C and hepatitis B

Stigma The Causal Chain He Wants You to Carry More stigma → fewer people get tested → fewer people tell their partners → fewer people get treated → more transmission. So reducing stigma is not a nicety bolted onto the medicine. It is a transmission-control intervention . His script for a patient is worth borrowing almost verbatim: chlamydia is the most commonly reported infectious disease ; many people will have it at some point; it does not mean you are a bad person , and it does not mean you made some uncharacteristic mistake. It means you are a human being who had sex, like almost everyone does.

His Three Takeaways STIs are common, a major public health issue, and rising — largely because barrier use has fallen, thanks to effective contraception and PrEP. "Treatable" does not mean "minor." The long-term costs are infertility, antimicrobial resistance, and other adverse health effects . Your job has three parts: have the conversations, reduce stigma , and report . And the practical instruction: bookmark the Canadian Guidelines on Sexually Transmitted Infections . You are not meant to memorise them — you are meant to be able to find them, which is exactly the caveat flagged on 4.6 .

Learning Objectives Describe clinical symptoms and findings for various STI presentations. Outline diagnostic criteria for common STIs. Apply treatment regimens to common STIs. Define PID, its treatment and clinical outcomes. Dr. Stephanie Black's 30-minute module. She discloses an advisory board affiliation with Bayer regarding intrauterine contraception, which does not come up in this talk.

What Counts as an STI Any condition primarily acquired through sexual activity — vaginal, oral, anal, or a combination. Bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic and protozoal. This talk focuses on the bacterial and viral ones.

Chlamydia Chlamydia trachomatis — small gram-negative intracellular bacterium. Cannot be cultured on artificial media. The majority are asymptomatic. When symptomatic: discharge, mucopurulent cervicitis (the yellow-green pus at the os in the photo), pelvic pain, urethritis. Most common STI worldwide — the deck's figure is 4 million women annually . London, Ontario has one of the highest chlamydia incidence rates in Canada. Screen opportunistically. Routine physicals, Pap appointments and other visits are the moment to raise it — especially in people with HIV or who are immunocompromised. Dr. Black's slide. Specimen Notes Cervical or vaginal swab Most accurate. A patient-collected vaginal swab is as accurate as a clinician-collected cervical swab — a finding that matters a lot for access Urine Must be first-catch , not the clean-catch you send for a UTI, and the patient must not have voided in the last 2 hours Reportable disease — public health is notified. Sexual partners must be contacted and treated. No sexual contact until both she and her partners have completed treatment. Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days , or azithromycin 1 g PO × 1 . Test of cure is not routine. Do it only for: pregnancy · suspected poor compliance · ongoing symptoms · risk of repeat exposure . And wait 4 weeks — non-viable organisms hang around and cause false positives . Dr. Black's slide. Concept Check When should a test of cure for chlamydia be performed? a) If the infected person is pregnant · b) If asymptomatic at diagnosis · c) If they have PID at diagnosis · d) 2 weeks after treatment Answer: (a) pregnancy. Note why (d) is wrong — 2 weeks is too early, and you would get a false positive from dead organisms. Why untreated chlamydia matters. Laparoscopic views of a dilated, scarred tube . Scarring blocks the tube → infertility and ectopic pregnancy . Up to 30% of untreated chlamydia progresses to PID . The liver image is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis — perihepatic adhesions, pathognomonic for previous PID.

Gonorrhea Gram-negative diplococcus , incubation 3–7 days . Inhabits the periurethral glands and endocervix . Does not survive outside the body. Urethritis is the commonest symptom — dysuria, frequency, purulent discharge. Mild or absent in 50%. Identical to the chlamydia slide — which is the point. Dr. Black's slide. Same swab as chlamydia — you do not need two samples. Urine rules are identical (first-catch, 2 hours). Also ascends to cause PID , in 10–49% of women with cervical gonorrhea. Reportable , and partners must be treated. The Co-Infection Rule — It Only Runs One Way If a patient is gonorrhea-positive, they usually also have chlamydia , so you treat for both. The inverse is not true: chlamydia commonly exists on its own. The deck's regimen: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM (or cefixime 400 mg PO) plus azithromycin 1 g PO × 1 for the chlamydia. See the dating caveat at the top of this page — the ceftriaxone dose has since increased. Disseminated gonococcal infection — 0.5–3% if unrecognised. The classic triad: acute polyarthralgia + tenosynovitis + dermatitis . May present as purulent arthritis with no skin lesions. Dr. Black's slide.

Syphilis The spirochete Treponema pallidum . It burrows into the mucosa and will not grow in culture . Dr. Black's slide. Primary: a painless ulcer (chancre) at the inoculation site, 10–90 days after infection. Self-resolving , and because it is painless it is easily missed — while being highly contagious . Secondary: weeks to months later, lasting 4–6 weeks . Non-specific systemic symptoms plus a rash on the palms and soles — most other rashes spare those. Condyloma lata: large flat warts on the genitals in secondary syphilis. Distinguish from HPV warts , which are cauliflower-like . Diffuse lymphadenopathy is also part of the secondary picture. Dr. Black's slide. Stage Timing Features Primary 10–90 days Painless chancre ; highly contagious Secondary Weeks–months; lasts 4–6 weeks Fever, headache, malaise · rash on palms and soles · condyloma lata · lymphadenopathy Latent Can last 20+ years Asymptomatic carrier, serologically positive. Can be transmitted vertically to the fetus Tertiary 1–30 years after primary Neurosyphilis (general paresis, tabes dorsalis ) · cardiovascular (aortitis) · gummatous (granulomatous nodular lesions in skin and bone). Life-threatening. One Claim Worth Flagging The recording states that syphilis is not sexually transmitted during the latent stage , only vertically. That is too absolute . The standard division is early latent (within about the first year), where relapses of infectious secondary lesions can occur and sexual transmission is possible, versus late latent , where it is generally not. Vertical transmission remains possible throughout. The slide itself only says "asymptomatic carriers, serologically positive" — it does not make the claim. Worth confirming with your tutor which version the exam wants. Dr. Black's slide. 1 Scrape the chancre and look under darkfield microscopy — or, far more commonly, 2 VDRL , a blood screening test. 3 If positive, confirm with a fluorescent treponemal antibody test . 4 Treat: penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose . There is no alternative regimen for penicillin allergy. The only satisfactory treatment is desensitization, followed by penicillin . Remember that one — it is unusual, and therefore examinable. Concept Check Which accurately describes secondary syphilis? a) Neurosyphilis with CNS involvement · b) Formation of a painless ulcer (chancre) · c) Asymptomatic and non-transmittable · d) Condyloma lata, diffuse lymphadenopathy and a rash involving palms and soles Answer:

Hepatitis B The serology table in miniature. Dr. Black's slide. Marker Means HBsAg Present in both acute and chronic infection — on its own it does not distinguish them IgM anti-HBc Diagnostic of acute or recently acquired infection anti-HBs Produced after a resolved infection , and is the only HBV antibody marker present after vaccination HBsAg + anti-HBc, IgM anti-HBc negative Chronic HBV infection Total anti-HBc alone Could be acute, resolved, chronic, or a false positive No specific therapy — treatment is supportive . Vaccination is preventative and part of routine immunization. Caption warning: the auto-transcript of this section repeatedly writes "HPV" where the lecturer says HBV , and garbles the antibody names. The table above is taken from the slide, not the transcript.

HIV Dr. Black's slide. Transmitted in: blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, breast milk. Not in saliva. Acute HIV is a non-specific influenza-like illness , often short-lived and easily missed. Untreated, it becomes a multi-year chronic illness with progressive CD4+ T cell depletion → AIDS . Diagnosis: HIV-1/2 antigen–antibody combination immunoassay . Treatment: antiretroviral therapy.

The Case Dr. Black's slide. Work It Through 17-year-old · unwell with fevers, chills, nausea · generalized pelvic pain · dyspareunia · foul-smelling discharge · β-hCG negative · WBC 22 · chandelier sign . The chandelier sign is cervical motion tenderness : moving the cervix on bimanual exam reproduces exquisite pain — supposedly enough to make the patient reach for the chandelier. Diagnosis: PID. Note the order of operations — the negative pregnancy test comes first , because ectopic pregnancy is the thing that kills her (see 4.9 ).

What PID Is An acute infection of the upper genital tract — uterus, tubes, ovaries, surrounding organs. More than cervicitis or vaginitis. Polymicrobial , with chlamydia and gonorrhea the two commonest associated STIs. The definitional boundary matters: PID is a community-acquired infection initiated by a sexually transmitted agent . A pelvic infection or abscess after a D&C or other procedure is not PID — nor are infections from pregnancy or primary abdominal processes. Dr. Black's slide. The Counselling Point She Spends the Most Time On Fewer than 50% of women with PID culture positive for chlamydia or gonorrhea. Normal vaginal organisms — anaerobes, Gardnerella vaginalis , Haemophilus influenzae , enteric gram-negative rods, streptococci — can ascend and cause PID given the opportunity. So do not assume, or imply, that a patient or her partner has been unfaithful. Being told you are being tested for gonorrhea and chlamydia is alarming; frame it as ruling things out, not accusing. Because it is polymicrobial, treatment requires broad-spectrum coverage . The mechanism. The endocervical canal is the barrier between the sterile upper tract and the polymicrobial lower tract. Alter the cervical mucus — sexual activity, an STI — and bacteria ascend. Two routes of spread: up through the uterus and out the tube (→ tubo-ovarian abscess ), and lymphatic/haematogenous spread out to the parametrium .

Epidemiology and Presentation Dr. Black's slide. ~100,000 cases annually in Canada. 10–15% of reproductive-age women will have at least one episode. Symptoms: pelvic pain · dyspareunia · vaginal discharge · fever · cervicitis · cervical motion tenderness · pelvic mass · "stuck pelvis" from adhesions binding the uterus to the sidewalls. Dr. Black's slide. Investigation Why Pregnancy test Always. Rules out ectopic CBC, electrolytes Degree of inflammatory response, baseline Vaginal, urine ± blood cultures Blood cultures if she is unwell Ultrasound Usually. Looking for tubo-ovarian abscess , which changes management MRI Rarely, in unclear cases Surgery If the diagnosis is unclear or she is not responding . PID is largely a clinical diagnosis Left: a red, angry cervix with mucopurulent discharge — classic cervicitis. Right: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatic adhesions. Tubo-ovarian abscess at laparoscopy. Structures are hard to identify because of the dense adhesions — which is precisely why operating here threatens fertility.

Treatment Dr. Black's slide. Admit if… Because Cannot rule out a surgical emergency Ectopic, appendicitis Failed oral therapy, or non-compliant Needs IV and supervision Severely ill (nausea, vomiting, fever) Cannot tolerate oral medication Tubo-ovarian abscess Needs IV antibiotics for penetration into the abscess Pregnant More serious — always inpatient Youth / adolescent Often, but not always. Usually driven by psychosocial factors — access to antibiotics, compliance The Counterintuitive One A tubo-ovarian abscess is treated with IV antibiotics, not with incision and drainage. That is the opposite of how you treat abscesses almost everywhere else in the body. Surgical or interventional-radiology drainage is only for patients who fail to respond. Inpatient. A: cefoxitin 2 g IV q6h + doxycycline 100 mg IV/PO q12h → after 24 h improved, doxycycline PO BID to complete 14 days . B: clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h + gentamicin (2 mg/kg load, then 1.5 mg/kg q8h) → clindamycin 450 mg QID + doxycycline to 14 days. Outpatient. A: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM × 1 (or cefoxitin 2 g IM + probenecid 1 g PO) + doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 14 days ; consider adding metronidazole 500 mg BID × 14 days for anaerobes. B: ofloxacin or levofloxacin + metronidazole × 14 days. The number to hold onto: 14 days for PID, versus 7 days for uncomplicated chlamydia. That contrast is exactly the kind of thing an exam asks. "PID is NOT easily treated surgically while maintaining fertility." The adhesions are dense and the tubes and ovaries are easily damaged in trying to free them. Dr. Black's slide. Concept Check Which of the following is FALSE regarding PID? a) If left untreated, PID can lead to pelvic and liver adhesions, chronic pain and infertility · b) Individuals with PID test positive for chlamydia and/or gonorrhea in the majority of cases · c) PID should be treated as an inpatient in pregnancy · d) PID is a polymicrobial infection Answer: (b) is the false one. Fewer than 50% culture positive. The other three are all true.

Herpes, Warts and Trichomonas Genital herpes. Incubation 3–7 days ; painful blisters or ulcers within 24–72 h; may cause urinary retention ; resolves in 2–6 weeks . Transmissible from asymptomatic carriers . Diagnose by unroofing a lesion for PCR ; treat with acyclovir, famciclovir or valacyclovir . Condylomata acuminata — genital warts, caused by HPV . May remain dormant for years. Usually a clinical diagnosis; biopsy when uncertain. Treat topically (podophyllin, imiquimod, liquid nitrogen, TCA) or surgically. The HPV story continues in 4.8 . Trichomonas. Flagellated protozoan; survives 24 h in tap water and hot tubs ; humans are the only natural host . Full treatment detail is on 4.5 . "Strawberry cervix" — punctate haemorrhages. Famous, but present in only about 2% of cases. Likewise the classic "frothy" discharge shows up in fewer than 10% . The deck also covers granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) , lymphogranuloma venereum , molluscum contagiosum and pediculosis pubis in its interest-only section. For anything you need to actually prescribe from, the lecture points you to the CDC and Health Canada / Public Health Agency of Canada STI guidelines .

The Comparison Table STI Organism Classic presentation Diagnosis Treatment (as on the slides) The must-know Chlamydia C. trachomatis — gram-negative, intracellular ; can't be cultured on artificial media Mostly asymptomatic. Mucopurulent cervicitis, discharge, pelvic pain, urethritis Cervical or vaginal swab ( self-collected vaginal = as accurate ), or first-catch urine, ≥2 h since voiding Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 d or azithromycin 1 g PO × 1 Most common STI. Up to 30% untreated → PID → infertility, ectopic. Test of cure only if pregnant , poor compliance, ongoing symptoms or re-exposure — and wait 4 weeks Gonorrhea N. gonorrhoeae — gram-negative diplococcus ; incubation 3–7 d; doesn't survive outside the body Urethritis — dysuria, frequency, purulent discharge. Mild or absent in 50% Same swab as chlamydia — one sample tests both Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM (or cefixime 400 mg PO) + azithromycin 1 g — dose is out of date, see top of page Gonorrhea-positive → treat chlamydia too (not the reverse). PID in 10–49%. Disseminated GC (0.5–3%): polyarthralgia + tenosynovitis + dermatitis Syphilis Treponema pallidum — spirochete ; won't grow in culture 1° painless chancre (10–90 d) · 2° rash on palms and soles , condyloma lata, lymphadenopathy · latent (20+ y) · 3° neuro, aortitis, gummas (1–30 y) Darkfield of chancre scraping, or VDRL screen → FTA confirm Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM × 1 Penicillin allergy: no alternative — desensitize, then give penicillin. Learning Objectives Describe the changes in vaginal discharge over the menstrual cycle. Describe the assessment of vaginal discharge. Dr. Laura Sovran's 25-minute module. The lecture itself is short and deliberately sends you to a self-study table covering BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis and atrophic vaginitis — that table is reproduced in full further down. The cycle underneath all of this is in 3.3 .

The Estrogen–Glycogen–Lactobacillus–pH Chain The one causal chain to hold onto. Dr. Sovran's slide. 1 Estrogen acts on the vaginal mucosa and drives glycogen production. 2 Vaginal flora — chiefly lactobacilli The dominant healthy vaginal bacteria. They ferment glycogen to lactic acid, which is what keeps the pH low. — metabolize the glycogen , generating lactic acid. 3 The pH falls (normal is under 4.5). 4 The low pH protects against pathogens , and the moist mucosa provides barrier function and prevents water loss. Why This Matters at the Two Ends of Life This chain only runs when estrogen is present — that is, during the reproductive years. Before puberty and after menopause there is little estrogen , so little glycogen, fewer lactobacilli, a higher pH , and a thin fragile mucosa. That is exactly why postmenopausal women get atrophic vaginitis and recurrent urinary tract infections . Heads up: the auto-transcript of this lecture garbles this passage badly — it says the estrogen effect happens "in the menopausal phase" and that premenopausal women don't have much estrogen, which is backwards. The slide and the rest of the talk make the direction clear; the version above is the correct one. High-estrogen states make a lot of discharge. Pregnancy is the obvious one. Some patients are genuinely bothered by the volume of normal physiologic discharge — once you have ruled out BV, trichomoniasis and recurrent yeast, and you have looked at the cervix, reassurance is the treatment .

Discharge Across the Cycle The cycle you already know from 3.3 : growing follicles, ovulation, corpus luteum, and the estradiol and progesterone curves that drive everything below. The same month, seen from the patient's side. The two superimposed — the slide worth actually understanding. Dr. Sovran's slide. Phase Hormone Discharge Just after the period Estradiol at its lowest Dry phase — relatively little discharge Follicular (roughly days 1–13) Estrogen rising Increasing white, creamy discharge — normal Ovulation (~days 10–14 of a 28-day cycle) Estrogen peaks Clear, stretchy, "egg-white" mucus — Spinnbarkeit The stretchiness of cervical mucus. At ovulation it can be drawn out several centimetres between two fingers without breaking. . It stretches a long way Luteal Progesterone dominant Thickened cervical mucus and discharge; some describe it as slightly yellowish The Clinical Hook This is the physiology behind fertility awareness / natural family planning . Stretchy egg-white mucus means the fertile window — so it is the worst time to have unprotected intercourse if you are avoiding pregnancy, and the best time if you are trying. See 4.3 for how well that actually works as a method.

entries.t: Colour Is a Clue, Not a Diagnosis
entries.x: Colour Is a Clue, Not a Diagnosis The lecturer's own annotation says it: "Not quite this simple. Can be used as a guideline but you need to know how to assess the patient." Dr. Sovran's slide. White discharge is not automatically yeast. Plenty of healthy discharge is white. Even classic "grey" BV discharge rarely looks convincingly grey. What is more telling is how it coats the vaginal walls — thinly and evenly, adherent all the way round. Watery discharge deserves a good look at the cervix. Cervical cancer can present this way.

The Structure Dr. Sovran's slide. What You Will Actually Do in Family Practice In a family medicine office you will probably only do a vaginal swab , and the lecturer is explicit that this is perfectly fine . If you have looked at the vulva, the vagina and the cervix, inspected the discharge, and taken a swab, you have done your job . The pH strip, whiff test and wet mount are here so you understand the descriptions in the lab report and in the table below — and because some offices do have a microscope.

History Dr. Sovran's slide. Ask Why Amount, frequency, colour Establishes what "abnormal" means for her Odour vs odourless A fishy odour points hard at BV (or trichomonas) When it started; better or worse with anything Cyclical → likely physiologic. After a new partner → think BV or STI What has she tried, and how did she use it? Half-finished OTC azoles are common. "How did you use it" matters — people do get this wrong Douching, "potions and lotions" Douching is a risk factor for BV ; topical products cause contact dermatitis Itch, rash, other symptoms Itch pushes you toward candida or a dermatologic cause Recent antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, immunosuppression All risk factors for yeast . Pregnancy is a mildly immunosuppressed state The lecturer's framing is worth stealing: every question you ask is simultaneously gathering risk factors and building the clinical picture, not just filling in a form.

Physical Examination "The vulva and vagina are not the highway to the cervix — they too have pathology." Dr. Sovran's slide. Vulva: architecture, lesions, hair pattern or removal . Shaving causes folliculitis and ingrown hairs, which itch — and broken hairs suggest scratching. Vagina: is it wet or dry? Are there lesions, masses, ulcerations ? Does the mucosa bleed or look friable when you open the speculum? Cervix: what does the surface look like? Is there mucopurulent discharge from the os (cervicitis)? Is there anything that worries you about cancer ? Discharge: where is it, what does it coat, how does it behave? The Habit She's Trying to Build "You can just quickly do a speculum examination, but that's the wrong approach. You actually have to look and see and appreciate what you're looking at ." The more deliberately you do it, the more you pick up.

entries.t: Swabs: Where You Take Them Matters
entries.x: Swabs: Where You Take Them Matters Swab Taken from Why there Chlamydia & gonorrhea (if cervicitis is suspected) The cervix, within the cervical os That is where the organisms live (see 4.6 ) Vaginal swab (wet mount / culture) The lateral vaginal walls Away from the cervix pH sample Lateral walls, not near the cervix Blood has a pH of 7 and even invisible blood near the cervix will falsely raise your reading

pH and the Whiff Test pH strips 3.5–7. Place the secretions on the strip and read while still wet . Whiff test. A couple of drops of 10% KOH on the secretions. Why the whiff test works: KOH alkalizes the amines produced by the anaerobic bacteria that overgrow in BV, releasing them as a gas. The result is the fishy odour . A positive whiff test is one of the Amsel criteria. The lecturer's description of a strongly positive test — that it will take your breath away — is not an exaggeration.

The Wet Mount Three steps. The hinge angle on the coverslip is what stops you trapping air bubbles. Dr. Sovran's slide. What you are hunting for: white blood cells, yeast, trichomonads, bacteria and epithelial cells. Use both low and high power . Clue cells (BV). An epithelial cell so coated in adherent bacteria that its borders disappear — the classic description is a cell "rolled in sand." Yeast. C. albicans (90% of cases) gives pseudohyphae plus budding yeast . C. glabrata gives individual oval yeasts scattered about, with no pseudohyphae. Trichomonads. Look for the tail and, critically, motility . Leave the slide more than 10–15 minutes and they stop moving, and you will miss them. Everything else. Size is your guide: RBCs small with no nucleus · WBCs a bit bigger, with nuclei · epithelial cells much larger. Sperm are often on the slide too. Honest Caveat From the Lecturer Reading a wet mount takes practice . Background artifact can be mistaken for pseudohyphae by a novice, and trichomonads are "really difficult and finicky." Do not over-trust your own early readings.

Quick Comparison BV Candidiasis Trichomoniasis Atrophic Rank #1 infectious vaginitis #2 (75% of women in their lifetime) #3 Postmenopausal STI? No No Yes No Discharge Grey, thin , thinly coating the walls "Cottage cheese" , adherent white Profuse, purulent, yellow, malodorous Scant; dryness Symptom Fishy odour Itch , burning, fissuring, "splash" dysuria Itch, odour Dyspareunia , postcoital bleeding pH >4.5 <4.5 (normal) >4.5 Can be >4.5 Whiff Positive Negative Negative — Microscopy Clue cells Budding yeast, pseudohyphae Motile trichomonads Parabasal cells , ↑ WBCs First-line Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 d Fluconazole 150 mg PO × 1 , or a topical azole × 7 d Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 d or 2 g × 1 Local estrogen

Bacterial Vaginosis It is not an infection with one organism and it is not an STI. It is an alteration of the normal flora to anaerobic predominance — Gardnerella , Mobiluncus , Mycoplasma and others. Risk factors: new sexual partner, IUD, sexual activity, douching , smoking, Black ethnicity. Culture is not required — and is not useful. Amsel Criteria — 3 of 4 1. pH >4.5 · 2. >20% clue cells · 3. Homogeneous thin white discharge smoothly coating the vaginal walls · 4. Positive KOH whiff test The gold standard is a Gram stain scored by the Nugent criteria (relative concentrations of lactobacilli versus gram-negative and gram-variable rods and cocci), but Amsel is what you use in clinic. Situation Treatment First episode Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 d Alternatives: metronidazole gel 0.75%, 5 g PV daily × 5 d · clindamycin 300 mg BID × 7 d · clindamycin 2% cream 5 g PV qhs × 7 d Recurrent Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 10–14 d , or metronidazole gel daily × 10 d then twice weekly for 3–6 months Pregnancy Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 d or clindamycin 300 mg PO BID × 7 d, then test of cure in 1 month . Must be oral — topical will not reduce the pregnancy risks No alcohol with metronidazole. In pregnancy , BV raises the risk of preterm labour, PPROM, chorioamnionitis and post-caesarean endometritis . Routine screening is not recommended, though high-risk women may be screened at the first antenatal visit. BV also raises the risk of PID, post-abortal PID, post-hysterectomy cuff infection and abnormal Pap results . Practical tip from the table: if a swab reports "altered vaginal flora" and the patient is symptomatic, treat it like BV .

Candidiasis Symptoms: vulvar pruritus , "cottage cheese" discharge, vulvar burning and fissuring , external "splash" dysuria (it stings as urine passes over inflamed skin — unlike the internal dysuria of a UTI). Risk factors: diabetes, pregnancy, antibiotics, immunosuppression . On exam: vulvar and labial erythema and edema , satellite pustulopapular lesions, erythematous vagina with adherent white discharge, a normal cervix , and pH <4.5 . Culture only if it fails therapy. And note: 20% of women have a positive culture and no symptoms — which is why you treat the patient, not the swab. Situation Treatment Symptomatic OTC azole (miconazole 100 mg PV × 7 d; clotrimazole 1% cream 5 g PV × 7–14 d) or fluconazole 150 mg PO × 1 Recurrent (>4 in 12 months) Fluconazole 150 mg q72h × 3 doses Maintenance Fluconazole 150 mg weekly × 6 months Resistant / non-albicans Boric acid 600 mg PV daily × 2 weeks Pregnancy Topical azole × 7 d . Boric acid is contraindicated Boric acid is toxic if swallowed. Say so out loud when you prescribe it. C. albicans in 90% ; others are C. glabrata and C. tropicalis . Long-term antifungals can be hepatotoxic , and cross-react with calcium channel blockers, warfarin, oral hypoglycemics and phenytoin .

Trichomoniasis A flagellated protozoan , Trichomonas vaginalis . Sexually transmitted — and it survives in hot tubs (up to 24 hours in tap water). Discharge: profuse, purulent, yellow, malodorous — the table's phrase is "dripping down the leg." Plus vulvar pruritus. pH >4.5 , negative whiff test. Colpitis macularis ("strawberry cervix") — patchy vaginal erythema with punctate haemorrhages. Classic, but only in a small minority of cases. Diagnosis: NAAT is the gold standard . Wet mount is neither sensitive nor specific. Culture on Diamond's media was the pre-molecular gold standard (100% specific, 75–96% sensitive). Treatment: metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 d, or 2 g PO × 1. Do not use the vaginal gel — it is not effective enough. Treat partners from the last 6 months. Pregnancy: increased risk of PPROM, preterm birth, small for gestational age . Same regimen as non-pregnant. Coexists with BV in 60% of cases.

Atrophic Vaginitis Who: postmenopausal women, or any hypoestrogenic state . Symptoms: dyspareunia , postcoital bleeding . On exam: vulvovaginal atrophy, loss of vaginal rugae , friable mucosa. Microscopy: predominant parabasal epithelial cells and increased leukocytes ; pH can be >4.5. It is an inflammatory reaction to atrophy — the estrogen chain at the top of this page, running in reverse. Option Detail Premarin (CEE) cream 0.5–1 g PV daily × 1–2 weeks, then 0.5–1 g PV twice weekly. Systemic absorption at the start , because the epithelium is thin. No progestin needed Estring Estradiol 5–10 µg/day, changed every 3 months Vagifem Estradiol 10 µg PV qhs × 1–2 weeks, then twice weekly Conservative Vaginal moisturizers and regular sexual activity Two things to warn about: local estrogen can cause postmenopausal bleeding (which always needs its own work-up), and atrophic vaginitis often travels with recurrent UTIs .

The Original Table The self-study document, reproduced above in pieces. Here it is whole — it is a genuinely good reference to keep. Page 1 — bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis . Page 2 — trichomoniasis and atrophic vaginitis .

Learning Objectives Describe different lesions of the vulva. List the various differential diagnoses for the various lesions. Compare and contrast vulvar conditions with other skin lesions. Describe the presentation of vulvar malignancy. List benign masses of the vulva with clinical presentations. Dr. Laura Sovran's 30-minute module. She frames it explicitly: this "may seem a bit advanced for a medical student," and the goal is to be a resource you come back to as a general practitioner — so don't try to memorize all 82 slides. What she says you must take away is at the top of this page. Vulvar hygiene was covered in a separate lecture; the HPV biology behind the HPV-related cancers is in 4.8 , and the infectious differential is 4.5 and 4.6 .

entries.t: The Comparison That Does the Work
entries.x: The Comparison That Does the Work Her summary slide reduces the three to a 3×3 grid. Learn this first, then read the detail. Lichen sclerosus (LS) Lichen planus (LP) Lichen simplex chronicus (LSC) Symptom Itch or burn Itch or burn ++++ Itch Scarring Scars Scars No scar Site Not in vagina In vagina AND mouth Not in vagina Cancer risk Yes — ~4% SCC Yes — 2–3% SCC Not intrinsically * Treatment Topical superpotent steroid Topical superpotent steroid (+ vaginal) Treat the cause , then the skin * Her caveat, verbatim in substance: LSC does not carry a cancer risk of its own, "but prolonged inflammation in any system can technically increase your risk of cancer." The Single Most Useful Discriminator Architecture. LSC is itch and thickening with normal anatomy — labia minora still present, no adhesions. LS and LP destroy architecture : the clitoral hood agglutinates and buries the clitoris, the labia minora resorb and disappear, and the introitus narrows. So her clinical habit is worth copying — when the labia minora look absent, ask the patient directly: "do you remember ever having larger labia minora?" Some women simply have small ones, and that question separates normal variation from disease.

Lichen Simplex Chronicus Essentially vulvar eczema — and, as she puts it, the end stage of the itch cycle . Itch → scratch → itch. Worse with heat, humidity, stress and irritation. The last line is the clinical problem: scratching feels so good , which is why patient education is treatment. LSC is a reaction pattern, not a diagnosis . Anything that makes her itch causes it — including lichen sclerosus and lichen planus themselves , diabetes , and VIN . So finding LSC means you keep looking. What her case looked like: a 36-year-old with a very itchy rash flaring with heat and friction, not responding to topical steroids, scratching all night, with hay fever and environmental allergies. On the photograph she points to the left interlabial sulcus being noticeably thicker with increased skin markings than the other side — the signature of rubbing. Other clues: a fractured hair pattern from scratching, hyperpigmentation from the thickening, and, decisively, normal architecture with both labia minora present . Her LSC was probably driven by underlying yeast. Why the Hyperpigmentation Is Not Lichen Sclerosus Her analogy: the vulva is a sweaty, occluded area, and chronically rubbed skin thickens — like fingertips going white and wrinkly after a long bath. The resulting hyperpigmentation is a consequence of thickening , not of sclerosis. Lichen sclerosus goes the other way: hypopigmented, thin, easily traumatized skin. Thick and dark = LSC. Thin, white and scarred = LS. Two halves. Above the red line: find and fix the cause — confirm with biopsy, treat infection ( fluconazole for yeast, cefadroxil if there are open wounds, and rule out MRSA), and stop the irritants , which includes excessive hygiene and over-washing. Below it: break the cycle — cool sitz baths and gel packs, night-time sedation ( doxepin or hydroxyzine PM, fluoxetine AM ) so she stops scratching in her sleep, and a tapering course of clobetasol 0.05% . Severe disease gets oral prednisone taper or IM triamcinolone. Dr. Sovran's slide.

Lichen Sclerosus Her case: a 60-year-old attending for a routine Pap , with hypothyroidism but otherwise well and with no complaints of her own . On the vulva: hyperpigmentation anteriorly , labia minora completely resorbed , petechial trauma at the introitus , and hypopigmented plaque . Adhesions of the clitoral hood with the glans buried beneath . A urethral caruncle alongside, consistent with being menopausal. Her line about it: "it's not okay to just do your Pap and be like, you're totally fine." The five numbers worth keeping. She adds that in her clinic it is closer to 1 in 300 than 1 in 1000 . Itch in 90% , pain/burning/soreness in 40% — but note the last bullet: asymptomatic . That is the case above. The figure-of-8 pattern — the classic distribution, running around the anterior vulva and around the perineal/perianal area, making an 8. It occurs in children (15% of cases), so you cannot dismiss it in a child. Harder to spot: the colour change is subtler and the vulvar architecture is not yet fully developed, so "loss of architecture" is a difficult judgement. What she points to in the paediatric photograph is thickened skin around the anus and perineal body from rubbing . In children the presenting symptom is often painful defecation , with fissures as thin skin splits on passing stool, and rectal bleeding . Associated with hypothyroidism → annual TSH. Why we care: a ~4% lifetime squamous cell carcinoma risk if untreated. That single number is the reason to treat an asymptomatic patient. Primary damage vs secondary damage. The top list is the disease destroying architecture; the bottom list is what the patient's own scratching adds on top. Separating them matters, because the secondary changes are the ones that resolve with treatment. Dr. Sovran's slide. What the photo series shows, in her words: loss of labia minora with a few petechial spots from rubbing · ulcerations where it is unclear whether the cause is scratching or the disease itself · concurrent yeast in one image · varying degrees of hyperpigmentation near the perineal body. In advanced disease : complete loss of architecture, skin so thin it is easily traumatized, with ecchymoses and petechiae . One image also shows a rectocele , which she flags as unrelated to the skin disease — a useful reminder not to attribute every finding to the diagnosis you came for. The dosing principle is the exam point: a tiny amount of superpotent steroid ointment, daily until the whiteness resolves , then m

Vulvar Melanosis Placed here deliberately, because it is what you see after the inflammation of lichen sclerosus — and because it mimics the thing you are most afraid of. Flat, smooth, 5–25 mm , on non-keratinized mucosa , and crucially unchanging . Benign course expected — but the natural-history data are thin, so periodic observation rather than discharge. It is a post-inflammatory reaction , commonly following lichen sclerosus or another inflammatory vulvar condition. The problem is that it can look like melanoma. Her practical answer: track it photographically so change is detectable, and biopsy if concerned. On a multi-spot lesion, biopsy the darkest area — the one most likely to be melanoma if it is. Skin tone changes the presentation. She makes this point explicitly: in Caucasian women inflammation tends to add pigment (melanosis), whereas in Black women pigment tends to be removed after inflammation . Both directions can obscure the diagnosis, and both are worth expecting. Photography has a second benefit — it lets the patient examine herself meaningfully between visits, because she knows what her own baseline looks like.

Lichen Planus Her case: a 50-year-old with dyspareunia , otherwise healthy. Her line: you might glance and say the vulva looks normal, but "if you look with the intent of seeing what you need to see" there is a lacy white pattern on the vulva extending up toward the labia minora, and red erosions medially on the vestibule . Erosion vs Ulceration — Worth Fixing Now A distinction she stops to make, and it is generally useful: ulcerations are deep , extend to the dermis, and have a yellow base . Erosions are superficial and look red , "almost like you've shaved a layer of skin off." That missing layer is exactly why erosive lichen planus hurts and causes dyspareunia. The distinguishing feature is in the last line. Always examine vulva, vagina AND mouth. Note also: on the genitals the erosive pattern is the commonest, not the classic lacy one. Three morphologies. The hypertrophic one "looks like lichen sclerosus" — which is why biopsy exists, and why it matters less than you'd think (see below). It gets into the vagina — unlike lichen sclerosus. So a speculum examination with routine monitoring is part of care, not optional. It gets into the mouth — she asks patients to tell their dentist the diagnosis. 2–3% squamous cell carcinoma risk. Less than lichen sclerosus, but real — her closing line makes a point of it: "lichen sclerosus is associated with cancer, but so is lichen planus." The complication to understand mechanically: two erosions facing each other — one on each side of the vagina, or one on each labium minus — can heal together . That agglutination can close off the introitus and, at the extreme, make it impossible to have intercourse or even to void. Same skeleton as lichen sclerosus, plus two vaginal additions — hydrocortisone suppositories (25 mg daily × 2 weeks, then MWF) and dilators . Dr. Sovran's slide. Two Practical Points She Adds Out Loud 1. If you cannot tell LS from LP, it matters less than you'd fear — "the treatments are the same": clobetasol 0.05% ointment daily until the visible signs resolve (red or white), then maintenance from twice weekly, titrated up or down. Biopsy still confirms it, but you are not paralysed while you wait. 2. A cost workaround. Compounded vaginal hydrocortisone suppositories are expensive; she instead uses over-the-counter Anusol-HC suppositories — made for hemorrhoids — inserted vaginally, for much less money. And the reason dilators or regular intercourse are prescribed is not comfort, it is keeping the vagi

Aphthous Ulcers Her case: a 17-year-old with a vulvar lesion for the third time, episodes years apart, each a day or two after strep throat . Initially not painful, then uncomfortable. The lesion is small — ~3 mm, dark, almost black, not raised but slightly depressed . That is the early presentation before it ulcerates . The pattern: a preceding viral or streptococcal illness , in a girl roughly 9–20 , with oral aphthae too but usually not at the same time . Pain can be severe enough to cause urinary retention. Treatment is oral prednisone plus vulvar care. Dr. Sovran's slide.

Vitiligo Autoimmune and therefore worth screening: TSH, anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin, fasting glucose , with an eye to pernicious anemia, SLE, Addison's, type 1 diabetes and hypopituitarism. Dr. Sovran's slide. Vitiligo vs Lichen Sclerosus — the Discriminator Both present as white vulvar skin, and she says outright it can be hard. The answer is again architecture : vitiligo is depigmentation of normal skin — no scarring, no architectural loss. So you look for scarring to tell them apart. Two complications she is honest about: patients can have both , and in extensive vulvar vitiligo the architecture may be hard to read at all. A confirmatory clue in her photograph — the vulvar hair is depigmented too , not just the skin. Distribution helps as well: vitiligo elsewhere favours acral areas, around body orifices, and extensor surfaces .

Seborrheic Keratoses and Molluscum "Stuck-on" verrucous papules — what patients call age spots. Nothing needs doing; treat only if irritated along the underwear line , or biopsy if you are unsure what it is. Poxvirus. Firm, flesh-coloured, dome-shaped 2–5 mm papules ; never on palms or soles . Self-limiting within ~2 months. Sites: vulva, groin, perianal area, inner thighs. Two counselling points she adds: molluscum is "sexually transmitted in a sense " — the lubrication of intercourse helps spread it from existing genital lesions — and tell her not to shave , because shaving spreads it. They are soft enough to be scratched off with a fingernail, which is also how they spread.

Yeast Vulvitis Her headline: yeast vulvitis is often underdiagnosed , and — the thing people get wrong — you do not need vaginitis or clumpy white discharge to have it. It can be a purely vulvar, purely skin problem. Four risk factors with good evidence. Diabetes leads — and her case below is why. Fissures are one of the top vulvar causes — "like little papercuts." Note splash dysuria and satellite lesions . Two Signs Explained Splash dysuria is not urethral pain. It does not hurt while the urine is coming out — it hurts when urine touches the broken vulvar skin . That tells you the problem is the skin, not the urinary tract, and it is a discriminator you can get from history alone. Satellite lesions are small separate red papules just outside the main confluent rash, which will eventually coalesce into it. They are what makes a confluent red rash candidal rather than simply irritant. The case worth remembering: a ~36-year-old with groin fissures, a red confluent rash with flaking edges, satellite papules, and lichenification from scratching — so she had both LSC and yeast vulvitis . She turned out to be diabetic and did not know it. Yeast vulvitis is a reason to check a glucose. "Air it out" is a real prescription, not a throwaway — she asks patients to spend 30 minutes a day deliberately airing the vulva, and points out that sleeping without underwear is not enough because the legs stay closed. Topical nystatin, miconazole or clotrimazole BID; fluconazole 200 mg PO daily × 3 days, then twice weekly for 3–6 weeks . Dr. Sovran's slide. A cost tip she volunteers: the 150 mg fluconazole is the over-the-counter one and is significantly more expensive — she deliberately prescribes 100–200 mg doses because they are cheaper. On patients taking multiple cardiac drugs she drops to 100 mg twice weekly × 3–6 weeks instead. Her compounding trick: hydrocortisone 1% + clotrimazole 1% mixed together — and she notes it makes an excellent diaper-rash cream. Think of this diagnosis in anyone who wears a diaper — infants through incontinent adults. She flags it as useful in paediatrics, family medicine, geriatrics and internal medicine, not just gynecology. Complicated cases exist — one of her patients has lupus and psoriasis and lives on suppressive fluconazole; another had erosions and lichenified groin skin from a tight, aggressively rubbing diaper strap.

Labial Adhesions Not a disease of its own — the end result of anything that scars . In her photograph, whether the cause was lichen sclerosus or lichen planus is no longer determinable. Two things follow: They may be completely asymptomatic , or cause real problems: if she is voiding through a tiny residual opening, she is at higher risk of voiding dysfunction and urine tracking back into the vagina . They can be opened in clinic under local freezing — not an operating-room problem.

Bartholin Gland Cyst and Abscess Learn the location and where the duct drains — that is the whole point of this slide. Figure from MyHealth Alberta, on Dr. Sovran's slide. Why She Spends a Slide on Anatomy Because of a specific, common error: Bartholin abscesses get referred from the emergency department, and the frequent confusion is with a labial abscess. Location is what distinguishes them — so knowing where the gland sits and where it drains is the diagnostic step, before any imaging or procedure. Cyst = often asymptomatic. Abscess = hurts a lot , with difficulty walking, sitting or having intercourse, and she can become systemically unwell. Carcinoma of the gland is rare but exists. Diagnosis is clinical . Abscesses are tender, warm, soft, fluctuant . Option What it is Incision and drainage The immediate relief Word catheter A tiny balloon catheter, like a miniature Foley, left in place so the gland re-epithelializes a drainage tract rather than simply re-sealing and recurring Marsupialization Cutting an opening through the skin and vestibule into the gland and sewing that hole open , creating a permanent drainage tract ± Antibiotics For skin flora Sitz baths / warm soaks Caught early, some resolve on this alone — but by the time gynecology sees them, a procedure is usually needed

Vulvar Lipoma Soft, painless nodules of mature fat, 1 cm to >10 cm. Ask about lipomas elsewhere — patients often have them, and that supports the diagnosis. If it is not bothering her, expectant management . Her illustrative photograph shows one on the mons . Dr. Sovran's slide.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma and VIN SCC is the commonest vulvar cancer. 3–5% of gynecologic cancers, 1–2 per 100,000 — and absolute numbers are expected to rise as the population ages . Pruritus is the commonest complaint — and 50% are asymptomatic . Which is the argument for actually looking at the vulva. The one classification table worth learning, because the two pathways look and behave differently. Dr. Sovran's slide. HPV-related Non-HPV-related Age Younger women Older women Number Multiple lesions Solitary lesion Appearance Flat-topped red, brown or skin-coloured papules and plaques Pink, red or white papule, nodule or ulcer Site Vestibule, labia majora , perivulvar, perianal Vestibule and labia minora Background HPV infection Frequently lichen sclerosus or lichen planus Biopsy In-situ carcinoma ( VIN ); invasion occasional Often already invasive Why This Table Is Clinically Loaded Two consequences fall straight out of it. The non-HPV pathway is the one that grows out of the lichens you just learned — which is the second reason to treat lichen sclerosus forever, and to biopsy any lichen sclerosus lesion that does not resolve or is refractory to therapy. And the non-HPV lesion is more often already invasive at biopsy , in an older woman, as a single lesion you might be tempted to watch. The HPV pathway, by contrast, is multifocal and recurrent — she notes of one VIN 3 case that being HPV-related gives it "a very high likelihood of recurring." Examination and Biopsy Four lines, all high-yield. Look AND feel. Firm. Often tender. Inguinal nodes. When in doubt = biopsy. Multiple biopsies if areas look different. 4 mm punch minimum. Additional points from her detailed examination slide: direct observation is best, with photographs for comparison ; inspect and palpate the vulva and groin for masses, ulceration and colour change; most VIN lesions are multifocal and sit in the non-hairy part of the vulva ; lesions are often raised or verrucous and white, but may be red, pink, grey or brown; macular lesions mostly occur on adjacent mucosal surfaces. And the mimics to know: lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, condyloma acuminata and condyloma lata can all mimic VIN. The rule that follows — if one of those is suspected clinically but the lesion does not completely resolve, or is refractory to therapy, biopsy it. What the malignancy photographs show, in her narration: VIN 3 with HPV — a verrucous growth, with two visibly different areas, so she would biopsy both. VIN 3

Melanoma and Basal Cell Carcinoma Older patient, 50–80. Basically black with red/white/blue variegation — and if it is pink or red, think amelanotic melanoma . Symptoms may be entirely absent , hence the last line. The anatomic rule is the memorable bit: BCC occurs only on keratinizing, non-mucosal skin — so labia majora and perianal area , never the mucosal vestibule. On the melanoma photographs she draws the distinction from melanosis directly: yes, it looks like melanosis — but this one is a raised dark patch, and one area looks distinctly different from the rest , so multiple biopsies are appropriate. Her framing of BCC is the thesis of the lecture restated: "skin is skin — just because it's skin on the vulva doesn't mean it does not occur there."

Extramammary Paget Disease <1% of vulvar malignancies , 60s–70s. Mostly intraepithelial — but 4–17% harbour invasive adenocarcinoma within or beneath the visible lesion . The appearance to recognize: eczematoid, well demarcated, slightly raised edges, red background dotted with small pale islands. Multifocal , starting on hair-bearing skin. The Association Not to Miss She raises something the slides only hint at: extramammary Paget disease may be primary or secondary , and the secondary form can be associated with another underlying malignancy — of the breast, or the genital or urinary tract . So the diagnosis obliges you to look further rather than treat it as an isolated skin lesion. It can also extend into the rectum, vagina or urinary tract directly.
